docs.title: About this book
docs.text: An introduction to the Constitution of India and the way the country is governed. The book follows the making of the Constitution, its Preamble, citizenship, Fundamental Rights and their remedies, the Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties, the Union executive, Parliament and law-making, the judiciary and the basic structure doctrine, federalism and Centre-State relations, State and local government, emergency provisions, amendment, the constitutional bodies, and elections and political parties, and closes with the Constitution in practice. Every chapter has learning outcomes, worked examples, figures or tables, a summary, exercises with answers and a quiz.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Amending the Constitution and the Basic Structure
docs.text:
How the Constitution is changed, the limits on that power, and the amendments that shaped it

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain why a constitution needs a procedure for amendment, and why India's is described as partly rigid and partly flexible;
  • describe the procedure of Article 368 step by step;
  • classify proposed changes according to the three methods of amendment;
  • trace the conflict between Parliament and the Supreme Court over the amending power, from Shankari Prasad to Minerva Mills;
  • explain the basic structure doctrine and list the elements the courts have recognised;
  • identify the most important amendments and what each did;
  • weigh the main arguments for and against the basic structure doctrine.

docs.title: 11.1 Why constitutions change
docs.text:
A constitution is meant to last, but no generation can foresee every need of the generations after it. A constitution that cannot be changed may break; one that can be changed too easily offers no protection. Every constitution must strike a balance between stability and adaptability.

Constitutions are often classified by how easily they can be changed. A flexible constitution, like the British, can be changed by the ordinary process of law-making. A rigid constitution, like the American, can be changed only by a special procedure; the United States Constitution needs the approval of two-thirds of each House of Congress and three-quarters of the states, and has been amended fewer than thirty times.

The framers of the Indian Constitution chose a middle course. Jawaharlal Nehru told the Constituent Assembly that while the framers wanted the Constitution to be as solid and permanent as they could make it, there was no permanence in constitutions, and a certain flexibility was needed to allow the nation to grow. The result is a Constitution that can be amended by Parliament with a special majority, with the States joining in for provisions that affect the federal structure. It has been amended far more often than the American Constitution: 106 amendments had been made by 2023 (check the official text for any later ones).

docs.title: 11.2 The procedure under Article 368
docs.text:
Article 368, in Part XX, gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution "by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision", and lays down the procedure.

  1. A bill to amend the Constitution can be introduced only in Parliament, in either House. It cannot be introduced in a State legislature.
  2. It may be introduced by a minister or by a private member, and does not need the prior permission of the President.
  3. It must be passed in each House by a special majority: a majority of the total membership of the House and a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
  4. Each House must pass it separately. There is no joint sitting for a constitutional amendment bill if the Houses disagree.
  5. If the bill seeks to amend certain federal provisions, it must also be ratified by the legislatures of not less than half of the States, by resolutions passed by a simple majority. No time limit is fixed for ratification.
  6. The bill is then presented to the President, who must give assent (since the 24th Amendment, 1971). The President can neither withhold assent nor return the bill.
  7. The bill then becomes a Constitution (Amendment) Act, and the Constitution stands amended.

Worked example 11.1: Counting votes for an amendment

Situation. A constitutional amendment bill is put to the vote in the Rajya Sabha, which has a total membership of 245 (no vacancies). 200 members are present and voting; 140 vote in favour and 60 against. Is the bill passed in the Rajya Sabha?

Answer. Two conditions must both be satisfied. (1) A majority of the total membership: more than half of 245, that is at least 123. 140 is more than 123, so this is met. (2) Two-thirds of those present and voting: \(\tfrac{2}{3} \times 200 = 133.3\), so at least 134. 140 is more than 134, so this is met too. The bill is passed in the Rajya Sabha. (Had 210 members been present and voting with 140 in favour, condition (2) would have needed 140, and the bill would just pass; with 211 present it would need 141 and fail.)

docs.title: 11.3 Three methods of amendment
docs.text:
Although Article 368 describes one procedure, the Constitution in fact provides for three methods, shown in Figure 11.1.

Figure 11.1 Three methods of amendment. Three ways of amending the Constitution. (1) By a simple majority of each House, outside Article 368, for matters such as new States, Legislative Councils, citizenship, quorum and several Schedules. (2) By a special majority of each House under Article 368, for most provisions including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. (3) By a special majority plus ratification by half the State legislatures, for federal provisions such as the election of the President, the judiciary, the distribution of legislative powers, the Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, the GST Council and Article 368 itself.

docs.title: 1. By a simple majority of Parliament
docs.text:
Several provisions can be changed by an ordinary law passed by a simple majority of each House. The Constitution itself says that such laws are not amendments for the purposes of Article 368. Examples include:

  • admission or establishment of new States, and the formation of new States or alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States (Articles 2 to 4);
  • creation or abolition of Legislative Councils in the States (Article 169);
  • the Second Schedule (emoluments of the President, Governors, judges and others);
  • quorum in Parliament, salaries and allowances of members, rules of procedure and privileges;
  • the number of judges of the Supreme Court and the conferment of additional jurisdiction on it;
  • the acquisition and termination of citizenship (Article 11);
  • elections to Parliament and the State legislatures, and delimitation of constituencies;
  • administration of the Union Territories, and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.

docs.title: 2. By a special majority of Parliament
docs.text: Most provisions, including the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles, are amended by the special majority of each House described in section 11.2, without ratification by the States.

docs.title: 3. By a special majority and ratification by the States
docs.text:
Provisions that concern the federal structure need, in addition, ratification by half of the State legislatures. The proviso to Article 368(2) lists them:

  • the election of the President and its manner (Articles 54 and 55);
  • the extent of the executive power of the Union and the States (Articles 73 and 162), and the High Courts for Union Territories (Article 241);
  • the Goods and Services Tax Council (Article 279A, added in 2016);
  • the Supreme Court and the High Courts (Chapter IV of Part V and Chapter V of Part VI);
  • the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States (Chapter I of Part XI);
  • any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule;
  • the representation of States in Parliament;
  • the provisions of Article 368 itself.

Worked example 11.2: Which procedure?

Name the method needed for each change.

  1. Changing the name of a State.
  2. Adding a new Fundamental Right.
  3. Moving a subject from the State List to the Concurrent List.
  4. Increasing the number of judges of the Supreme Court.
  5. Changing the method of electing the President.

Answers. (1) Simple majority, by a law under Article 3 (with the President's recommendation and reference to the State legislature for its views); by Article 4 it is not an amendment. (2) Special majority of each House under Article 368. (3) Special majority and ratification by half the States, because it changes a List of the Seventh Schedule; the 42nd Amendment's transfer of five subjects in 1976 was ratified in this way. (4) Simple majority, by a law under Article 124(1). (5) Special majority and ratification, since Articles 54 and 55 are in the proviso.

docs.title: 11.4 Parliament, the courts and the amending power
docs.text: Article 368 says how the Constitution may be amended. It does not say, in so many words, whether there are any limits on what may be amended. Could Parliament, by the special majority, take away Fundamental Rights altogether? Abolish judicial review? Replace the republic with a monarchy? For a quarter of a century this question was the centre of a struggle between Parliament and the Supreme Court.

docs.title: First phase: unlimited power (1951–1967)
docs.text: In Shankari Prasad v. Union of India (1951), the Supreme Court upheld the 1st Amendment, which had curtailed the right to property. It held that the word "law" in Article 13, which forbids laws that take away Fundamental Rights, refers to ordinary legislation, not to constitutional amendments. Parliament could therefore amend Part III. The Court took the same view in Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan (1965), upholding the 17th Amendment, although two judges expressed doubts.

docs.title: Second phase: no amendment of Fundamental Rights (1967–1973)
docs.text:
In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), a bench of eleven judges held, by six to five, that a constitutional amendment is "law" under Article 13, and that Parliament therefore cannot amend Fundamental Rights so as to take away or abridge them. To avoid upsetting earlier amendments, the Court applied its ruling only to future amendments (a doctrine called prospective overruling).

Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), which declared that Parliament may amend any provision of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, under Article 368; that Article 13 does not apply to constitutional amendments (Article 13(4)); and that the President must give assent to an amendment bill. The 25th Amendment (1971) curtailed the right to property further and added Article 31C (Chapter 4).

docs.title: Third phase: the basic structure (1973 onwards)
docs.text:
The validity of these amendments came before the largest bench in the Court's history: thirteen judges, in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, decided on 24 April 1973. By a majority of seven to six, the Court held:

  • Golaknath was overruled: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights; the 24th Amendment was valid;
  • but the power to amend is not a power to destroy: Parliament cannot alter the basic structure (or basic features, or framework) of the Constitution;
  • the first part of Article 31C was valid, but the second part, which barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to Article 39(b) and (c), was invalid.

The judges in the majority gave different examples of basic features, and the Court did not attempt a complete list. But the principle was clear: an amendment that damaged or destroyed the basic structure would be void.

Key idea

Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is the most important case in Indian constitutional law. Parliament can amend every part of the Constitution, but it cannot amend away its basic structure. The courts decide, case by case, what the basic structure includes.

docs.title: The doctrine tested
docs.text:
The doctrine was soon applied. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), the Court struck down a clause of the 39th Amendment that had placed disputes about the election of the Prime Minister and the Speaker beyond the reach of the courts and validated a disputed election. It held that free and fair elections and judicial review were part of the basic structure.

Parliament responded again. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added clauses (4) and (5) to Article 368, declaring that no amendment could be called in question in any court on any ground, and that there was no limitation whatever on Parliament's constituent power.

In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down both clauses. It held that:

  • limited amending power is itself a basic feature: since Parliament's power is limited, it cannot convert it into an unlimited power by amendment;
  • judicial review is a basic feature;
  • the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a basic feature, so the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles was invalid.

In Waman Rao v. Union of India (1981), the Court held that the basic structure doctrine applies only to amendments made after 24 April 1973, the date of Kesavananda. Amendments before that date, and laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before that date, are not open to challenge on this ground. I. R. Coelho (2007) later confirmed that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after that date can be tested against the basic structure.

Case Year Bench Holding on the amending power Shankari Prasad 1951 5 Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights; amendment is not "law" under Article 13 Sajjan Singh 1965 5 Same, by majority Golaknath 1967 11 Parliament cannot abridge Fundamental Rights (6:5) Kesavananda Bharati 1973 13 Parliament can amend any part, but not the basic structure (7:6) Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain 1975 5 Free and fair elections and judicial review are basic Minerva Mills 1980 5 Limited amending power, judicial review and balance of Parts III and IV are basic Waman Rao 1981 5 Doctrine applies to amendments after 24 April 1973

Table 11.1. The amending power in the Supreme Court.

docs.title: 11.5 What is the basic structure?
docs.text:
The Supreme Court has never given an exhaustive list. Over the years, it has recognised a number of features as part of the basic structure, including:

  • the supremacy of the Constitution;
  • the sovereign, democratic and republican form of government;
  • the secular character of the Constitution (S. R. Bommai, 1994);
  • the federal character of the Constitution (S. R. Bommai, 1994);
  • the separation of powers among the legislature, the executive and the judiciary;
  • the unity and integrity of the nation;
  • the rule of law and the principle of equality;
  • the freedom and dignity of the individual;
  • the parliamentary system of government;
  • free and fair elections (Indira Nehru Gandhi, 1975);
  • judicial review, including the powers of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 (Minerva Mills, 1980; L. Chandra Kumar, 1997) and of the Supreme Court under Article 32;
  • the independence of the judiciary (Fourth Judges case, 2015);
  • limited amending power (Minerva Mills, 1980);
  • the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (Minerva Mills, 1980);
  • the welfare state and the objective of social and economic justice.

The doctrine has been used to strike down a constitutional amendment only rarely. The most notable recent example is the 99th Amendment (2014), establishing the National Judicial Appointments Commission, which was struck down in 2015 as violating judicial independence. In other cases the Court has upheld amendments against basic structure challenges; for example, in Janhit Abhiyan (2022) the majority held that the 103rd Amendment's reservation for economically weaker sections did not violate the basic structure.

Worked example 11.3: Applying the doctrine

Situation. Suppose Parliament, with the special majority and the ratification of half the States, passed an amendment providing that elections to the Lok Sabha would be held only once every fifteen years and that no court could hear any challenge to the result of an election. Would it survive?

Answer. Almost certainly not. The provision on fifteen-year intervals would undermine democracy and free and fair elections, which are part of the basic structure; and excluding all judicial challenge to election results is very close to the provision struck down in Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), which also offends judicial review. Following the special procedure, even with State ratification, does not save an amendment that damages the basic structure. The test is not the procedure followed but the effect of the change on the identity of the Constitution.

docs.text:
Most amendments make modest, technical changes. A small number have reshaped the Constitution. The table lists those met most often in this book.

Part IXB and the States

The 97th Amendment (2011) added Part IXB on co-operative societies. In 2021, the Supreme Court held that the parts of Part IXB dealing with co-operative societies within a State were invalid, because the amendment affected a State List subject and had not been ratified by half the State legislatures as the proviso to Article 368(2) requires. The provisions relating to multi-State co-operative societies survived. The case shows that the ratification requirement is enforced.

docs.title: 11.7 Assessing the basic structure doctrine
docs.text:
The basic structure doctrine is not written in the Constitution; it is a creation of the Supreme Court. It has been both praised and criticised.

Arguments against the doctrine.

  • It allows unelected judges to override the considered will of the people's representatives, expressed by a large special majority and sometimes with the approval of the States.
  • It is vague: since there is no complete list of basic features, Parliament cannot know in advance what it may and may not do.
  • It is not found in the text of Article 368, which speaks of amending "any provision".

Arguments for the doctrine.

  • It protects the identity of the Constitution: the power to "amend" implies that the Constitution should survive the amendment, not be replaced by a different one.
  • It guards against the abuse of temporary majorities, as the experience of 1975–77 showed: without it, Parliament could have amended away elections, rights and judicial review.
  • In practice, the Court has used it sparingly, upholding the great majority of amendments, and it has gained wide acceptance. Courts in some other countries have adopted similar reasoning.

A balanced view is that the doctrine is a form of constitutional self-defence. It leaves Parliament very wide power to adapt the Constitution, as more than a hundred amendments show, while denying it the power to destroy the democratic, federal, secular and rights-based framework on which everything else rests.

Summary

  • Article 368 (Part XX) lets Parliament amend the Constitution by special majority of each House: a majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting. Bills start only in Parliament, in either House; there is no joint sitting; the President must assent.
  • There are three methods: simple majority (for matters outside Article 368, such as new States and citizenship), special majority (most provisions), and special majority with ratification by half the States (federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2)).
  • The courts first held the amending power unlimited (Shankari Prasad, 1951; Sajjan Singh, 1965), then held that Fundamental Rights could not be abridged (Golaknath, 1967). Parliament replied with the 24th Amendment (1971).
  • Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament can amend any part but not the basic structure; Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975), Minerva Mills (1980) and Waman Rao (1981) developed the doctrine.
  • Recognised basic features include supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, rule of law, free and fair elections, judicial review, independence of the judiciary and limited amending power.
  • Major amendments include the 1st, 7th, 24th, 42nd, 44th, 52nd, 61st, 73rd, 74th, 86th, 101st, 103rd and 106th.

docs.title: 11.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

State four features of the procedure under Article 368 that distinguish an amendment bill from an ordinary bill.

Answer

Any four of: it can be introduced only in Parliament, not in a State legislature; it needs a special majority in each House (majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting); there is no joint sitting if the Houses disagree; it may need ratification by half the States; it needs no prior recommendation of the President; the President must give assent and cannot return it.

Exercise 2

Which of the following require ratification by half the States? (a) An amendment to Article 21; (b) an amendment to the Union List; (c) an amendment to Article 368; (d) an amendment to Article 44.

Answer

(b) and (c). Amendments to Article 21 (a Fundamental Right) and Article 44 (a Directive Principle) need only the special majority of each House.

Exercise 3

What did Golaknath (1967) decide, and how did Parliament respond?

Answer

By six to five, an eleven-judge bench held that a constitutional amendment is "law" under Article 13, so Parliament cannot take away or abridge Fundamental Rights, though it applied this only prospectively. Parliament responded with the 24th Amendment (1971), which declared that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution including Part III, that Article 13 does not apply to amendments, and that the President must assent to amendment bills.

Exercise 4

Why is 24 April 1973 an important date?

Answer

It is the date of the judgment in Kesavananda Bharati, which established the basic structure doctrine. Under Waman Rao (1981) and I. R. Coelho (2007), amendments made, and laws placed in the Ninth Schedule, after that date can be challenged for violating the basic structure.

Exercise 5

Name the case and the amendment involved in each: (a) striking down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368; (b) striking down the National Judicial Appointments Commission.

Answer

(a) Minerva Mills (1980), the 42nd Amendment. (b) The Fourth Judges case, Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015), the 99th Amendment.

Exercise 6

Give one argument for and one against the basic structure doctrine.

Answer

For (any one): it preserves the identity of the Constitution and protects democracy, rights and judicial review against temporary majorities, as 1975–77 showed; it has been applied sparingly. Against (any one): it lets unelected judges override a large elected majority; it is vague and not found in the text of Article 368.

docs.title: Chapter 14: The Constitution in Practice
docs.text:
Separation of powers, conventions, citizens and the debates that keep the Constitution alive

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain why the working Constitution is more than its text, and name the sources that shape it;
  • describe the separation of powers in India and the checks and balances among the three organs;
  • give examples of constitutional conventions and explain the idea of constitutional morality;
  • use the main tools available to citizens: the vote, the Right to Information, grievance and court remedies, and participation in local government;
  • set out, in a balanced way, the main debates about the working of the Constitution;
  • analyse a new constitutional problem step by step, using the whole book.

docs.title: 14.1 A living document
docs.text:
The previous thirteen chapters described what the Constitution says and how the courts have read it. But a constitution in practice is more than its text. When the Constitution came into force in 1950, nobody knew exactly how the President and the Prime Minister would get on, how far the courts would go in protecting rights, or how much the Centre would leave to the States. These questions were answered over decades, by a combination of four things:

  1. The text, amended more than a hundred times.
  2. Judicial interpretation, which has given meaning to broad phrases such as "personal liberty", "equality before the law" and "the basic structure".
  3. Conventions: unwritten rules of political practice that are followed because they are regarded as binding.
  4. Political practice and public opinion: how governments, parties, officials and citizens actually behave.

The Constitution has survived wars, the assassination of national leaders, an emergency, many changes of government at the Centre and in the States, and great social and economic change. Every transfer of power at the Centre since 1950 has taken place through elections and parliamentary procedure. This is a considerable achievement, and it is worth asking what has made it possible, and what continues to test it.

docs.title: 14.2 Separation of powers and checks and balances
docs.text:
The doctrine of the separation of powers, associated with the French philosopher Montesquieu, holds that the three functions of government, making laws, carrying them out and judging disputes under them, should be given to separate organs, so that no single body has all power. In its strictest form, as in the United States, the three organs are separate in personnel as well as in function.

India does not follow the doctrine rigidly. In a parliamentary system the executive is drawn from the legislature and responsible to it, so the two are fused rather than separated. The Supreme Court observed in Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955) that the Constitution does not recognise the doctrine in its absolute rigidity, but that the functions of the different organs have been sufficiently differentiated, and one organ should not assume the essential functions of another. The judiciary, at least, is kept separate: Article 50 directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive, and judicial independence is part of the basic structure. In Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and later cases, the separation of powers itself was recognised as a basic feature.

What India has, instead of a strict separation, is a system of checks and balances, in which each organ can limit the others. Figure 14.1 shows the main checks.

Figure 14.1 Checks and balances. Checks and balances among the three organs. The legislature checks the executive through no-confidence motions, questions, committees, budget approval and impeachment of the President; the executive influences the legislature through ordinances, dissolution of the Lok Sabha, summoning and the veto. The judiciary reviews laws, amendments and executive action; the legislature can remove judges, change the law after a judgment, and fix the number of judges and their jurisdiction; the executive takes part in appointing judges and can grant pardons.

Key idea

India combines a fusion of the legislature and the executive (the parliamentary system) with a separate and independent judiciary that reviews both. No organ is supreme: Parliament is limited by the Constitution and judicial review; the courts are limited by the procedure for removal, by Parliament's power to change the law, and by their own self-restraint; the executive is limited by both.

Worked example 14.1: A judgment and a response

Situation. The Supreme Court interprets a statute in a way the government considers contrary to its policy. What constitutional responses are available, and what limits apply?

Answer. (1) If the judgment interprets an ordinary law, Parliament can amend the law to change its effect for the future (and sometimes retrospectively), provided the new law is within its competence and does not violate Fundamental Rights. It cannot simply declare the judgment void; it must change the legal basis on which the judgment rested. (2) If the judgment rests on the Constitution itself, Parliament can amend the Constitution by the procedure of Article 368, but the amendment will be reviewed against the basic structure. (3) The government may also seek a review of the judgment, or ask for a reference to a larger bench. These responses have all been used at different times. The relationship is one of dialogue, not of one organ simply overruling the other.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
A constitutional convention is an unwritten rule of political behaviour that is generally followed because those concerned regard it as binding, even though no court would enforce it directly. Conventions fill gaps in the text and adapt it to circumstances. Examples in India include:

  • the President invites the leader of the party or coalition with a majority in the Lok Sabha to be Prime Minister;
  • the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (now also required by Article 74);
  • the chairman of the Public Accounts Committee is from the opposition;
  • the Speaker, once elected, conducts the House impartially;
  • the Governor of a State is from outside that State, and the Chief Minister is consulted on the appointment;
  • the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court is appointed Chief Justice of India.

Conventions are only as strong as the willingness of political actors to observe them. Some have been broken at times, which has led to calls for them to be written into law or the Constitution.

docs.title: Constitutional morality
docs.text:
In the Constituent Assembly, Dr Ambedkar drew attention to the idea of constitutional morality, a phrase he took from the historian George Grote. He meant a habit of respect for the forms of the Constitution and for the limits it places on power, combined with freedom of criticism. Such a habit, he warned, is not natural; it has to be cultivated, and a democratic constitution can be undermined without changing its text if those who work it do not have it.

In recent decades the Supreme Court has used the phrase in a somewhat wider sense: the duty of the State to act according to the values of the Constitution (dignity, equality, liberty and fraternity), even where these conflict with prevailing social attitudes. Both senses point to the same truth: the Constitution depends on the conduct and values of those who work it, not only on its words.

docs.title: 14.4 The citizen and the Constitution
docs.text:
The Constitution is not only for governments and judges. It gives every citizen tools to take part in government and to defend their rights.

Tool What it allows Where it comes from The vote Choosing representatives at every level, and removing them at the next election Articles 325, 326; Representation of the People Acts Right to Information Obtaining information held by public authorities Right to Information Act, 2005; Article 19(1)(a) Writ petitions and PIL Going to the High Court or Supreme Court when rights are violated, including on behalf of others who cannot Articles 32, 226 Gram Sabha and ward committees Taking part directly in local planning and oversight Articles 243A, 243S Commissions and ombudsmen Complaints to human rights commissions, the commissions for SCs, STs and Backward Classes, the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Constitution and statutes (Chapter 12) Free legal aid and Lok Adalats Access to justice for those who cannot afford it; quick settlement of disputes Article 39A; Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 Free speech, assembly and association Criticising the government, organising and protesting peacefully Article 19(1)(a)–(c)

Table 14.1. A citizen's constitutional toolkit.

Worked example 14.2: Asking a question of the government

Situation. Meena wants to know how much her municipality spent on repairing the roads in her ward last year, and which contractors were paid.

Answer. Under the Right to Information Act, 2005, she may write to the Public Information Officer of the municipality, stating the information she wants; she need not give reasons. A reply is due within 30 days (48 hours where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person). If she receives no reply or an unsatisfactory one, she may file a first appeal with a senior officer of the municipality, and after that a second appeal or complaint to the State Information Commission. The Commission can order disclosure and impose penalties on officers who refuse information without reasonable cause. If the information reveals irregularities, she can raise them in the ward committee, with her elected councillor, with the State's audit authorities or, in serious cases, before the courts or anti-corruption bodies. This is the toolkit of Table 14.1 in action.

docs.title: 14.5 Debates about the working of the Constitution
docs.text:
A study of the Constitution would be incomplete without the debates that surround its working. The following are among the most discussed. In each case there are serious arguments on more than one side, and the aim here is to state them, not to decide them.

  • The role of Governors. Governors are appointed by the Centre and hold office at its pleasure. Some States have complained that Governors have delayed assent to bills, intervened in the formation of governments, or acted as agents of the Union government. Others argue that the Governor's role as a link between the Centre and the States is an essential part of the federal design. The Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions, S. R. Bommai and B. P. Singhal have all tried to define limits (Chapters 8, 9 and 10).
  • Federal balance. States seek more financial autonomy and a larger say in national policy; the Union stresses the need for national standards and unity. GST and the GST Council, the Finance Commissions' devolution and NITI Aayog are all part of this debate.
  • Judicial appointments and accountability. The collegium system protects judicial independence but has been criticised for lack of transparency; the attempt to replace it with the National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down in 2015 (Chapter 7). Pendency of cases is a separate and pressing problem.
  • Anti-defection law and the presiding officers. The Tenth Schedule has curbed frequent defections, but critics say it has reduced the independence of individual legislators, and the decisions of presiding officers on defection petitions have sometimes been delayed or contested (Chapter 6).
  • Ordinances. The power to make ordinances is meant for urgent situations when the legislature is not in session. Its frequent use, and re-promulgation, has been criticised by the Supreme Court (Chapter 5).
  • The functioning of Parliament. Observers and parliamentary research groups have noted fewer sitting days, frequent disruptions and a smaller share of bills referred to committees than in earlier decades. Others point to the continued vitality of question time, committee reports and debate on major issues.
  • Reservation. The extent and basis of reservation (caste, economic criteria, the 50 per cent ceiling, sub-classification within groups) continue to be debated, in Parliament and in the courts (Chapter 3).
  • Liberty and security. Laws on preventive detention, sedition-type offences and unlawful activities raise questions about the balance between national security and personal liberty, a balance the Constitution leaves to Parliament subject to judicial review.

Avoid one-sided answers

Examination questions on these debates often ask you to "critically examine" or "discuss". A good answer states the constitutional provisions, the relevant cases, the arguments on each side, and a reasoned conclusion. It does not treat any political party or government as simply right or wrong.

docs.title: 14.6 The framers' warnings
docs.text:
On 25 November 1949, the day before the Constitution was adopted, Dr Ambedkar made a speech in the Constituent Assembly that is still often quoted. He offered three warnings.

  1. Hold fast to constitutional methods. Now that the people had a democratic constitution, he argued, methods such as civil disobedience and non-cooperation, justified under foreign rule, should give way to constitutional methods of seeking change; otherwise disorder would follow.
  2. Beware of hero-worship. He warned against laying the people's liberties at the feet of any individual, however great. Gratitude to great leaders was natural, but devotion to a person in politics, he said, was a sure road to degradation and dictatorship.
  3. Make political democracy a social democracy. The Constitution gave every citizen one vote and one value, but Indian society remained deeply unequal. Ambedkar observed that India was "going to enter into a life of contradictions": political equality alongside social and economic inequality. Unless the contradiction was removed, he warned, those who suffered from inequality would one day blow up the structure of political democracy.

These warnings explain why the Constitution contains not only the machinery of government but also Directive Principles, reservations, the abolition of untouchability and the protection of the weaker sections. Seventy-five years on, they remain a useful test for judging how the Constitution is working.

docs.title: 14.7 Analysing a constitutional problem
docs.text:
The best way to consolidate what you have learnt is to use it. Faced with any new question ("Can the government do this?" "Is this law valid?"), work through a sequence of steps that draws on the whole book.

  1. Who is acting? The Union or a State? The legislature, the executive or a local body? (Chapters 5, 6, 9)
  2. Do they have the power? For a law: which list of the Seventh Schedule does it fall in, by pith and substance? For an executive act: is there a law or constitutional provision authorising it? (Chapter 8)
  3. Was the right procedure followed? The right majority, the right House, the President's or Governor's assent, consultation where required. (Chapters 6, 11)
  4. Does it violate a Fundamental Right? If it restricts a right, is the restriction on a permitted ground, by law, reasonable and proportionate? (Chapter 3)
  5. What do the Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties say? They may support the law's reasonableness. (Chapter 4)
  6. If it is a constitutional amendment, does it touch the basic structure? (Chapter 11)
  7. What remedy is available, and before which forum? Writs under Articles 32 or 226, a commission, an election petition, or political means. (Chapters 3, 7, 12, 13)

Worked example 14.3: A ban on single-use plastic

Situation. A State legislature passes a law banning the manufacture, sale and use of certain single-use plastic items in the State, with fines for violation. A manufacturer challenges it.

Answer. Work through the steps.

  1. Who is acting? A State legislature.
  2. Power. In pith and substance, the law concerns public health and sanitation, which is in the State List (and may also touch trade within the State). The State therefore has competence, even if the law incidentally affects trade and industry. If Parliament has made a law or rules on the same subject (for example, under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, made under Article 253), the court will examine whether the two can stand together, and whether any part of the State law is repugnant to Union law.
  3. Procedure. Passed by the legislature and assented to by the Governor; no special procedure appears to be needed.
  4. Fundamental Rights. The law restricts the manufacturer's freedom to carry on trade under Article 19(1)(g). Restrictions are permitted under Article 19(6) in the interests of the general public. The court will ask whether the ban is reasonable and proportionate: does it serve a legitimate aim (protecting health and the environment), is it suited to that aim, are less restrictive means available, and is a reasonable time allowed for compliance? Under Article 14, it will check that the items banned are chosen on an intelligible basis connected with the aim.
  5. Directive Principles and Duties. Article 48A (protection of the environment) and Article 47 (public health), together with the citizen's duty under Article 51A(g), support the reasonableness of the law.
  6. Basic structure. Not relevant: this is an ordinary law, not an amendment.
  7. Remedy. The manufacturer may file a writ petition in the High Court under Article 226, alleging violation of Article 19(1)(g) and lack of competence.

Likely result. If the ban is properly framed, gives notice and is not arbitrary in the items it covers, it is likely to be upheld as a reasonable restriction in the public interest. This conclusion depends on the facts; the method is what matters.

Summary

  • The working Constitution is shaped by its text, judicial interpretation, conventions and political practice. Its endurance since 1950, through many crises and changes of government, is a significant achievement.
  • India does not follow a rigid separation of powers: the executive and legislature are fused in the parliamentary system, while the judiciary is separate and independent. Each organ checks the others.
  • Conventions fill gaps in the text; constitutional morality, the habit of respecting constitutional limits, is necessary for the Constitution to work.
  • Citizens have a constitutional toolkit: the vote, the Right to Information, writ petitions and PIL, participation in Gram Sabhas and ward committees, commissions and ombudsmen, legal aid and Lok Adalats, and the freedoms of speech, assembly and association.
  • Continuing debates concern Governors, the federal balance, judicial appointments, anti-defection, ordinances, the functioning of Parliament, reservation, and liberty and security.
  • Dr Ambedkar's warnings of 1949 (constitutional methods, no hero-worship, social democracy) remain a test for the Constitution's working.
  • A constitutional problem can be analysed in seven steps: actor, power, procedure, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Duties, basic structure, and remedy.

docs.title: 14.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Does India follow the doctrine of separation of powers? Answer with reference to one case.

Answer

Not in a rigid form. In the parliamentary system the executive is drawn from and responsible to the legislature. But the functions of the organs are differentiated, the judiciary is separate and independent (Article 50), and no organ may usurp the essential functions of another. Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) said the Constitution does not recognise the doctrine in absolute rigidity; Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) recognised separation of powers as part of the basic structure.

Exercise 2

Give three examples of constitutional conventions in India.

Answer

Any three of: the President appoints as Prime Minister the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha; the President acts on ministerial advice; the Public Accounts Committee is chaired by an opposition member; the Speaker acts impartially; the Governor is from outside the State and the Chief Minister is consulted; the senior-most Supreme Court judge becomes Chief Justice of India.

Exercise 3

What did Dr Ambedkar mean by the "life of contradictions" that India would enter on 26 January 1950?

Answer

He meant that India would have political equality (one person, one vote, one value) while its social and economic life remained deeply unequal. He warned that if this contradiction was not removed, those who suffered from inequality might destroy the structure of political democracy. Political democracy had to be made a social democracy.

Exercise 4

A citizen's application under the Right to Information Act gets no reply in 30 days. What should she do next?

Answer

File a first appeal with the designated senior officer of the same public authority. If that fails, file a second appeal (or complaint) with the Central Information Commission or the State Information Commission, as appropriate, which can order disclosure and penalise the officer.

Exercise 5

Using the seven-step method, outline how you would analyse a Union law requiring all citizens to register their religion in a national database.

Answer

(1) Actor: Parliament. (2) Power: identify the list entry (for example, census or a residuary subject); likely within Union competence. (3) Procedure: ordinary law, simple majority. (4) Rights: the law affects privacy, recognised under Article 21 in K. S. Puttaswamy (2017), and freedom of conscience under Article 25; the court would apply the tests of legality, legitimate aim, necessity and proportionality, and look at safeguards for data. It may also raise Article 14 questions. (5) Directive Principles and Duties offer little support for compulsion in this area. (6) Basic structure: not relevant for an ordinary law. (7) Remedy: a writ petition under Article 32 in the Supreme Court. The outcome would depend on the law's purpose, necessity and safeguards; the method is to test it against each step.

Exercise 6

Choose one of the debates in section 14.5 and write a balanced paragraph stating the main argument on each side.

Answer

Example, on the collegium system. Supporters argue that letting senior judges choose judges protects the judiciary from political influence, which is essential since governments are the largest litigants before the courts, and that the Supreme Court found the alternative, the National Judicial Appointments Commission, to threaten judicial independence. Critics argue that the system is opaque, that it is not provided for in the text of the Constitution, and that it lacks accountability and diversity; they propose a transparent process with published criteria and a role for other branches. Many observers favour retaining judicial primacy while improving transparency, as even the 2015 judgment suggested. (Any other debate, treated with the same balance, is acceptable.)

docs.title: 14.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check yourself: the Constitution in practice

Exercise 1

Which article directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive?

  1. Article 39A
  2. Article 44
  3. Article 50
  4. Article 51
Answer

Exercise 2

Which case observed that the Constitution does not recognise the separation of powers in its absolute rigidity?

  1. Ram Jawaya Kapur
  2. Kesavananda Bharati
  3. Maneka Gandhi
  4. S. R. Bommai
Answer

Exercise 3

An unwritten rule of political practice that is regarded as binding is called...

  1. an ordinance
  2. a convention
  3. a directive
  4. a schedule
Answer

Exercise 4

Within how many days should a Public Information Officer normally reply to an RTI application?

  1. 7
  2. 15
  3. 30
  4. 60
Answer

Exercise 5

Who drew on the historian George Grote to speak of constitutional morality in the Constituent Assembly?

  1. Jawaharlal Nehru
  2. B. R. Ambedkar
  3. Rajendra Prasad
  4. B. N. Rau
Answer

Exercise 6

Match each check with the organ that exercises it.

ABNo-confidence motionJudiciaryJudicial review of lawsExecutiveOrdinancesLegislature Answer

docs.title: Chapter 12: Constitutional and Statutory Bodies
docs.text:
The Election Commission, the CAG, the Public Service Commissions, the Finance Commission and the other watchdogs

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • distinguish constitutional, statutory and executive bodies, and explain why some bodies are made independent of the government;
  • describe the composition, appointment, tenure, removal and functions of the Election Commission;
  • explain the role of the Comptroller and Auditor-General and the link with the Public Accounts Committee;
  • describe the Union and State Public Service Commissions;
  • recall the constitution and functions of the Finance Commission and the national commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Backward Classes;
  • outline the main statutory and executive bodies: NITI Aayog, the National Human Rights Commission, the Central Vigilance Commission, the Central Bureau of Investigation, the Information Commissions and the Lokpal;
  • choose the right body for a given grievance.

docs.title: 12.1 Why independent bodies?
docs.text:
In a parliamentary democracy, the government of the day controls the executive. But some functions are too important to be left to the government of the day, because the government itself has an interest in how they are performed. Who should conduct elections that decide whether the government stays in power? Who should audit the government's own spending? Who should select civil servants, so that jobs do not go to party supporters? The framers answered: bodies that are independent of the government, protected by the Constitution in the same way as judges.

Such bodies are of three kinds.

Kind Created by Examples Constitutional bodies The Constitution itself Election Commission, Comptroller and Auditor-General, Union and State Public Service Commissions, Finance Commission, National Commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Backward Classes, GST Council Statutory bodies An Act of Parliament (or a State legislature) National Human Rights Commission, Central Vigilance Commission, Central and State Information Commissions, Lokpal, National Commission for Women Executive (non-statutory) bodies A resolution or order of the government NITI Aayog; the Central Bureau of Investigation (which draws its legal powers from a statute)

Table 12.1. Three kinds of body.

A constitutional body cannot be abolished, nor its basic features changed, without a constitutional amendment. A statutory body can be changed by ordinary law. An executive body can be reshaped by the government itself.

Key idea

The independence of a body depends on the same safeguards that protect judges: a secure term, removal only by a difficult procedure, service conditions that cannot be worsened, expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund, and no prospect of further government office after retirement. When you study a body, check which of these safeguards it has.

docs.title: Composition and appointment
docs.text:
Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, to the State legislatures and to the offices of President and Vice-President in an Election Commission. The Commission consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President fixes. It was a single-member body from 1950 to 1989; after a brief period with additional commissioners in 1989–90, it has been a three-member body since 1993, with decisions taken by majority.

The commissioners are appointed by the President, subject to any law made by Parliament. For many years there was no such law, and appointments were made on the advice of the government. In Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023), the Supreme Court directed that, until Parliament made a law, appointments should be made on the advice of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and the Chief Justice of India. Parliament then enacted the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, under which appointments are made on the recommendation of a selection committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (or the leader of the largest opposition party) and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister. Commissioners hold office for six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.

docs.title: Independence
docs.text:
• The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court (Article 324(5)).
  • Other Election Commissioners can be removed only on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner.
  • The conditions of service of the Chief Election Commissioner cannot be varied to his or her disadvantage after appointment.

Critics have pointed out some gaps: the Constitution does not bar commissioners from later government appointments, and the protection of the other commissioners is weaker than that of the Chief Election Commissioner.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
The Election Commission:

  • prepares and periodically revises the electoral rolls and registers voters;
  • fixes the schedule of elections and supervises the whole process, from nomination to counting;
  • recognises political parties and allots election symbols, and decides disputes about them;
  • enforces the Model Code of Conduct for parties and candidates;
  • monitors election expenditure;
  • advises the President and the Governors on the disqualification of members of Parliament and of State legislatures (Articles 103 and 192);
  • can cancel polls in the event of rigging, booth capturing or violence.

Chapter 13 discusses elections in more detail. Elections to panchayats and municipalities are conducted not by the Election Commission but by State Election Commissions (Articles 243K and 243ZA).

docs.title: Office and independence
docs.text:
Article 148 provides for a Comptroller and Auditor-General of India (CAG), appointed by the President. Dr Ambedkar regarded the CAG as perhaps the most important officer under the Constitution, since he or she is the guardian of the public purse. The CAG's independence is protected in several ways:

  • the CAG can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court;
  • the term is six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier (under a law of 1971);
  • the CAG's salary and conditions of service are fixed by Parliament and cannot be varied to his or her disadvantage; the salary equals that of a Supreme Court judge;
  • the administrative expenses of the office, including salaries, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India;
  • after ceasing to hold office, the CAG is not eligible for further office under the Government of India or of any State.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
The CAG audits all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India and of each State (and of Union Territories having legislatures), the Contingency Funds and the Public Accounts, and the accounts of government companies and other bodies substantially financed by government. The audit covers not only whether money was spent according to law and rules (compliance audit), but also whether it was spent wisely and economically (performance audit).

The CAG's reports on the accounts of the Union are submitted to the President, who causes them to be laid before Parliament; reports on the accounts of a State are submitted to the Governor, who lays them before the State legislature (Article 151). In Parliament, the Public Accounts Committee examines the reports, with the CAG acting as its guide and adviser.

Comptroller in name, auditor in fact

In Britain, the Comptroller and Auditor-General controls the issue of money from the treasury as well as auditing it. In India, money is withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund by the executive, without the CAG's prior approval. The Indian CAG is therefore an auditor, not a comptroller, despite the title; his or her control is exercised after the money has been spent.

docs.title: The Union Public Service Commission
docs.text:
Part XIV (Articles 315 to 323) provides for a Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and a Public Service Commission for each State. The UPSC was preceded by a Public Service Commission set up in 1926 and a Federal Public Service Commission under the Government of India Act, 1935.

  • Composition and appointment. A chairman and members appointed by the President. At least half of the members must have held office under the Government of India or of a State for at least ten years.
  • Term. Six years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
  • Removal. By the President, on the ground of misbehaviour, after the Supreme Court, on a reference, has inquired and advised removal (Article 317). The President may also remove a member who is adjudged insolvent, takes up paid employment outside his or her duties, or is unfit because of infirmity of mind or body.
  • Independence. Expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund; conditions of service cannot be varied to a member's disadvantage; the chairman is not eligible for further government employment, and a member may be appointed only as chairman of the UPSC or a State Commission.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Under Article 320, the UPSC:

  • conducts examinations for appointment to the All-India Services and the Central services;
  • is consulted on methods of recruitment, principles for appointments, promotions and transfers, disciplinary matters affecting civil servants, and claims for legal expenses and pensions in certain cases.

The UPSC's advice is not binding on the government. But the government must lay before Parliament the UPSC's annual report, with a memorandum explaining any case in which its advice was not accepted, and the reasons (Article 323). The UPSC is not consulted on reservation of posts for backward classes (Article 320(4)).

docs.title: State Public Service Commissions
docs.text: Each State has a State Public Service Commission, whose chairman and members are appointed by the Governor for six years or until the age of 62. They can, however, be removed only by the President, in the same way as members of the UPSC. Parliament may also create a Joint State Public Service Commission for two or more States at their request.

docs.title: 12.5 The Finance Commission and the GST Council
docs.text:
The Finance Commission (Article 280) and the GST Council (Article 279A) were described in Chapter 8. In brief:

  • The Finance Commission is constituted by the President every five years, with a chairman and four other members whose qualifications are laid down by a law of 1951. It recommends the share of the States in the divisible pool of Union taxes, its distribution among the States, the principles of grants-in-aid, and measures to supplement the resources of local bodies. Its recommendations are laid before Parliament with an explanatory memorandum; they are advisory, but generally accepted.
  • The GST Council is a permanent body of the Union Finance Minister, a Union Minister of State, and the finance ministers of all States. It recommends GST rates and rules, and its decisions require three-fourths of the weighted votes, with the Union holding one-third and the States two-thirds of the weight.

docs.title: 12.6 Commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Backward Classes
docs.text:
The Constitution makes special provision for bodies to protect disadvantaged groups.

  • National Commission for Scheduled Castes (Article 338). Originally a single commission covered both Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. The 89th Amendment (2003) divided it into two commissions.
  • National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A). Created by the same amendment.
  • National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B). A statutory body since 1993, it was given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (2018).

Each commission consists of a chairperson, a vice-chairperson and other members appointed by the President. Each investigates and monitors the safeguards provided for its group, inquires into specific complaints of deprivation of rights and safeguards, participates in and advises on planning for the group's development, and reports to the President, who lays the reports before Parliament. While investigating, the commissions have the powers of a civil court, such as summoning witnesses.

The Constitution also provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (Article 350B, added in 1956), who investigates matters relating to the safeguards for linguistic minorities and reports to the President.

docs.title: NITI Aayog
docs.text: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. Like its predecessor, it was created by a resolution of the Union Cabinet, not by the Constitution or a law. The Prime Minister is its chairperson; its Governing Council includes the Chief Ministers of all States and of Union Territories with legislatures, and the Lieutenant Governors of other Union Territories; it has a Vice-Chairperson and a Chief Executive Officer. Unlike the Planning Commission, it does not allocate funds to States; it works as a policy think tank and a forum for co-operative federalism.

docs.title: National Human Rights Commission
docs.text: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) was set up in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. Its chairperson must be a person who has been Chief Justice of India or a judge of the Supreme Court; its members include judges and persons with knowledge of human rights, and the chairpersons of several national commissions are members ex officio. It inquires into complaints of violation of human rights by public servants, can intervene in court proceedings, visits jails, and recommends compensation or prosecution. Its recommendations are not binding, though they usually carry weight. States have State Human Rights Commissions under the same Act.

docs.title: Central Vigilance Commission
docs.text: The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was set up in 1964 by an executive resolution, on the recommendation of the Santhanam Committee on prevention of corruption, and was given statutory status by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003. It consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and up to two Vigilance Commissioners, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Union Home Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, for four years or until the age of 65. It supervises vigilance administration in central government organisations and superintends the investigation of certain corruption offences.

docs.title: Central Bureau of Investigation
docs.text: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) was set up in 1963 by a resolution of the Union Ministry of Home Affairs. It derives its legal powers from the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946. It investigates corruption, serious economic offences and other important crimes, often on reference from the government or on the orders of the courts. Because police and public order are State subjects, the CBI generally needs the consent of a State government to investigate in that State, unless a constitutional court orders it.

docs.title: Information Commissions
docs.text: The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives citizens the right to obtain information held by public authorities, subject to listed exemptions, and sets up a Central Information Commission and State Information Commissions to hear appeals and complaints. The Central Information Commission consists of a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The right to information has been described by the courts as part of the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

docs.title: Lokpal and Lokayuktas
docs.text: The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 created the Lokpal, an anti-corruption ombudsman at the Union level, and required States to set up Lokayuktas. The Lokpal consists of a chairperson and up to eight members, at least half of them judicial members, and at least half from among Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, minorities and women. They are appointed on the recommendation of a selection committee of the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the Lok Sabha, the Leader of the Opposition, the Chief Justice of India (or a judge nominated by the Chief Justice) and an eminent jurist. The Lokpal's jurisdiction extends to the Prime Minister, with safeguards, ministers, members of Parliament and public servants. The first Lokpal was appointed in 2019.

docs.title: Other national commissions
docs.text:
Other statutory bodies include the National Commission for Women (under an Act of 1990, constituted in 1992), the National Commission for Minorities (under an Act of 1992) and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (under an Act of 2005).

Worked example 12.1: Where should the complaint go?

Name the body most suited to each complaint.

  1. A government department has refused, without valid reason, to give a citizen copies of documents she applied for under the Right to Information Act, and her first appeal within the department has failed.
  2. A person alleges that his brother died after being beaten in police custody.
  3. A newspaper reports that a ministry spent large sums on equipment that was never used.
  4. A member of a Scheduled Caste alleges that he was denied a promotion in a central government office because of his caste.
  5. A citizen alleges that a Union minister took a bribe.

Answers. (1) The Central Information Commission (or the State Information Commission, for a State department), by second appeal or complaint under the Right to Information Act. (2) The National Human Rights Commission (or the State Human Rights Commission); the family may also approach a court by writ petition. (3) This is a matter for audit by the CAG, whose report would be examined by the Public Accounts Committee. (4) The National Commission for Scheduled Castes, which can inquire into complaints of deprivation of safeguards. (5) The Lokpal, which has jurisdiction over ministers under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.

Summary

  • Independent bodies perform functions in which the government of the day has an interest: elections, audit, recruitment, sharing of revenue, protection of disadvantaged groups. They may be constitutional, statutory or executive.
  • The Election Commission (Article 324), a three-member body since 1993, superintends, directs and controls elections to Parliament, State legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. The Chief Election Commissioner is removable only like a Supreme Court judge. Appointments are now governed by a law of 2023.
  • The CAG (Articles 148–151) audits Union and State accounts, reports to the President and Governors, and works with the Public Accounts Committee; the office is protected like a judgeship.
  • The UPSC and State Public Service Commissions (Articles 315–323) conduct recruitment and advise on service matters; their advice is not binding, but departures must be explained to the legislature.
  • The Finance Commission (280) and the GST Council (279A) govern fiscal federalism. Articles 338, 338A and 338B create national commissions for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Backward Classes.
  • Statutory bodies include the NHRC, CVC, Information Commissions and the Lokpal; NITI Aayog and the CBI rest on executive resolutions.

docs.title: 12.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Distinguish a constitutional body from a statutory body, with two examples of each.

Answer

A constitutional body is created by the Constitution, and its basic features can be changed only by amendment: for example, the Election Commission and the CAG (also the UPSC and the Finance Commission). A statutory body is created by an Act of Parliament or a State legislature and can be changed by ordinary law: for example, the NHRC and the Central Vigilance Commission (also the Information Commissions and the Lokpal).

Exercise 2

How is the Chief Election Commissioner protected from removal, and how does this differ from the protection of other Election Commissioners?

Answer

The Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court: by an address of both Houses of Parliament passed by special majority for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Other Election Commissioners can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner, which is a weaker protection.

Exercise 3

Why is the CAG described as an auditor rather than a comptroller in India?

Answer

In India, money is withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund by the executive without the CAG's prior approval; the CAG audits expenditure after it has been incurred. Unlike the British CAG, the Indian CAG does not control the issue of money, so in practice the office is that of an auditor.

Exercise 4

Is the advice of the UPSC binding on the government? What check exists if the government does not accept it?

Answer

No, it is advisory. But under Article 323 the government must lay the UPSC's annual report before Parliament, with a memorandum explaining the cases in which the advice was not accepted and the reasons. Parliament can then question the government.

Exercise 5

Which amendments gave constitutional status to (a) a separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes and (b) the National Commission for Backward Classes?

Answer

(a) The 89th Amendment (2003), which divided the earlier joint commission into Article 338 (SCs) and Article 338A (STs). (b) The 102nd Amendment (2018), which inserted Article 338B.

Exercise 6

Name one body each that was created by (a) an executive resolution and (b) the Right to Information Act, 2005.

Answer

(a) NITI Aayog (2015) (or the Planning Commission before it, or the CBI in 1963). (b) The Central Information Commission (and State Information Commissions).
