docs.title: Chapter 4: Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties
docs.text:
The goals the Constitution sets for the State, and the duties it asks of citizens

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain what the Directive Principles of State Policy are and why they were made non-justiciable;
  • classify the Directive Principles into socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groups, with their articles;
  • identify the principles added by later amendments;
  • trace the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles through the main cases, from Champakam Dorairajan to Minerva Mills;
  • give examples of laws and policies that implement the Directive Principles;
  • list the Fundamental Duties and explain their status.

docs.title: 4.1 The idea of Directive Principles
docs.text:
Part III of the Constitution tells the State what it must not do: it must not discriminate, must not take away liberty without fair procedure, must not suppress speech without good reason. But the framers also wanted to tell the State what it should do: secure a decent livelihood for all, protect workers and children, spread education, raise nutrition and public health, protect the environment. These positive goals are set out in Part IV, the Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36 to 51).

The idea came from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which contained "directive principles of social policy". Dr Ambedkar compared the Directive Principles to the Instruments of Instructions that the British government used to issue to the Governor-General and Governors under the Government of India Act, 1935: the difference was that these instructions were addressed to the governments of free India, and the people would judge them by how well they followed them.

docs.title: Article 37: not enforceable, but fundamental
docs.text:
Article 37 states the legal character of Part IV in two sentences. The provisions of Part IV "shall not be enforceable by any court", but the principles laid down in it are "nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country", and it shall be "the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws".

Why were they made non-justiciable? The usual reasons are these.

  • Resources. In 1950 the State did not have the money to provide, for example, work, education and public assistance for all at once. A court cannot order the State to do what it cannot afford.
  • Flexibility. Different governments might choose different means and different speeds. The framers did not want to tie the hands of future legislatures to a particular economic programme.
  • Backwardness and diversity. Conditions varied widely across the country, and uniform enforcement would have been impractical.

Article 36 gives "the State" in Part IV the same meaning as in Part III (Article 12), so the directives are addressed to the Union, the States, and local and other authorities.

Key idea

Fundamental Rights are limits on the State and are enforced by the courts. Directive Principles are goals for the State and are enforced by the political process: by legislation, by policy and ultimately by voters. Article 37 makes them non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.

Fundamental Rights Directive Principles Part III (Articles 12–35) IV (Articles 36–51) Nature Mostly negative: prohibitions on the State Positive: instructions to the State Enforceable in court? Yes (Articles 32 and 226) No (Article 37) Aim Political democracy; protection of the individual Social and economic democracy; a welfare state Effect on laws A law violating them is void A law is not void for violating them Source United States (Bill of Rights) Ireland Suspension Can be suspended in an emergency (except Articles 20, 21) Not applicable

Table 4.1. Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles compared.

docs.title: 4.2 The principles, classified
docs.text: The Constitution does not group the Directive Principles, but they are usually arranged in three broad categories according to the ideas behind them.

docs.title: Socialist principles
docs.text:
These reflect the ideal of a welfare state and aim at social and economic justice.

  • Article 38: the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order in which justice, social, economic and political, informs all institutions of national life; and (clause 2, added in 1978) shall strive to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.
  • Article 39: the State shall direct its policy towards securing (a) an adequate means of livelihood for all citizens, men and women equally; (b) that the ownership and control of the material resources of the community are distributed to subserve the common good; (c) that the operation of the economic system does not result in the concentration of wealth and means of production to the common detriment; (d) equal pay for equal work for men and women; (e) that the health and strength of workers and the tender age of children are not abused; and (f) that children are given opportunities to develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity.
  • Article 39A: equal justice and free legal aid.
  • Article 41: the right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, within the limits of the State's economic capacity.
  • Article 42: just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
  • Article 43: a living wage and a decent standard of life for all workers.
  • Article 43A: participation of workers in the management of industries.
  • Article 47: raising the level of nutrition and the standard of living, and improving public health.

docs.title: Gandhian principles
docs.text:
These reflect the programme of reconstruction associated with Mahatma Gandhi.

  • Article 40: organise village panchayats and give them the powers needed to function as units of self-government.
  • Article 43: promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.
  • Article 43B: promote the voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.
  • Article 46: promote with special care the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections, in particular the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and protect them from social injustice and exploitation.
  • Article 47: bring about the prohibition of the consumption, except for medicinal purposes, of intoxicating drinks and of drugs injurious to health.
  • Article 48: prohibit the slaughter of cows and calves and other milch and draught cattle, and improve their breeds.

docs.title: Liberal-intellectual principles
docs.text:
These reflect the ideals of liberalism and modern administration.

  • Article 44: secure for citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.
  • Article 45: provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete the age of six years.
  • Article 48: organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines.
  • Article 48A: protect and improve the environment and safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.
  • Article 49: protect monuments and places and objects of artistic or historic interest declared to be of national importance.
  • Article 50: separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
  • Article 51: promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

Overlapping categories

Articles 43, 47 and 48 appear in two categories because they contain more than one idea. Article 47 joins nutrition and public health (socialist) with prohibition (Gandhian); Article 48 joins scientific agriculture (liberal) with the protection of cattle (Gandhian). The classification is a teaching aid, not part of the Constitution.

docs.title: Principles added by amendments
docs.text:
Amendment Change 42nd (1976) Article 39(f) (healthy development of children); Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid); Article 43A (workers' participation in management); Article 48A (environment, forests and wildlife) 44th (1978) Article 38(2) (minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities) 86th (2002) Article 45 substituted: early childhood care and education until six (free and compulsory education from six to fourteen became a Fundamental Right in Article 21A) 97th (2011) Article 43B (co-operative societies)

Table 4.2. Directive Principles added or changed by amendments.

Directives outside Part IV

A few directions to the State appear elsewhere in the Constitution and are also non-justiciable: Article 335 (the claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes to services, consistently with efficiency of administration), Article 350A (instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children of linguistic minorities) and Article 351 (development of the Hindi language).

docs.title: 4.3 Rights versus directives: from conflict to harmony
docs.text:
Because the Directive Principles ask the State to redistribute wealth and land, and the Fundamental Rights originally protected property, the two were bound to clash. The history of that clash is a history of exchanges between the courts and Parliament, shown in Figure 4.1.

Figure 4.1 Rights and directives, 1951 to 1980. A timeline of the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles: Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the 1st Amendment (1951), Golaknath (1967), the 24th and 25th Amendments (1971), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the 42nd Amendment (1976) and Minerva Mills (1980).
  1. Rights prevail (1951). In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Supreme Court struck down a government order reserving seats in medical and engineering colleges by community. It held that the Directive Principles must conform to and run subsidiary to the Fundamental Rights. Parliament responded with the 1st Amendment (1951), which added Article 15(4) and the Ninth Schedule.
  2. Rights cannot be amended (1967). In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Court held that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights at all, even to implement the Directive Principles.
  3. Parliament replies (1971). The 24th Amendment asserted Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Part III. The 25th Amendment inserted Article 31C: a law giving effect to the principles in Article 39(b) and (c) shall not be void for violating Articles 14 or 19, and no such law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to those principles shall be questioned in court on the ground that it does not give such effect.
  4. The basic structure (1973). In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Court overruled Golaknath: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights, but not the basic structure. It upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the second part, the declaration that barred judicial review.
  5. Directives above rights (1976). The 42nd Amendment extended the protection of Article 31C to laws implementing any of the Directive Principles, not only Article 39(b) and (c).
  6. Balance is basic (1980). In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down this extension. It held that the Constitution rests on the balance and harmony between Parts III and IV; giving absolute primacy to one over the other would disturb that harmony, and the harmony itself is part of the basic structure. Article 31C stands as it was after Kesavananda, covering Article 39(b) and (c) only.

Key idea

The present position comes from Minerva Mills (1980): Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary, neither is subordinate to the other, and the balance between them is part of the basic structure. Laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c) are protected from challenge under Articles 14 and 19 by Article 31C.

docs.title: Directives as a guide to interpretation
docs.text:
Apart from this history, the courts use the Directive Principles in two everyday ways.

  • To interpret rights. Many rights read into Article 21, such as livelihood, health, education, legal aid and a clean environment, draw directly on Articles 39A, 41, 45, 47 and 48A.
  • To judge reasonableness. A restriction on a Fundamental Right that promotes a Directive Principle is more likely to be held reasonable. For instance, a law regulating a trade in order to protect public health (Article 47) is more easily upheld under Article 19(6).

Material resources of the community

In 2024 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court considered the meaning of "material resources of the community" in Article 39(b). The majority held that not every privately owned resource falls within the phrase merely because it meets a material need; whether a particular resource does depends on its nature and its effect on the community. Questions of this kind show that the boundary between Parts III and IV is still being worked out.

Worked example 4.1: A law and the Directive Principles

Situation. A State enacts a law fixing a ceiling on agricultural landholdings and distributing the surplus land to landless labourers. A landowner challenges it under Article 14, saying it treats large landowners unfairly. The law states that it is for giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c).

Answer. Article 31C protects a law giving effect to Article 39(b) (distribution of material resources for the common good) and 39(c) (preventing concentration of wealth) from being declared void for violating Article 14 or 19. Since Kesavananda Bharati, however, the declaration in the law is not conclusive: the court can examine whether the law really has a reasonable connection with those principles. If it does, the challenge under Article 14 fails. (Land reform laws are also commonly protected by Article 31A, and many have been placed in the Ninth Schedule, subject to I. R. Coelho.)

docs.title: 4.4 How the directives have been implemented
docs.text:
Although no court can order it, governments have passed many laws and launched many programmes in pursuit of the Directive Principles. A few examples:

Directive Laws and policies that implement it 39(b), (c) Land reform laws: abolition of intermediaries such as zamindars, tenancy reform, land ceilings 39(d) Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 (now part of the Code on Wages, 2019) 39A Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; free legal aid through legal services authorities; Lok Adalats 40 73rd Amendment (1992): constitutional status for panchayats 41 Social security pensions; the rural employment guarantee under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 42 Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 43B 97th Amendment (2011) on co-operative societies 45 Integrated Child Development Services and early childhood education 47 Nutrition programmes; prohibition laws in some States 48A Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980; Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 50 Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which separated judicial magistrates from the executive (its successor, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, keeps the separation)

Table 4.3. Examples of implementation.

docs.title: The uniform civil code
docs.text:
Article 44 asks the State to "endeavour to secure" a uniform civil code for citizens: a common set of laws on marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption and succession, in place of the personal laws of different religious communities. It is the most debated directive. Supporters argue that a common code would advance equality, especially gender equality, and national integration. Others argue that personal laws are part of religious and cultural freedom, that reform should come from within communities, and that uniformity should not be imposed. The Supreme Court has more than once urged the State to act on Article 44, for example in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985) and Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995). Goa has long had a common civil code inherited from the Portuguese period, and Uttarakhand enacted a uniform civil code law in 2024. There is no nationwide code.

Common confusion

Do not write that the uniform civil code is "required by the Constitution". Article 44 is a Directive Principle: it asks the State to endeavour to secure such a code, but it cannot be enforced by a court, and the form and timing of any code are left to the legislature.

docs.title: Origin
docs.text: The original Constitution had no list of duties. During the emergency of 1975–77, the government set up the Swaran Singh Committee, which recommended adding duties of citizens. The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part IVA, with one article, Article 51A, listing ten duties. The idea was influenced by the constitution of the former USSR. The 86th Amendment (2002) added an eleventh duty.

docs.title: The eleven duties
docs.text:
Article 51A says that it shall be the duty of every citizen of India:

  1. to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem;
  2. to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom;
  3. to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India;
  4. to defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so;
  5. to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood among all the people of India, transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities, and to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women;
  6. to value and preserve the rich heritage of the country's composite culture;
  7. to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures;
  8. to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform;
  9. to safeguard public property and to abjure violence;
  10. to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity, so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement;
  11. who is a parent or guardian, to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen years (added in 2002).

(The list above follows the order of clauses (a) to (k) of Article 51A, in paraphrase.)

docs.title: Status and enforcement
docs.text:
• Citizens only. Unlike many Fundamental Rights, the duties are addressed to citizens, not to all persons.
  • Non-justiciable. The Constitution provides no direct penalty or court remedy for failing to perform them. They can, however, be enforced through ordinary laws that Parliament chooses to make.
  • An aid to interpretation. Courts may refer to the duties in deciding whether a restriction on a right is reasonable. A law that gives effect to a Fundamental Duty, for example a law punishing insults to the National Flag, is more easily upheld.
  • Many are already enforced by law. A committee chaired by Justice J. S. Verma, reporting in 1999 on how the duties could be put into practice, pointed to existing laws that give effect to several of them: the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971; the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, among others.

Some duties mirror directives

Several Fundamental Duties are the citizen's side of a Directive Principle. Article 48A asks the State to protect the environment; Article 51A(g) asks the citizen to do the same. Article 45 and Article 21A concern the State's provision of education; Article 51A(k) asks the parent to provide the opportunity.

Worked example 4.2: Can a duty be enforced?

Situation. A resident association asks a court to order a neighbour to stop dumping waste into a lake, citing the neighbour's duty under Article 51A(g) to protect the natural environment.

Answer. The court cannot enforce Article 51A(g) directly as a duty: Fundamental Duties are not justiciable in themselves. But the association is not without a remedy. The dumping is likely to violate environmental and municipal laws, which can be enforced against the neighbour, and the authorities' failure to act may be challenged as a violation of the right to a clean environment under Article 21, read with Article 48A. The court can use Article 51A(g) to support its reasoning.

Summary

  • Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36–51), borrowed in idea from Ireland, are goals for the State. Under Article 37 they cannot be enforced by any court but are fundamental in governance, and the State must apply them in making laws.
  • They are commonly classified as socialist (38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47), Gandhian (40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48) and liberal-intellectual (44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51).
  • Amendments added 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A (42nd), 38(2) (44th), the present Article 45 (86th) and 43B (97th).
  • The relationship with Fundamental Rights moved from rights prevailing (Champakam Dorairajan, 1951) through Article 31C (1971) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973) to the doctrine of harmony and balance (Minerva Mills, 1980).
  • Many laws implement the directives: land reform, legal aid, panchayats, labour and environmental laws. The uniform civil code (Article 44) remains a subject of debate.
  • Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A) were added by the 42nd Amendment (ten duties) and the 86th Amendment (the eleventh). They apply to citizens, are non-justiciable in themselves, and guide interpretation and legislation.

docs.title: 4.6 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Quote the key words of Article 37 that state the legal status of the Directive Principles.

Answer

The provisions of Part IV "shall not be enforceable by any court", but the principles are "nevertheless fundamental in the governance of the country", and it is "the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws".

Exercise 2

Classify the following as socialist, Gandhian or liberal-intellectual: Article 40, Article 44, Article 39(d), Article 48A, Article 46.

Answer

Article 40 (village panchayats): Gandhian. Article 44 (uniform civil code): liberal-intellectual. Article 39(d) (equal pay for equal work): socialist. Article 48A (environment): liberal-intellectual. Article 46 (interests of weaker sections, SCs and STs): Gandhian.

Exercise 3

What did the Supreme Court decide in Minerva Mills (1980) about the relationship between Parts III and IV?

Answer

It held that the Constitution is founded on the balance and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, that giving absolute primacy to the directives over the rights would destroy this balance, and that the balance is part of the basic structure. It therefore struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles; Article 31C protects only laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c).

Exercise 4

Name four Directive Principles inserted by the 42nd Amendment.

Answer

Article 39(f) (opportunities for healthy development of children), Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), Article 43A (workers' participation in management) and Article 48A (protection of the environment, forests and wildlife).

Exercise 5

How many Fundamental Duties are there now, which amendment added the last one, and what does it say?

Answer

Eleven. The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 51A(k): a parent or guardian must provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the ages of six and fourteen.

Exercise 6

"Directive Principles are useless because they cannot be enforced." Give two arguments against this statement.

Answer

Any two of: (1) They guide legislation, and a large body of law (land reform, labour, legal aid, panchayats, environment) has been made to implement them. (2) Courts use them to interpret Fundamental Rights, especially Article 21, and to judge whether restrictions are reasonable. (3) They are a standard by which voters can judge governments. (4) Since Minerva Mills, the balance between rights and directives is part of the basic structure, and Article 31C protects laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c).

docs.title: Chapter 13: Elections and Political Parties
docs.text:
The franchise, electoral systems, the conduct of elections, parties and electoral reform

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • state the constitutional provisions on elections (Part XV) and the two Representation of the People Acts;
  • explain universal adult franchise and the system of electoral rolls;
  • compare the first-past-the-post system with proportional representation by single transferable vote, and work simple examples of each;
  • explain delimitation and reserved constituencies;
  • describe the stages of an election, the Model Code of Conduct, voting machines and NOTA, and how election disputes are settled;
  • explain the role of political parties, how they are registered and recognised, and how the party system has changed;
  • discuss the main electoral reforms and the issues still debated.

docs.title: 13.1 Elections in a democracy
docs.text:
In a representative democracy, elections are the means by which the people choose their representatives and hold them to account. An election is democratic only if certain conditions are met: every adult can vote, every vote counts equally, voters can choose freely among real alternatives, the poll is secret, the count is honest, and those who lose accept the result. The Indian Constitution tries to secure these conditions through Part XV (Articles 324 to 329) and through laws made by Parliament.

Article Provision 324 Superintendence, direction and control of elections vested in the Election Commission 325 One general electoral roll for every constituency; no one excluded on grounds only of religion, race, caste or sex 326 Elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage 327 Parliament may make laws on elections to Parliament and State legislatures 328 State legislatures may make such laws for their own elections, so far as Parliament has not done so 329 Courts may not question laws on delimitation or the allotment of seats; elections may be questioned only by an election petition

Table 13.1. Part XV of the Constitution.

The main laws are the Representation of the People Act, 1950, which deals with the allocation of seats, delimitation, the qualifications of voters and the preparation of electoral rolls, and the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which deals with the conduct of elections, the qualifications and disqualifications of members, corrupt practices and election disputes.

Article 325 deserves a special note. Under British rule, Muslims and some other groups had separate electorates: they voted only for candidates of their own community in seats reserved for it. The Constitution rejected this. There is one general roll for each constituency, and even in constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes, all voters vote together.

docs.title: 13.2 The franchise and the electoral roll
Universal adult franchise
docs.text:
Article 326 gives the vote to every citizen who is at least 18 years old on the qualifying date fixed by law and is not otherwise disqualified (for example, for non-residence, unsoundness of mind, or crime or corrupt practices). The voting age was 21 until the 61st Amendment (1988) lowered it to 18. There are no qualifications of property, income, education or sex.

The first general elections, held between October 1951 and February 1952 under the first Chief Election Commissioner, Sukumar Sen, were then the largest elections ever held. Most voters could not read, so each party was identified by a symbol, a practice that continues.

docs.title: Electoral rolls
docs.text:
A citizen can vote only if his or her name is on the electoral roll of a constituency in which he or she is ordinarily resident. The rolls are prepared and revised by the Election Commission through Electoral Registration Officers, usually with an annual summary revision and continuous updating. Since 2022, the law has provided four qualifying dates in a year (1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October), so that young people can register soon after turning eighteen. Voters are issued an Electors Photo Identity Card.

Common confusion

Article 326 guarantees adult suffrage, but the right to vote in India has been described by the Supreme Court as a statutory right, conferred and regulated by the Representation of the People Acts, rather than a Fundamental Right. The freedom of voting (the choice of whom to vote for, or not to vote for anyone) is, however, protected as part of freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a).

docs.title: 13.3 Electoral systems
docs.text: An electoral system is the method by which votes are turned into seats. India uses two.

docs.title: First past the post
docs.text:
Elections to the Lok Sabha and the State Legislative Assemblies use the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, also called the simple plurality system. The country (or the State) is divided into single-member constituencies. Each voter has one vote. The candidate who receives more votes than any other candidate wins, even if he or she does not have a majority of the votes cast.

The framers chose FPTP for its simplicity, which mattered in a country where most voters were voting for the first time, and because it tends to produce stable governments with a clear link between each constituency and its representative. Its main drawback is that the share of seats a party wins can differ greatly from its share of votes.

Worked example 13.1: Votes and seats under FPTP

Situation. A small State has three constituencies of 100,000 voters each, all of whom vote. Three parties, A, B and C, contest every seat. The results are:

  • Constituency 1: A 40,000; B 35,000; C 25,000.
  • Constituency 2: A 38,000; B 37,000; C 25,000.
  • Constituency 3: A 20,000; B 50,000; C 30,000.

Who wins each seat, and how do vote shares compare with seat shares?

Answer. A wins Constituencies 1 and 2 (with 40 and 38 per cent), and B wins Constituency 3. Overall votes: A \(= 98{,}000\) (32.7 per cent), B \(= 122{,}000\) (40.7 per cent), C \(= 80{,}000\) (26.7 per cent). Seats: A 2 (66.7 per cent), B 1 (33.3 per cent), C 0. Party B won the most votes but fewer seats than A, and C won more than a quarter of the votes but no seat at all. This is the typical distortion of FPTP: what matters is where votes are cast, not just how many.

docs.title: Proportional representation by single transferable vote
docs.text:
Indirect elections use proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (STV). It is used for the elections of the President and the Vice-President (Chapter 5), of members of the Rajya Sabha by the State Legislative Assemblies, and of members of the State Legislative Councils.

Where several seats are to be filled, as in a Rajya Sabha election, each voter ranks the candidates in order of preference. A candidate is elected on reaching a quota, calculated as

\[ \text{quota} = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{number of valid votes}}{\text{number of seats} + 1} \right\rfloor + 1 . \]

Votes in excess of the quota (the surplus) are transferred to the voters' next preferences, and if seats remain unfilled, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and his or her votes are transferred, until all seats are filled. (In practice, each vote is given a value of 100 to allow fractional transfers.)

Worked example 13.2: A Rajya Sabha election

Situation. A State Legislative Assembly has 120 elected members, all of whom vote. Four seats in the Rajya Sabha are to be filled. Party P has 70 members and Party Q has 50. Assuming every member votes for his or her own party's candidates, how many seats will each party win?

Answer. Quota \(= \lfloor 120 / (4 + 1) \rfloor + 1 = 24 + 1 = 25\) votes. Party P, with 70 votes, can fill two quotas (\(2 \times 25 = 50\)) with 20 votes to spare; Party Q, with 50 votes, can fill exactly two quotas. So P wins 2 seats and Q wins 2, even though P has a clear majority in the Assembly. P's remaining 20 votes are not enough for a third quota. (Under FPTP-style voting for each seat, P would have won all four.) The STV system gives a minority party in the Assembly representation roughly proportional to its strength.

docs.title: Delimitation
docs.text:
Delimitation means drawing the boundaries of constituencies. Under Article 82 (and Article 170 for the States), after each census the allocation of seats and the division into constituencies are to be readjusted by an authority set up by Parliament. Parliament has set up Delimitation Commissions under laws of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002. A Delimitation Commission is an independent body, usually chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge, with the Chief Election Commissioner (or an Election Commissioner) and the State Election Commissioners as members. Its orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court (Article 329(a)).

As Chapter 6 explained, the number of seats allotted to each State has been frozen on the basis of the 1971 census until the first census after 2026. The last Commission, constituted under the 2002 law, redrew constituency boundaries within each State on the basis of the 2001 census without changing the number of seats per State. A new delimitation after the next census will affect both the allocation of seats among States and the coming into force of the reservation of seats for women under the 106th Amendment. It is expected to be a significant political question, since States differ greatly in population growth.

docs.title: Reserved constituencies
docs.text: Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies in proportion to their population (Articles 330 and 332), until 2030 (104th Amendment). The Delimitation Commission decides which constituencies are reserved, choosing for Scheduled Tribes those where their share of the population is highest, and for Scheduled Castes, constituencies spread across the State where their share is relatively high. In a reserved constituency only members of the group can stand as candidates, but all registered voters vote. There is no reservation of seats for any religious community.

docs.title: The stages of an election
docs.text:
1. Announcement. The Election Commission announces the schedule. The Model Code of Conduct comes into force at once.
  2. Notification. The President (for the Lok Sabha) or the Governor (for an Assembly) issues a notification calling on the constituencies to elect members, on the Commission's recommendation.
  3. Nominations. Candidates file nomination papers with the Returning Officer, along with an affidavit disclosing their criminal record (if any), assets and liabilities, and educational qualifications. A candidate must make a security deposit (₹25,000 for the Lok Sabha and ₹10,000 for an Assembly, halved for SC and ST candidates), which is forfeited if he or she polls less than one-sixth of the valid votes.
  4. Scrutiny and withdrawal. The Returning Officer examines the nominations; candidates may withdraw within a fixed period.
  5. Campaign. Parties and candidates campaign, subject to limits on expenditure fixed by rules for each candidate. Campaigning must stop 48 hours before the close of polling.
  6. Polling. Voting takes place by secret ballot on electronic voting machines. Large elections are held in several phases so that security forces can be deployed.
  7. Counting and results. Votes are counted under the supervision of the Returning Officer and observers, and the result is declared.

docs.title: The Model Code of Conduct
docs.text: The Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines for parties, candidates and governments during elections. It forbids, among other things, appeals to caste or communal feelings, the use of places of worship for campaigning, and the announcement of new schemes, projects or grants by ministers after elections are announced. It is not a law, but the Election Commission enforces it through warnings, orders to stop campaigning for a period, and transfers of officials; violations that are also offences can be prosecuted.

docs.title: Voting machines, VVPAT and NOTA
docs.text:
Electronic voting machines (EVMs) were first used experimentally in a by-election in Kerala in 1982, and have been used in all constituencies since the Lok Sabha election of 2004. A voter-verifiable paper audit trail (VVPAT) unit attached to each machine prints a slip that the voter can see through a window for a few seconds before it drops into a sealed box. VVPAT was introduced following a direction of the Supreme Court in 2013, and the slips from a sample of machines in each constituency are counted and matched with the machine counts. The Supreme Court has declined petitions to return to paper ballots.

Since People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2013), voting machines have included a "None of the Above" (NOTA) option, which lets a voter reject all candidates while keeping the secrecy of the vote. NOTA votes are counted and announced, but they do not affect the result: the candidate with the most votes wins even if NOTA receives more.

docs.title: Election disputes
docs.text: Under Article 329(b) and the Representation of the People Act, 1951, an election can be challenged only by an election petition filed in the High Court within 45 days of the declaration of the result, by a candidate or an elector, on grounds such as corrupt practices, improper acceptance or rejection of nominations, or non-compliance with the law. An appeal lies to the Supreme Court. Corrupt practices under the Act include bribery, undue influence, appeals on grounds of religion, race, caste, community or language, and spending beyond the limit. A person found guilty of a corrupt practice can be disqualified for up to six years. Disputes about the election of the President and the Vice-President go directly to the Supreme Court (Article 71).

docs.title: The role of parties
docs.text: Political parties are not mentioned in the original Constitution; they first appeared in its text with the Tenth Schedule in 1985. Yet parliamentary government cannot work without them. Parties select candidates, present programmes to voters, form governments or act as the opposition, organise legislative business and connect citizens with the State.

docs.title: Registration and recognition
docs.text:
An association of citizens can apply to the Election Commission to be registered as a political party under Section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. It must commit itself, in its constitution, to bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and to the principles of socialism, secularism and democracy, and to uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.

Registered parties that perform well in elections may be recognised as national or State parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. Recognition brings advantages: a reserved symbol for the party's candidates throughout the country (national party) or the State (State party), free broadcasting time on public radio and television, copies of electoral rolls, and a larger number of "star campaigners" whose travel costs are not counted in the candidate's expenses.

A party is recognised as a national party if it fulfils any one of three conditions:

  1. it secures at least 6 per cent of the valid votes in four or more States in a general election to the Lok Sabha or the Assemblies, and in addition wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha; or
  2. it wins at least 2 per cent of the seats in the Lok Sabha (that is, 11 seats) from at least three States; or
  3. it is recognised as a State party in at least four States.

A party is recognised as a State party in a State if it meets criteria based on its share of votes and seats in that State at a general election (for example, 6 per cent of the valid votes in the State together with two seats in the Assembly). The Election Commission reviews recognition after general elections, so the list of recognised parties changes over time.

Worked example 13.3: National party status

Situation. After a general election, Party R has won 6 per cent or more of the valid votes in five States and three seats in the Lok Sabha. It is recognised as a State party in two States. Is it a national party?

Answer. Check each condition. (1) It has 6 per cent of the votes in four or more States (five), but it also needs four Lok Sabha seats; it has only three, so it fails. (2) It needs 11 Lok Sabha seats from at least three States; it has three, so it fails. (3) It needs State party recognition in four States; it has two, so it fails. Party R is not a national party, though it remains a recognised State party in two States. Winning one more Lok Sabha seat would satisfy condition (1).

docs.title: How the party system has changed
docs.text: For about two decades after independence, the Indian National Congress won national elections comfortably and governed most States, while opposition parties were numerous but fragmented. Political scientists described this as a one-party dominant system. From 1967, non-Congress governments came to power in several States, and in 1977 a non-Congress government was formed at the Centre for the first time. From 1989 to 2014 no single party won a majority in the Lok Sabha, and India was governed by coalitions, which strengthened the role of regional parties. A single party won a majority in 2014 and again in 2019; in 2024 no party won a majority on its own, and a coalition government was formed. The party system is now best described as a multi-party system in which national and regional parties both play important roles.

docs.title: 13.7 Electoral reforms
docs.text:
Electoral law has changed considerably since 1950, often under pressure from the courts and the Election Commission. The main reforms and debates include the following.

  • Disclosure by candidates. In Union of India v. Association for Democratic Reforms (2002) and People's Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2003), the Supreme Court held that voters have a right to know the criminal antecedents, assets and educational qualifications of candidates, as part of the freedom of expression. Candidates now file affidavits disclosing them. Later judgments have required parties to publicise the criminal records of their candidates and the reasons for choosing them.
  • Disqualification on conviction. In Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013), the Court struck down the provision that let sitting legislators continue in office pending appeal after conviction; a conviction with a sentence of two years or more now disqualifies at once.
  • NOTA and VVPAT, described above.
  • Anti-defection law, strengthened by the 91st Amendment (2003) (Chapter 6).
  • Funding of parties. Party finance has long been considered a weak spot. The electoral bonds scheme, introduced in 2018, allowed anonymous donations to parties through bonds bought from a bank. In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (February 2024), a five-judge bench unanimously struck down the scheme, holding that it violated voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a). Proposals for State funding of elections have been made by committees such as the Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998), but have not been adopted.
  • Criminalisation of politics. Concern about candidates facing serious criminal charges remains. Proposals include disqualification on the framing of charges (rather than on conviction) and fast-track trials of legislators.
  • Simultaneous elections. Elections to the Lok Sabha and all State Assemblies were held together from 1951–52 until 1967, after which the cycles separated. A high-level committee recommended in 2024 that simultaneous elections be restored, and constitutional amendment bills for this purpose were introduced in Parliament in December 2024 and referred to a joint parliamentary committee. Supporters cite lower costs and less disruption to governance; critics raise concerns about federalism and accountability. Check the current position.

Key idea

Much of Indian electoral reform has come from the Supreme Court, applying the voter's right to information and the guarantee of free and fair elections (a part of the basic structure), and from the Election Commission's enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct. Parliament retains the power to legislate on elections, and the debates over party funding, criminalisation and simultaneous elections continue.

Summary

  • Part XV (Articles 324–329) vests control of elections in the Election Commission, guarantees one general roll per constituency without separate electorates, and adult suffrage at 18 (61st Amendment, 1988). The Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951 supply the details.
  • The Lok Sabha and Assemblies are elected by first past the post in single-member constituencies; the President, Vice-President, Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils by proportional representation by single transferable vote.
  • Delimitation Commissions draw constituency boundaries; their orders cannot be challenged in court. Seat allocation per State is frozen on the 1971 census until after the first census following 2026. SC and ST seats are reserved until 2030.
  • Elections pass through announcement, notification, nomination, scrutiny, campaign, polling and counting; the Model Code of Conduct applies from announcement; EVMs with VVPAT are used; NOTA is available; disputes go to the High Court by election petition.
  • Parties are registered under Section 29A and recognised as national or State parties under the Symbols Order, 1968. The party system has moved from one-party dominance through coalitions to a competitive multi-party system.
  • Reforms include disclosure by candidates, immediate disqualification on conviction, NOTA, VVPAT and the striking down of electoral bonds; party funding, criminalisation and simultaneous elections remain under debate.

docs.title: 13.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What does Article 325 provide, and what colonial practice did it end?

Answer

There shall be one general electoral roll for every territorial constituency, and no person shall be ineligible for inclusion in it on grounds only of religion, race, caste or sex. It ended the colonial system of separate electorates, under which certain communities voted separately for their own representatives.

Exercise 2

In a constituency, the votes are: Candidate X 45,000; Candidate Y 42,000; Candidate Z 33,000; NOTA 5,000. Who wins? Did the winner obtain a majority of votes cast?

Answer

X wins, having the most votes. Total votes cast (including NOTA) \(= 125{,}000\); X has \(45{,}000 / 125{,}000 = 36\) per cent, which is not a majority. Under first past the post, a plurality is enough, and NOTA votes do not affect the result.

Exercise 3

A State Assembly of 150 members elects three members of the Rajya Sabha. What is the quota? If Party M has 95 members and Party N has 55, and all vote on party lines, how many seats does each win?

Answer

Quota \(= \lfloor 150 / (3 + 1) \rfloor + 1 = 37 + 1 =\) 38. Party M's 95 votes fill two quotas (\(2 \times 38 = 76\)) with 19 to spare, not enough for a third. Party N's 55 votes fill one quota with 17 to spare. Two M candidates and one N candidate reach the quota, which fills all three seats: M wins 2 and N wins 1.

Exercise 4

Why can the orders of a Delimitation Commission not be challenged in court?

Answer

Article 329(a) provides that the validity of any law relating to the delimitation of constituencies or the allotment of seats, made under Article 327 or 328, shall not be called in question in any court. The Delimitation Acts give the Commission's orders the force of law, so they enjoy this protection. The purpose is to prevent elections from being held up by litigation over boundaries.

Exercise 5

State the three alternative conditions for recognition as a national party.

Answer

(1) At least 6 per cent of the valid votes in four or more States in a general election to the Lok Sabha or the Assemblies, plus at least four Lok Sabha seats; or (2) at least 2 per cent of Lok Sabha seats (11 seats) from at least three States; or (3) recognition as a State party in at least four States.

Exercise 6

What did the Supreme Court decide about electoral bonds in 2024, and on what ground?

Answer

In Association for Democratic Reforms v. Union of India (February 2024), a five-judge bench unanimously struck down the electoral bonds scheme and related amendments, holding that anonymous funding of parties violated the voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a), which is essential to free and fair elections.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Emergency Provisions
docs.text:
National emergency, President's rule in the States and financial emergency

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain why the Constitution contains emergency provisions and where they come from;
  • state the grounds, procedure, approval, duration and revocation of a national emergency under Article 352;
  • describe the effects of a national emergency on Centre-State relations, Parliament and Fundamental Rights;
  • state the grounds, approval and duration of President's rule under Article 356, and explain its effects;
  • summarise the guidelines laid down in S. R. Bommai (1994) and the cases in which Article 356 is and is not properly used;
  • explain the financial emergency under Article 360;
  • list the safeguards added by the 44th Amendment (1978) after the emergency of 1975–77.

docs.title: 10.1 Why emergency provisions?
docs.text:
Every constitution must face the possibility that ordinary government will not be enough: an invasion, an armed rebellion, the collapse of a State government, or a financial crisis. The framers of the Indian Constitution had just lived through partition, communal violence and the integration of the princely states. They gave the Union extraordinary powers to deal with such situations, in Part XVIII (Articles 352 to 360).

The Constitution provides for three kinds of emergency:

  1. a national emergency (Article 352), on the ground of war, external aggression or armed rebellion;
  2. failure of constitutional machinery in a State (Article 356), popularly called President's rule or State emergency;
  3. a financial emergency (Article 360).

During an emergency, the federal system can become, in effect, unitary: the Union can direct the States, legislate on State subjects and, in the case of President's rule, take over the government of a State. The emergency provisions draw on the Government of India Act, 1935 (for the structure of central powers) and on the Weimar Constitution of Germany (for the suspension of Fundamental Rights).

The provisions were much debated in the Constituent Assembly. Some members feared they would be misused to destroy State autonomy and civil liberties. The experience of 1975–77 showed that the fears were not groundless, and the 44th Amendment (1978) added important safeguards, which this chapter notes at each step.

Figure 10.1 Approval and duration of emergencies. Approval and duration rules for the three emergencies. A national emergency must be approved by a special majority of each House within one month and renewed every six months, with no maximum. President's rule must be approved by a simple majority within two months and renewed every six months, up to three years, with conditions beyond one year. A financial emergency must be approved within two months and then continues until revoked.

docs.title: Grounds
docs.text:
The President may proclaim a national emergency if satisfied that a grave emergency exists whereby the security of India, or of any part of it, is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion. The proclamation may be issued before the actual occurrence of war, aggression or rebellion, if the President is satisfied that there is imminent danger of it. Since the 42nd Amendment (1976), it may apply to the whole of India or to a part only.

When the ground is war or external aggression, the emergency is sometimes called an external emergency; when it is armed rebellion, an internal emergency. Originally the third ground was "internal disturbance"; the 44th Amendment replaced it with the narrower words "armed rebellion", so that a mere disturbance of law and order cannot justify a national emergency.

docs.title: Procedure and approval
docs.text:
• The President can proclaim an emergency only on the written communication of a decision of the Union Cabinet (the Prime Minister and Cabinet Ministers), not on the advice of the Prime Minister alone. This was added by the 44th Amendment.
  • The proclamation must be laid before both Houses of Parliament and approved by each House within one month (two months before the 44th Amendment). Otherwise it ceases to operate.
  • Approval requires a special majority: a majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of the members present and voting (a simple majority before the 44th Amendment).
  • If the Lok Sabha has been dissolved, or is dissolved during the month, and the Rajya Sabha approves the proclamation, it continues until thirty days after the first sitting of the new Lok Sabha, which must approve it within that time.

docs.title: Duration and revocation
docs.text:
Once approved, the emergency continues for six months, and can be extended indefinitely by further approvals of both Houses, each by special majority, every six months. (Before 1978, an approved emergency continued until revoked, without any need for renewal.)

The President may revoke the proclamation at any time by a further proclamation, which needs no parliamentary approval. The President must revoke it if the Lok Sabha passes a resolution disapproving its continuation, by a simple majority. If one-tenth of the total members of the Lok Sabha give written notice to the Speaker (or to the President, if the House is not in session) of their intention to move such a resolution, a special sitting must be held within fourteen days to consider it. These provisions too were added in 1978, to ensure that the Lok Sabha could end an emergency even if the government did not want to.

Key idea

A national emergency needs: a written decision of the Cabinet; approval by a special majority of each House within one month; renewal every six months, again by special majority. It can be ended by the President at any time, and must be ended if the Lok Sabha disapproves by a simple majority.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
On Centre-State relations. The federal division of powers is not suspended, but the Union's powers expand:

  • executive: the Union may give directions to any State on any matter (Article 353), not only on the matters covered by Articles 256 and 257;
  • legislative: Parliament may make laws on any subject in the State List (Article 250). Such laws cease to have effect six months after the emergency ends. The State legislatures are not suspended, but their laws give way to Union laws;
  • financial: the President may modify the constitutional distribution of revenues between the Union and the States (Article 354), subject to approval by Parliament, until the end of the financial year in which the emergency ends.

On the life of the Lok Sabha and Assemblies. During a national emergency, Parliament may by law extend the term of the Lok Sabha by one year at a time, without limit, but not beyond six months after the emergency has ceased (Article 83(2)). The terms of State Legislative Assemblies may be extended in the same way (Article 172(1)). The term of the fifth Lok Sabha was extended in this way during 1976.

On Fundamental Rights. As explained in Chapter 3:

  • under Article 358, the six freedoms of Article 19 are suspended automatically when an emergency is proclaimed on the ground of war or external aggression (not armed rebellion). The State may then make laws or take executive action restricting those freedoms, and they cannot be challenged during the emergency;
  • under Article 359, the President may by order suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights named in the order, except Articles 20 and 21. The order must be laid before Parliament.

Since the 44th Amendment, only laws that contain a recital that they are made in relation to the emergency are protected from challenge under Articles 358 and 359; other laws and executive actions remain open to challenge.

Article 358 and Article 359 are different

Article 358 works automatically and only for Article 19, and only in an emergency on the ground of war or external aggression. Article 359 needs a Presidential order, can cover any Fundamental Right named in it except Articles 20 and 21, and applies whatever the ground of the emergency. Article 358 suspends the right itself; Article 359 suspends only its enforcement in court.

docs.title: Use so far
docs.text:
A national emergency has been proclaimed three times.

Proclamation Ground Circumstances October 1962 External aggression Chinese aggression on the northern frontier; revoked in January 1968 December 1971 External aggression War with Pakistan; revoked in March 1977 June 1975 Internal disturbance Proclaimed while the 1971 emergency was still in force; revoked in March 1977

Table 10.1. Proclamations of national emergency.

The emergency of 1975–77 is the one usually meant by "the Emergency". It was proclaimed on the ground of internal disturbance on 25 June 1975. During it, many political leaders and others were detained under preventive detention laws, the press was censored, elections were postponed by extending the term of the Lok Sabha, and Parliament passed far-reaching amendments, including the 38th, 39th and 42nd. General elections were held in March 1977, after which the emergency was revoked. The new government set up the Shah Commission of Inquiry, under a former Chief Justice of India, J. C. Shah, to inquire into excesses committed during the period, and Parliament enacted the 44th Amendment.

docs.title: Judicial review
docs.text: The 38th Amendment (1975) declared the President's satisfaction in proclaiming an emergency final and beyond the review of any court. The 44th Amendment (1978) deleted that provision. In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court held that a proclamation of emergency can be challenged if it is shown to be mala fide, or based on wholly extraneous or irrelevant grounds, or absurd or perverse.

docs.title: Grounds
docs.text: Under Article 356, if the President, on receipt of a report from the Governor of a State or otherwise, is satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, the President may proclaim President's rule in that State. Under Article 365, if a State fails to comply with directions given by the Union, the President may treat this as such a situation.

docs.title: Approval, duration and revocation
docs.text:
• The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months, by a simple majority.
  • Once approved, it continues for six months and may be extended by further approvals every six months, to a maximum of three years.
  • Since the 44th Amendment, it can be continued beyond one year only if (a) a national emergency is in operation in the whole of India or in the whole or part of the State, and (b) the Election Commission certifies that general elections to the State Assembly cannot be held because of difficulties. (Exceptions to these limits were made by specific amendments for Punjab in the late 1980s and early 1990s.)
  • The President may revoke the proclamation at any time; no parliamentary approval is needed for revocation.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
When President's rule is proclaimed:

  • the President takes over the functions of the State government and the powers of the Governor, and in practice the State is administered by the Governor on behalf of the President, assisted by advisers;
  • the President declares that the powers of the State legislature shall be exercised by Parliament, which may delegate them to the President (laws made in this way are often called President's Acts);
  • the Legislative Assembly is either dissolved or kept in suspended animation;
  • Parliament (or, when the Lok Sabha is not in session, the President) may authorise expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State;
  • the High Court continues to function normally; President's rule does not affect the judiciary;
  • laws made during President's rule continue in force after it ends, until the State legislature alters or repeals them.

Worked example 10.1: Counting the months

Situation. President's rule is proclaimed in a State on 1 January. Parliament approves it on 20 February. No national emergency is in force. For how long, at most, can President's rule continue?

Answer. The proclamation was approved within two months, so it survives. Once approved, it lasts six months, counted from the date of the proclamation: to 30 June. It can be extended for a further six months by both Houses, to 31 December, completing one year. Because no national emergency is in force, the 44th Amendment's conditions for going beyond one year cannot be met (both a national emergency and a certificate from the Election Commission are needed). So, unless a national emergency is proclaimed, President's rule must end after one year, by 31 December. If both conditions were met, it could be extended by six months at a time up to a maximum of three years.

docs.title: Use and misuse
docs.text:
President's rule has been imposed well over a hundred times since 1950, beginning with Punjab in 1951. Some impositions were clearly justified: when no party could form a stable government after an election, or when law and order had broken down completely. Others were widely criticised as being motivated by party considerations: for example, the dismissal of an elected State government that still had a majority in its Assembly, or the dissolution of several State Assemblies together after a change of government at the Centre, as happened in 1977 and again in 1980. Dr Ambedkar had told the Constituent Assembly that he hoped the article would never be called into operation and would remain a dead letter.

The Sarkaria Commission (1988) studied the use of Article 356 and recommended that it be used sparingly, as a last resort, after a warning to the State and after exploring the possibility of an alternative government.

Proper use (examples) Improper use (examples) A hung Assembly in which no party or coalition can form a government Dismissing a ministry that still has a majority, without a floor test A ministry has lost its majority and no alternative government is possible Dismissing a government on charges of maladministration or corruption alone A complete breakdown of law and order, or a physical breakdown of administration Using it to settle internal problems of the ruling party A State government deliberately acting against the Constitution, or refusing to comply with constitutional directions Imposing it for partisan political reasons, or without giving the State a chance to correct itself

Table 10.2. Proper and improper uses of Article 356 (as summarised from the Sarkaria Commission and S. R. Bommai).

docs.title: The Bommai judgment
docs.text:
In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court laid down the main principles that now govern Article 356.

  1. A proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review. The court can examine whether there was relevant material for the President's satisfaction, and whether it was mala fide or based on irrelevant grounds. The burden lies on the Union to show the relevant material.
  2. The question whether a ministry has lost majority support must be decided on the floor of the House, not by the Governor's subjective assessment.
  3. The State Assembly should not be dissolved until both Houses of Parliament have approved the proclamation. Until then, it may only be kept in suspended animation.
  4. If the court strikes down the proclamation, it can restore the dismissed government and revive the Assembly.
  5. Secularism and federalism are part of the basic structure. A State government that pursues anti-secular policies may be dismissed under Article 356.

Following Bommai, the use of Article 356 declined considerably. The courts have applied it since; for example, in Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court held the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly in 2005 to be unconstitutional.

Key idea

After S. R. Bommai (1994), President's rule is subject to judicial review; majority is tested on the floor of the House; the Assembly may not be dissolved before Parliament approves; and a wrongly dismissed government can be restored. Article 356 is meant to be a last resort.

docs.title: 10.4 Financial emergency (Article 360)
docs.text:
Under Article 360, the President may proclaim a financial emergency if satisfied that a situation has arisen whereby the financial stability or credit of India, or of any part of it, is threatened.

  • The proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months, by a simple majority.
  • Once approved, it continues indefinitely until it is revoked; no periodical approval is needed.
  • The President may revoke it at any time.

During a financial emergency:

  • the Union may direct any State to observe canons of financial propriety, and give any other directions it considers necessary;
  • the Union may require the States to reduce the salaries and allowances of persons serving in connection with the affairs of the State, and to reserve money bills and other financial bills for the President's consideration after the State legislature passes them;
  • the President may direct the reduction of salaries and allowances of persons serving the Union, including the judges of the Supreme Court and the High Courts.

A financial emergency has never been proclaimed, even during the balance-of-payments crisis of 1991. As with the national emergency, the 38th Amendment had made the President's satisfaction immune from review, and the 44th Amendment removed that immunity.

docs.title: 10.5 The emergency provisions compared, and the 44th Amendment
docs.text:
National emergency (352) President's rule (356) Financial emergency (360) Ground War, external aggression or armed rebellion Failure of constitutional machinery in a State Threat to financial stability or credit Approval within One month Two months Two months Majority for approval Special Simple Simple Duration once approved Six months, renewable indefinitely Six months, renewable up to three years (conditions beyond one year) Until revoked Effect on State government Continues, subject to Union direction and legislation Taken over by the President Continues, subject to financial directions Effect on Fundamental Rights Articles 358 and 359 None directly None directly Revocation President, or must on Lok Sabha disapproval President President Times used Three Well over a hundred Never

Table 10.3. The three emergencies compared.

The 44th Amendment (1978) is the key to the present form of the emergency provisions. Its main changes were:

  1. "Internal disturbance" replaced by "armed rebellion" as a ground for national emergency.
  2. Proclamation only on the written decision of the Cabinet.
  3. Approval within one month (instead of two) by special majority (instead of simple).
  4. Renewal every six months by special majority.
  5. Lok Sabha disapproval by simple majority forces revocation; one-tenth of members can require a special sitting.
  6. Article 358 applies only to emergencies on the ground of war or external aggression.
  7. Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359.
  8. President's rule beyond one year only with a national emergency in force and an Election Commission certificate.
  9. The immunity from judicial review given by the 38th Amendment removed.

Summary

  • Part XVIII provides for three emergencies: national (352), failure of constitutional machinery in a State (356) and financial (360).
  • A national emergency may be proclaimed for war, external aggression or armed rebellion, on the Cabinet's written advice; it must be approved within one month by a special majority of each House and renewed every six months; the Lok Sabha can force its revocation by a simple majority.
  • During it the Union can direct States on any matter and legislate on State subjects; the Lok Sabha's term can be extended a year at a time; Article 19 is suspended automatically in an external emergency (358), and enforcement of other rights except Articles 20 and 21 can be suspended by Presidential order (359).
  • National emergencies were proclaimed in 1962, 1971 and 1975; the last two were revoked in March 1977.
  • President's rule requires approval within two months by simple majority, lasts six months at a time up to three years, and beyond one year only with a national emergency and an Election Commission certificate. S. R. Bommai (1994) made it subject to judicial review and the floor test.
  • A financial emergency needs approval within two months and then lasts until revoked; it has never been proclaimed.
  • The 44th Amendment (1978) added the main safeguards against misuse.

docs.title: 10.6 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What are the three grounds for a national emergency? Which ground was replaced in 1978, and why?

Answer

War, external aggression and armed rebellion. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion", because the vaguer phrase had been used to justify the emergency of 1975, and a mere disturbance of public order should not be enough.

Exercise 2

The Lok Sabha has 543 members. During a national emergency, 60 members give written notice of a resolution disapproving its continuation. Must a special sitting be held? If the resolution is then passed by 260 votes to 240, what happens?

Answer

One-tenth of 543 is 54.3, so 55 members are needed; 60 is enough, and a special sitting must be held within fourteen days. A disapproval resolution needs only a simple majority of members present and voting; 260 to 240 is a simple majority, so the President must revoke the proclamation.

Exercise 3

Explain the difference between Articles 358 and 359.

Answer

Article 358 suspends the freedoms of Article 19 automatically when a national emergency is proclaimed on the ground of war or external aggression; the State can then act as if Article 19 did not exist. Article 359 allows the President, by order, to suspend the right to move the courts for the enforcement of any Fundamental Rights named in the order, except Articles 20 and 21, whatever the ground of the emergency.

Exercise 4

Give two principles laid down in S. R. Bommai (1994).

Answer

Any two of: the proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, with the burden on the Union to show relevant material; majority must be tested on the floor of the House; the Assembly should not be dissolved until Parliament has approved the proclamation; the court can restore a dismissed government if the proclamation is invalid; secularism and federalism are part of the basic structure, and anti-secular conduct by a State government can justify Article 356.

Exercise 5

How does a financial emergency differ from President's rule in its duration?

Answer

A financial emergency, once approved by both Houses within two months, continues until revoked, with no need for renewal and no maximum. President's rule must be renewed every six months, cannot ordinarily go beyond one year, and can never exceed three years.

Exercise 6

During a national emergency, can the State legislatures still make laws on State subjects? What happens if a State law conflicts with a law made by Parliament under Article 250?

Answer

Yes. The State legislatures are not suspended. But Parliament may also legislate on State subjects, and in case of conflict, the law made by Parliament prevails. Parliament's law ceases to have effect six months after the emergency ends.

docs.text:
