docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Official sources and standard books for going further

docs.title: The text and official sources
docs.text:
• The Constitution of India. The authoritative, up-to-date text is published by the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India, and can be read on its website. Always check provisions against it: amendments are frequent.
  • Constituent Assembly Debates. The full record of the debates of 1946–1950, published by the Lok Sabha Secretariat. Indispensable for understanding why provisions were adopted.
  • B. Shiva Rao (ed.), The Framing of India's Constitution (Indian Institute of Public Administration, 1966–1968). Documents and studies on the making of the Constitution, in several volumes.
  • Judgments of the Supreme Court of India, available on the Court's website. The landmark cases cited in this book can be read in full there.
  • Websites of Parliament (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), the Election Commission of India and other constitutional bodies, for rules of procedure, reports and current figures.

docs.title: Introductory books
docs.text:
• NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work (textbook in political science for Class XI). A clear, accessible introduction.
  • Subhash C. Kashyap, Our Constitution: An Introduction to India's Constitution and Constitutional Law (National Book Trust, several editions). A readable short account by a former Secretary-General of the Lok Sabha.
  • Madhav Khosla, The Indian Constitution (Oxford University Press, Oxford India Short Introductions, 2012). A brief, analytical introduction.
  • M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity (McGraw Hill, many editions). A comprehensive reference widely used by students preparing for competitive examinations.

docs.title: Standard textbooks and commentaries
docs.text:
• D. D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India (LexisNexis, many editions). The classic student text.
  • M. P. Jain, Indian Constitutional Law (LexisNexis, many editions). A detailed treatment of constitutional law with extensive case law.
  • H. M. Seervai, Constitutional Law of India (4th edition, in three volumes). A critical commentary by a leading constitutional lawyer.

docs.title: History and interpretation
docs.text:
• Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation (Oxford University Press, 1966). The classic study of the making of the Constitution.
  • Granville Austin, Working a Democratic Constitution: The Indian Experience (Oxford University Press, 1999). The working of the Constitution from 1950 to the 1980s.
  • Sujit Choudhry, Madhav Khosla and Pratap Bhanu Mehta (eds), The Oxford Handbook of the Indian Constitution (Oxford University Press, 2016). Essays by many scholars on every major area.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
• Report of the Commission on Centre-State Relations (the Sarkaria Commission, 1988).
  • Report of the Commission on Centre-State Relations (the Punchhi Commission, 2010).
  • Reports of the Finance Commissions, which explain the sharing of revenues between the Union and the States.
  • Reports of the Second Administrative Reforms Commission (2005–2009), especially those on governance, local government and ethics.

How to use these sources

Start with an introductory book to get the overall picture, then read the relevant articles of the Constitution itself. When a topic interests you, look up the landmark judgment and read at least its summary and conclusions. For any current figure, such as the number of seats, members or amendments, rely on the official websites rather than on any book, including this one.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms used in this book, with the chapter where each is explained

docs.title: A–B
docs.text: Absolute majority More than half of the total membership of a House, counting vacant seats. Part of the special majority under Article 368. (Chapter 6) Adjournment Suspension of a sitting of a House for a stated time, by the presiding officer. Adjournment sine die ends a sitting without fixing a date for the next. (Chapter 6) Adjournment motion A motion in the Lok Sabha to set aside normal business and discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance; needs the support of 50 members. (Chapter 6) Advisory jurisdiction The power of the Supreme Court under Article 143 to give its opinion on a question referred by the President. (Chapter 7) All-India Services Services common to the Union and the States (the IAS, IPS and Indian Forest Service), recruited by the Union and serving in the States. (Chapter 8) Amendment A change in the text of the Constitution made under Article 368 by addition, variation or repeal. (Chapter 11) Appropriation Bill The bill that authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of the sums voted by the Lok Sabha and charged on the Fund (Article 114). (Chapter 6) Basic structure The essential features of the Constitution that Parliament cannot destroy by amendment, according to Kesavananda Bharati (1973). (Chapter 11) Bicameral Having two Houses. Parliament is bicameral; some State legislatures are bicameral. (Chapters 6, 9)

docs.title: C
docs.text: Cabinet The inner group of senior ministers (Cabinet Ministers) within the Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister. (Chapter 5) Casting vote The vote of a presiding officer used only to break a tie. (Chapter 6) Certiorari A writ by which a higher court quashes an order of a lower court or tribunal made without or in excess of jurisdiction, or with an error of law. (Chapter 3) Charged expenditure Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India by the Constitution or by law, which is not put to the vote of Parliament (Article 112(3)). (Chapter 6) Citizenship Full membership of the State, with civil and political rights. India has a single citizenship. (Chapter 2) Collective responsibility The principle that the Council of Ministers stands or falls together and is answerable as a body to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)). (Chapter 5) Collegium The body of the Chief Justice of India and the senior-most judges of the Supreme Court that recommends appointments of judges. (Chapter 7) Comptroller and Auditor-General (CAG) The constitutional authority that audits the accounts of the Union and the States (Articles 148 to 151). (Chapter 12) Concurrent List List III of the Seventh Schedule; subjects on which both Parliament and the State legislatures may make laws. (Chapter 8) Consolidated Fund of India The fund into which all revenues, loans raised and loan repayments received by the Union are credited, and from which money is spent only under appropriation by law (Article 266). (Chapter 6) Constituent Assembly The body that framed the Constitution between December 1946 and November 1949. (Chapter 1) Constitutional morality A habit of respect for the forms and limits of the Constitution; in later usage, action according to constitutional values. (Chapter 14) Contingency Fund of India A fund at the disposal of the President for unforeseen expenditure pending authorisation by Parliament (Article 267). (Chapter 6) Convention An unwritten rule of political practice regarded as binding by those concerned. (Chapter 14) Cut motion A motion to reduce a demand for grant during the budget: a policy cut, an economy cut or a token cut. (Chapter 6)

docs.title: D–E
docs.text: Delimitation The drawing of constituency boundaries, carried out by a Delimitation Commission whose orders cannot be challenged in court. (Chapter 13) Directive Principles of State Policy The goals for the State in Part IV (Articles 36 to 51), not enforceable by courts but fundamental in governance. (Chapter 4) Dissolution The ending of the life of the Lok Sabha or a State Legislative Assembly, followed by a general election. (Chapter 6) Doctrine of eclipse The rule that a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is overshadowed rather than dead, and revives if the conflict is removed. (Chapter 3) Effective majority More than half of the then members of a House (total membership minus vacancies). (Chapter 6) Election petition The only means of challenging an election to Parliament or a State legislature, filed in the High Court (Article 329). (Chapter 13) Electoral college The body of electors that elects the President (Article 54) or the Vice-President (Article 66). (Chapter 5) Emergency A situation in which the President may exercise extraordinary powers under Part XVIII: national (Article 352), in a State (Article 356) or financial (Article 360). (Chapter 10)

docs.title: F–G
docs.text: Federalism A system in which power is divided between a central government and regional governments by a written constitution. (Chapter 8) Finance Commission The body constituted every five years under Article 280 to recommend the sharing of Union taxes with the States and grants-in-aid. (Chapters 8, 12) Financial bill A bill dealing with fiscal matters that does not meet the strict definition of a money bill (Article 117). (Chapter 6) First past the post An electoral system in which the candidate with the most votes in a single-member constituency wins. (Chapter 13) Fundamental Duties The duties of citizens listed in Article 51A (Part IVA), added in 1976 and 2002. (Chapter 4) Fundamental Rights The rights guaranteed in Part III (Articles 12 to 35), enforceable in the courts. (Chapter 3) Gram Sabha The body of all registered voters of a village (Article 243A). (Chapter 9) GST Council The body of the Union and State finance ministers that recommends rates and rules for the Goods and Services Tax (Article 279A). (Chapter 8)

docs.title: H–L
docs.text: Habeas corpus A writ ordering a person who has detained another to produce the detained person before the court, so that the lawfulness of the detention can be examined. (Chapter 3) Impeachment The quasi-judicial procedure for removing the President for violation of the Constitution (Article 61). (Chapter 5) Joint sitting A sitting of both Houses of Parliament together, called by the President to resolve a deadlock on an ordinary bill (Article 108). (Chapter 6) Judicial review The power of the courts to examine whether laws, executive actions and amendments are consistent with the Constitution, and to declare them void if not. (Chapter 7) Locus standi The right to bring a case to court; relaxed for public interest litigation. (Chapter 3) Lok Adalat A forum for the amicable settlement of disputes under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, whose awards are final. (Chapter 7)

docs.title: M–O
docs.text: Mandamus A writ commanding a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed to perform. (Chapter 3) Model Code of Conduct Guidelines for parties, candidates and governments during elections, enforced by the Election Commission. (Chapter 13) Money bill A bill containing only the matters listed in Article 110, such as taxation and appropriation; it originates in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations. (Chapter 6) No-confidence motion A motion in the Lok Sabha expressing lack of confidence in the Council of Ministers; if adopted, the Council must resign. (Chapters 5, 6) NOTA "None of the Above", an option on voting machines that lets a voter reject all candidates. (Chapter 13) Ordinance A temporary law made by the President (Article 123) or a Governor (Article 213) when the legislature is not in session. (Chapters 5, 9) Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) A status for foreign citizens of Indian origin, giving a lifelong visa and certain rights; not citizenship. (Chapter 2)

docs.title: P–Q
docs.text: Panchayati Raj The system of rural local self-government given constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment (1992). (Chapter 9) Pith and substance The doctrine by which the courts decide which list a law falls under by looking at its true nature, not its incidental effects. (Chapter 8) Pocket veto The President's power to keep a bill pending indefinitely, since Article 111 fixes no time limit. (Chapter 5) Preamble The introduction to the Constitution, stating its source of authority, the nature of the State, its objectives and the date of adoption. (Chapter 2) Preventive detention Detention without trial to prevent a person from acting against security or public order, permitted by Article 22 with safeguards. (Chapter 3) Prohibition A writ by which a higher court forbids a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction in a pending case. (Chapter 3) Prorogation The ending of a session of a House by the President; pending bills do not lapse. (Chapter 6) Public interest litigation (PIL) Litigation brought in the public interest, often on behalf of those unable to approach the court themselves. (Chapters 3, 7) Quo warranto A writ by which a court inquires into the authority of a person holding a public office. (Chapter 3) Quorum The minimum number of members needed for a sitting; one-tenth of the total membership for each House of Parliament. (Chapter 6)

docs.title: R–S
docs.text: Reasonable classification A classification permitted under Article 14, based on an intelligible differentia with a rational nexus to the object of the law. (Chapter 3) Repugnancy Conflict between a Union law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject; the Union law prevails unless Article 254(2) applies. (Chapter 8) Republic A State whose head is elected rather than hereditary. (Chapter 2) Residuary powers The power to legislate on subjects not in any of the three lists; it belongs to Parliament (Article 248). (Chapter 8) Rule of law The principle that no one is above the law and that government acts only according to law. (Chapter 3) Schedule A part at the end of the Constitution containing lists and details; there are twelve. (Chapter 1) Secularism In the Indian sense, a State with no religion of its own that treats all religions equally and guarantees freedom of religion. (Chapter 2) Separation of powers The division of legislative, executive and judicial functions among separate organs; applied in India in a modified form. (Chapter 14) Simple majority More than half of the members present and voting. (Chapter 6) Single transferable vote A preferential voting system used for indirect elections in India, in which votes are transferred according to voters' rankings. (Chapters 5, 13) Sovereign Free from any external authority in internal and external affairs. (Chapter 2) Speaker The presiding officer of the Lok Sabha (or of a State Legislative Assembly), elected by its members. (Chapter 6) Special majority Under Article 368, a majority of the total membership of a House and two-thirds of the members present and voting. Under Article 249, two-thirds of members present and voting. (Chapters 6, 11) Suspensive veto The President's power to return a bill (other than a money bill) for reconsideration once. (Chapter 5)

docs.title: T–Z
docs.text: Tenth Schedule The anti-defection law, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985). (Chapter 6) Union Territory A territory administered by the President through an administrator (Article 239); some have legislatures. (Chapter 9) Universal adult franchise The right of every adult citizen to vote, without qualification of property, education, sex, religion or caste (Article 326). (Chapters 1, 13) Vote on account An advance grant by the Lok Sabha for part of the financial year, pending the passing of the full budget (Article 116). (Chapter 6) Writ A formal order of a court; the Supreme Court and High Courts issue writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. (Chapter 3) Zero Hour An informal period after Question Hour in which members raise urgent matters without notice. (Chapter 6)

docs.title: Chapter 1: The Making of the Constitution
docs.text:
The Constituent Assembly, its sources and the salient features of the document it produced

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • say what a constitution does and why a newly independent India needed a written one;
  • outline the colonial laws and political demands that led to the Constituent Assembly;
  • describe how the Constituent Assembly was composed, how it worked and how long it took;
  • match the main features of the Constitution with the constitutions and laws they were drawn from;
  • list and explain the salient features of the Constitution;
  • find your way around the document: its Parts, articles and Schedules.

docs.title: 1.1 What a constitution does
docs.text:
Every society that governs itself has to answer a few basic questions. Who makes the rules? Who carries them out? Who settles disputes about them? What may those in power never do? How are they chosen, and how are they removed? A constitution is the set of fundamental rules that answers these questions. It creates the organs of government, gives each its powers, sets limits on those powers and states the relationship between the government and the people.

Some countries have constitutions that are not written down in a single document. The United Kingdom is the usual example: its constitution is spread across Acts of Parliament, court judgments and long-standing conventions. Most countries, and India among them, have a written constitution: one document, adopted at a particular moment, that stands above ordinary law. A law that conflicts with it can be struck down by the courts.

Why did India, in particular, need a written constitution in 1947? There were at least four reasons.

  1. Legitimacy. Until 1947 India was governed under laws made by the British Parliament. A free country needed a framework that came from its own people.
  2. Diversity. India was, and is, a country of many religions, languages, castes and regions. A written document could set out guarantees that every group could rely on, and that no temporary majority could quietly take away.
  3. Federation. Power had to be divided between a central government and the provinces (soon to be States), and the princely states had to be brought in. A division of power needs a written text that both sides can point to.
  4. Social change. The leaders of the national movement wanted the new State to end untouchability, reduce inequality and widen opportunity. A constitution could commit the State to these goals.

Key idea

A constitution is the supreme law of a country. It creates and limits the institutions of government, and it states the basic relationship between the State and the people. In India, any law or executive action that conflicts with the Constitution can be declared void by the courts.

docs.title: 1.2 The road to the Constituent Assembly
docs.text:
The Constitution did not appear from nowhere. For nearly a century before 1947, India had been governed under a series of laws passed by the British Parliament, and each of them left something behind.

Law What it introduced Government of India Act, 1858 Transferred rule from the East India Company to the British Crown; a Secretary of State for India in London. Indian Councils Act, 1861 Associated a few Indians, nominated by the government, with law-making. Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley–Minto reforms) Enlarged legislative councils with some elected members; introduced separate electorates for Muslims. Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu–Chelmsford reforms) Dyarchy in the provinces (some subjects run by ministers answerable to the legislature, others reserved); a bicameral central legislature. Government of India Act, 1935 A proposed All-India Federation with lists of federal, provincial and concurrent subjects; provincial autonomy; a Federal Court; public service commissions. Indian Independence Act, 1947 Ended British rule; created the dominions of India and Pakistan; gave each Constituent Assembly full power.

Table 1.1. Colonial laws that shaped Indian government before 1950.

The Government of India Act, 1935 was by far the most important of these. It was a long and detailed law, and many of its administrative arrangements passed into the Constitution: the lists of subjects, the office of Governor, the Federal Court (which became the Supreme Court), the public service commissions and the emergency powers. The federation it proposed never came into being, because the princely states did not join, but provincial autonomy did operate from 1937.

Alongside these laws ran a political demand that Indians should write their own constitution. The Nehru Report of 1928, prepared by a committee of the All Parties Conference under Motilal Nehru, was an early Indian attempt at a constitution, with a list of fundamental rights. In 1935 the Indian National Congress formally demanded a Constituent Assembly elected by the people. The British government accepted the idea in principle during the Second World War, and after the war the Cabinet Mission of 1946 laid down how the Assembly was to be formed.

The Cabinet Mission plan

The Cabinet Mission, three members of the British Cabinet, came to India in 1946. Its plan of May 1946 proposed a Constituent Assembly elected not directly by the people but by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies, with seats allotted to each province roughly in proportion to its population, and divided among the main communities. Representatives of the princely states were to be nominated by their rulers.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
Under the Cabinet Mission plan the Assembly was to have 389 members: 296 from the provinces of British India and 93 from the princely states. The elections to the provincial seats were held in July and August 1946. Because the provincial legislatures had themselves been elected on a limited franchise, the Assembly was indirectly elected and not by universal adult suffrage. It was nevertheless broadly representative: it included members of every major religious community, of the Scheduled Castes, of the tribal areas, and fifteen women.

The Muslim League, after first taking part in the elections, boycotted the Assembly. When the country was partitioned in August 1947, the members from the areas that went to Pakistan left to form Pakistan's own Constituent Assembly, and the strength of the Indian Assembly fell to 299.

docs.title: Working
docs.text:
The Assembly met for the first time on 9 December 1946. Dr Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member, was its temporary chairman, and on 11 December Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected its permanent President. Sir B. N. Rau, a senior civil servant and jurist, was appointed constitutional adviser; he prepared the first draft from which the Drafting Committee worked.

On 13 December 1946 Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution. It stated that India would be an independent sovereign republic, that all power and authority would come from the people, and that the Constitution would secure to all the people justice, equality and freedom, with adequate safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas and depressed classes. The Assembly adopted it on 22 January 1947. The Objectives Resolution is the ancestor of the Preamble, and the two should be read together.

The Assembly did much of its work through committees. The most important were the Union Powers Committee and the Union Constitution Committee (both chaired by Nehru), the Provincial Constitution Committee and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas (both chaired by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel), and the Steering Committee and Rules of Procedure Committee (chaired by Rajendra Prasad).

On 29 August 1947 the Assembly set up the Drafting Committee, with Dr B. R. Ambedkar as its chairman. Its seven members were B. R. Ambedkar, N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, K. M. Munshi, Syed Mohammad Saadullah, B. L. Mitter (later replaced by N. Madhava Rau) and D. P. Khaitan (who died in 1948 and was replaced by T. T. Krishnamachari). The Committee published a draft in February 1948. The public, the provincial governments and members were invited to comment, and the draft was then debated clause by clause.

The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949, a day now observed as Constitution Day. The members signed the document on 24 January 1950, and on the same day the Assembly elected Rajendra Prasad as the first President of India. The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. The date was chosen because on 26 January 1930 the Congress had celebrated Purna Swaraj (complete independence) day.

The whole process took a little under three years: two years, eleven months and eighteen days from the first sitting to adoption.

Figure 1.1 The making of the Constitution. A timeline of the making of the Constitution, from the Cabinet Mission plan of May 1946 to the Constitution coming into force on 26 January 1950.

A body with two roles

After independence, under the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the Constituent Assembly also served as the legislature of the Dominion of India. It met as a constitution-making body on some days and as an ordinary legislature on others. After 26 January 1950 it continued as the Provisional Parliament until the first Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha were constituted after the general elections of 1951–52.

Common confusion

Not every provision came into force on 26 January 1950. Article 394 brought some provisions into force on the day of adoption, 26 November 1949. Among them were the provisions on citizenship, elections, the Provisional Parliament and certain temporary and transitional provisions. These were needed to prepare for the new system.

docs.title: How the Assembly decided
docs.text:
The Assembly was dominated by members of the Congress, but it was not a one-party body in its thinking. Members held very different views on almost every question: a strong or weak Centre, the place of religion, the official language, property rights, the protection of minorities. Most decisions were reached through long debate and compromise rather than by narrow votes. The historian Granville Austin, in his study of the Assembly, described its method as decision by consensus and accommodation. The debates were recorded in full and published as the Constituent Assembly Debates; they are still read by courts trying to understand what a provision was meant to do.

Worked example 1.1: Reading the timeline

Question. A classmate says: "The Constitution was made after independence, so the Constituent Assembly must have been elected by free India." Is this right?

Answer. No. The Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission plan and elected in July–August 1946, a year before independence, by the members of provincial legislatures who had themselves been elected under the Government of India Act, 1935 on a limited franchise. It first met on 9 December 1946. After independence on 15 August 1947 it continued its work, now as the sovereign constitution-making body of the Dominion of India, with full power under the Indian Independence Act, 1947.

docs.title: 1.4 The sources of the Constitution
docs.text:
The framers studied the constitutions of many countries. They were not trying to be original for its own sake; they wanted what had been shown to work, adapted to Indian conditions. Dr Ambedkar defended this openly in the Assembly: there was nothing to be ashamed of in borrowing, he argued, since nobody holds a patent on the fundamental ideas of a constitution.

Source Features drawn from it Government of India Act, 1935 Federal scheme and lists of subjects, office of Governor, judiciary, public service commissions, emergency provisions, many administrative details United Kingdom Parliamentary government, rule of law, legislative procedure, single citizenship, cabinet system, prerogative writs, parliamentary privileges, bicameralism United States Fundamental rights, independence of the judiciary, judicial review, impeachment of the President, removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges, post of Vice-President Ireland Directive Principles of State Policy, nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha, method of election of the President Canada Federation with a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, appointment of State Governors by the Centre, advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court Australia Concurrent List, freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse, joint sitting of the two Houses Weimar Germany Suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency Former USSR Fundamental Duties, the ideal of social, economic and political justice in the Preamble France Republic, and the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble South Africa Procedure for amendment of the Constitution, election of members of the Rajya Sabha Japan "Procedure established by law" in Article 21

Table 1.2. The main sources of the Constitution, as usually listed.

Borrowed, but not copied

The table can give the impression that the Constitution is a patchwork. It is better read as a synthesis. Each borrowed idea was changed to fit India. Judicial review came from the United States, but Indian courts were not given the American "due process" clause in Article 21. Parliamentary government came from Britain, but the Indian Parliament is not sovereign as the British Parliament is: it is limited by a written Constitution and by Fundamental Rights. The Directive Principles came from Ireland, but they were made far more detailed.

Worked example 1.2: Tracing a provision to its sources

Question. The emergency provisions of Part XVIII allow the President to proclaim an emergency, and during it the enforcement of some Fundamental Rights can be suspended. Where do these ideas come from?

Answer. Two sources meet here. The general structure of emergency powers, by which the Centre takes over powers normally exercised by the provinces, comes from the Government of India Act, 1935. The idea that Fundamental Rights may be suspended during an emergency comes from the Weimar Constitution of Germany. The framers combined them, and later amendments (especially the 44th Amendment of 1978, discussed in Chapter 10) added safeguards that neither source had.

docs.title: 1.5 Salient features of the Constitution
docs.text: The features below are the ones that give the Indian Constitution its character. Each will be studied in detail later; here the aim is the overall picture.

docs.title: The lengthiest written constitution
docs.text: The Constitution as adopted had 395 articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules. Amendments have added many articles (numbered with letters, such as 21A or 243ZH, so that the original numbering is kept) and four Schedules; there are now 12 Schedules and well over 450 articles. It is the longest written national constitution in the world. The reasons are many: the country's size and diversity; the inclusion of the constitutions of the States in the same document; detailed provisions on administration borrowed from the 1935 Act; long lists of rights and directives; and special provisions for particular regions and groups.

docs.title: Rigid and flexible at once
docs.text: A rigid constitution needs a special procedure to be amended; a flexible one can be amended like an ordinary law. The Indian Constitution is a mixture. Some provisions can be changed by a simple majority of Parliament; most need a special majority of both Houses; and a few, those that affect the federal structure, also need the consent of half the States. Chapter 11 explains the three procedures.

docs.title: Federal, with a unitary bias
docs.text: The Constitution sets up two levels of government, the Union and the States, divides powers between them in three lists, and makes the Constitution supreme and the judiciary independent. These are federal features. But it also gives the Centre more power than a classic federation would: a single citizenship, Governors appointed by the Centre, residuary powers with the Union, the power to change State boundaries, and emergency powers that can make the system unitary for a time. The word "federation" does not appear in the text; Article 1 calls India a Union of States. Chapter 8 discusses how to describe this design.

docs.title: Parliamentary government
docs.text: At both the Union and State levels the Constitution adopts the British parliamentary system: a nominal head (the President or Governor), a real executive (the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister or Chief Minister) drawn from the legislature and collectively responsible to the lower House. The framers preferred this to the American presidential system because, in their view, it gave daily accountability rather than periodic accountability.

docs.title: Parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy, balanced
docs.text: In Britain, Parliament is sovereign and courts cannot strike down its laws. In the United States, the courts can strike down laws on broad grounds. India takes a middle path. Parliament can amend most of the Constitution, but the courts can review both laws and amendments. Since Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Parliament cannot amend the basic structure of the Constitution (Chapter 11).

docs.title: An integrated and independent judiciary
docs.text: There is a single hierarchy of courts, with the Supreme Court at the top, High Courts in the States and subordinate courts below them, enforcing both Union and State laws. Unlike the United States, India has no separate federal and state court systems. The independence of judges is protected by security of tenure, fixed service conditions and the difficulty of removal.

docs.title: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties
docs.text: Part III guarantees Fundamental Rights that can be enforced in court. Part IV lays down Directive Principles of State Policy, goals for the State that cannot be enforced in court but are fundamental in the governance of the country. Part IVA, added in 1976, lists Fundamental Duties of citizens. Chapters 3 and 4 study all three.

docs.title: A secular State
docs.text: The Constitution gives no religion a special status. It guarantees freedom of conscience and religion to all persons, forbids discrimination on grounds of religion, and forbids taxes for the promotion of any particular religion. The word "secular" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976), but the secular character of the State was present in the original text, and the Supreme Court has held it to be part of the basic structure.

docs.title: Universal adult franchise
docs.text: Every adult citizen has the right to vote, without any qualification of property, education, sex, religion or caste (Article 326). This was a bold step in 1950, in a country where most people could not read; many older democracies had extended the vote gradually. The voting age was 21 at first and was lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment (1988).

docs.title: Single citizenship
docs.text: Although India is federal, there is only one citizenship, the citizenship of India. There is no separate State citizenship, as there is in the United States.

docs.title: Independent bodies
docs.text: The Constitution sets up bodies that are meant to work independently of the government of the day: the Election Commission, the Comptroller and Auditor-General, the Union and State Public Service Commissions, and the Finance Commission, among others (Chapter 12).

docs.title: Emergency provisions
docs.text: Three kinds of emergency are provided for: a national emergency (Article 352), failure of constitutional machinery in a State (Article 356) and a financial emergency (Article 360). Chapter 10 explains each.

docs.title: Three tiers of government
docs.text:
The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to panchayats in rural areas and municipalities in urban areas, creating a third tier of government below the Union and the States (Chapter 9).

Key idea

Almost every salient feature of the Constitution is a balance: rigid and flexible, federal and unitary, parliamentary sovereignty and judicial review, individual rights and social goals. When you are asked to "describe" a feature, state both sides of the balance.

docs.title: 1.6 Finding your way around the document
docs.text:
The Constitution is divided into Parts, each covering a subject, and each Part into articles. The Schedules at the end contain lists and details that would clutter the main text.

Part Subject Articles I The Union and its territory 1–4 II Citizenship 5–11 III Fundamental Rights 12–35 IV Directive Principles of State Policy 36–51 IVA Fundamental Duties 51A V The Union (executive, Parliament, judiciary, CAG) 52–151 VI The States 152–237 VIII The Union Territories 239–242 IX The Panchayats 243–243O IXA The Municipalities 243P–243ZG XI Relations between the Union and the States 245–263 XII Finance, property, contracts and suits 264–300A XIV Services under the Union and the States 308–323 XV Elections 324–329 XVIII Emergency provisions 352–360 XX Amendment of the Constitution 368

Table 1.3. Selected Parts of the Constitution. (Part VII, on the former Part B States, was repealed in 1956.)

Schedule Contents First Names of the States and Union Territories and their territories Second Emoluments and allowances of the President, Governors, presiding officers, judges and the CAG Third Forms of oaths and affirmations Fourth Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha Fifth Administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes Sixth Administration of tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram Seventh The Union, State and Concurrent Lists Eighth Languages recognised by the Constitution (22 at present; 14 originally) Ninth Laws protected from challenge on certain grounds (added 1951) Tenth Disqualification on the ground of defection (added 1985) Eleventh Subjects for panchayats (added 1992) Twelfth Subjects for municipalities (added 1992)

Table 1.4. The twelve Schedules.

Worked example 1.3: Locating a provision

Question. Where in the Constitution would you look for (a) the rule on who may become a citizen at the commencement of the Constitution, (b) the list of subjects on which a State legislature may make laws, and (c) the procedure for disqualifying a legislator who changes party?

Answer. (a) Part II, Articles 5 to 11, on citizenship. (b) The State List, which is List II of the Seventh Schedule; the general rule that States legislate on it is in Article 246 in Part XI. (c) The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985), read with Articles 102(2) and 191(2).

docs.title: 1.7 Criticisms and responses
docs.text:
The Constitution has had its critics from the start. The main criticisms, and the usual answers to them, are these.

  • "A borrowed constitution." Critics said it contained little that was original. The answer is that the framers borrowed deliberately, chose with care and adapted what they took; the combination is distinctively Indian.
  • "A carbon copy of the 1935 Act." Large administrative portions do follow the 1935 Act. But the 1935 Act had no fundamental rights, no universal franchise and no responsible government at the Centre, and its purpose was to preserve British control. The Constitution's purpose was the opposite.
  • "Too long and too detailed." Some argued that a constitution should state principles and leave details to law. The framers answered that in a new democracy, details left to ordinary law could be manipulated, and that putting them in the Constitution gave them protection.
  • "Not representative." The Assembly was indirectly elected on a limited franchise and dominated by one party. In reply, it is pointed out that it included every major group, that its debates were open and recorded, and that the first general elections, held under the new Constitution on universal adult franchise, endorsed the system it created.
  • "Un-Indian." Some members wished the Constitution had been built on village self-government and Indian traditions. This criticism was partly met later by the 73rd and 74th Amendments on local government.

Summary

  • A constitution creates, empowers and limits the organs of government. India chose a single written constitution, supreme over ordinary law.
  • Colonial laws, above all the Government of India Act, 1935, shaped the administrative framework; the national movement supplied the demand for rights, democracy and self-rule.
  • The Constituent Assembly, formed under the Cabinet Mission plan of 1946, first met on 9 December 1946, was led by Rajendra Prasad, drafted through a committee chaired by B. R. Ambedkar, and adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949. It came into force on 26 January 1950.
  • The framers drew on many sources: the 1935 Act, the United Kingdom, the United States, Ireland, Canada, Australia and others.
  • Salient features include length, a mix of rigidity and flexibility, a federal system with a unitary bias, parliamentary government, judicial review limited by the basic structure doctrine, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Duties, secularism, universal adult franchise, single citizenship, independent bodies, emergency provisions and three tiers of government.

docs.title: 1.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give two reasons why the Constituent Assembly could not be described as directly elected by the people of India.

Answer

First, its provincial members were elected by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies, not by voters directly. Second, those legislatures had themselves been elected on a limited franchise under the Government of India Act, 1935, so most adults had no vote at all. (The representatives of the princely states were, in addition, nominated.)

Exercise 2

On what dates was the Constitution (a) adopted, (b) signed by the members, and (c) brought fully into force? Why was the last date chosen?

Answer

(a) 26 November 1949; (b) 24 January 1950; (c) 26 January 1950. The date 26 January was chosen because the Congress had observed 26 January 1930 as Purna Swaraj (complete independence) day.

Exercise 3

Name the source of each feature: (a) Directive Principles of State Policy; (b) residuary powers with the Centre; (c) the Concurrent List; (d) Fundamental Duties; (e) the procedure for amending the Constitution.

Answer

(a) Ireland; (b) Canada; (c) Australia; (d) the former USSR; (e) South Africa.

Exercise 4

Explain, in about 100 words, why the Indian Constitution is said to have "a federal system with a unitary bias".

Answer

The Constitution has the main federal features: two levels of government, a written and supreme constitution, a division of powers in the Seventh Schedule, an independent judiciary to settle disputes, and the need for State consent to amend federal provisions. But it gives the Centre more power than a classic federation: residuary powers belong to the Union, Governors are appointed by the Centre, Parliament can alter State boundaries by ordinary law, there is a single citizenship and an integrated judiciary, the Rajya Sabha does not give States equal representation, and emergency provisions can make the system unitary for a time. Hence "federal with a unitary bias".

Exercise 5

What was the Objectives Resolution, who moved it, and how is it related to the Preamble?

Answer

It was a resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in the Constituent Assembly on 13 December 1946 and adopted on 22 January 1947. It declared India's resolve to become an independent sovereign republic, all authority coming from the people, with justice, equality and freedom for all and safeguards for minorities and backward groups. Its ideals were later expressed, in shorter form, in the Preamble.

Exercise 6

The original Constitution had 8 Schedules; there are now 12. Name the four added Schedules and say what each contains.

Answer

Ninth (1951): laws protected from challenge on certain grounds. Tenth (1985): disqualification on the ground of defection. Eleventh (1992): subjects for panchayats. Twelfth (1992): subjects for municipalities.

docs.text:

Exercise 3

Exercise 4
