docs.title: Chapter 2: The Preamble, the Union and Citizenship
docs.text:
The ideals of the Constitution, the territory of India and who belongs to it

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • quote the Preamble and identify its four parts;
  • explain each key word of the Preamble and the words added in 1976;
  • state how the Supreme Court has answered the question whether the Preamble is part of the Constitution and whether it can be amended;
  • explain Articles 1 to 4 and how new States are formed;
  • describe the citizenship provisions of Part II;
  • apply the rules of the Citizenship Act, 1955 on acquiring and losing citizenship to simple cases;
  • explain what Overseas Citizenship of India is and what the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 provides.

docs.title: 2.1 The Preamble
docs.text:
A preamble is an introduction. It states the purpose of the document that follows and the spirit in which it should be read. The Preamble to the Constitution of India is short enough to quote in full. As amended in 1976, it reads:

The Preamble to the Constitution of India

WE, THE PEOPLE OF INDIA, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens:

JUSTICE, social, economic and political;

LIBERTY of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship;

EQUALITY of status and of opportunity;

and to promote among them all

FRATERNITY assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation;

IN OUR CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do HEREBY ADOPT, ENACT AND GIVE TO OURSELVES THIS CONSTITUTION.

Source: the Constitution of India, as amended by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976.

The Preamble is based on the Objectives Resolution moved by Jawaharlal Nehru in December 1946 (Chapter 1). It can be read as four statements, shown in Figure 2.1.

Figure 2.1 The structure of the Preamble. The Preamble read as four parts: the source of authority (the people of India), the nature of the State (sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic), the objectives (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity) and the date of adoption (26 November 1949).
  1. The source of authority. "We, the people of India" says that the Constitution draws its authority from the people, not from any king, foreign parliament or assembly acting on its own account.
  2. The nature of the Indian State. India is to be a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic.
  3. The objectives. Justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
  4. The date of adoption. 26 November 1949.

Key idea

The Preamble tells you where the Constitution's authority comes from (the people), what kind of State it creates (a sovereign socialist secular democratic republic), what it aims at (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity) and when it was adopted (26 November 1949).

docs.title: 2.2 The key words of the Preamble
Sovereign
docs.text: India is sovereign: it is not subject to any external authority, and it is free to conduct its own internal and external affairs. India remained a member of the Commonwealth after becoming a republic, under an arrangement agreed in 1949 by which the British monarch is recognised only as a symbol of the free association of its members. This membership is voluntary and does not limit India's sovereignty.

docs.title: Socialist
docs.text: The word socialist was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), although many Directive Principles already pointed in that direction. Indian socialism is usually described as democratic socialism: the aim of reducing inequality of income, status and opportunity is to be pursued by democratic means, in a mixed economy where public and private sectors coexist. It does not mean the abolition of private property. Economic policy has changed a great deal since 1991, towards a larger role for markets, but the word remains in the Preamble as a statement of the goal of social and economic justice.

docs.title: Secular
docs.text: Secular was also added in 1976. The Indian idea of secularism is not a wall between religion and the State. It means that the State has no religion of its own, treats all religions with equal respect, does not discriminate on grounds of religion, and guarantees freedom of religion to all, subject to public order, morality and health. The State may, however, regulate secular activities connected with religion and carry out social reform (Article 25(2)). The Supreme Court held in S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) that secularism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution.

docs.title: Democratic
docs.text: Democratic means that the government draws its authority from the will of the people, expressed through periodic elections held on universal adult franchise. India is a representative democracy, in which the people elect representatives who make laws and hold the executive to account. The Preamble's wider objectives show that the framers meant more than political democracy: they wanted social and economic democracy as well.

docs.title: Republic
docs.text: A republic is a State whose head is elected rather than hereditary. India's head of State, the President, is elected indirectly for a fixed term of five years. The word also means that all public offices are open to every citizen without discrimination, and that there is no privileged class.

docs.title: Justice, liberty, equality, fraternity
docs.text:
• Justice in three forms. Social justice means equal treatment of all citizens without distinctions based on caste, religion, sex or race, and the removal of disadvantages. Economic justice means that differences of wealth and income should not become unjust. Political justice means equal political rights: the vote, access to office and a voice in government.
  • Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship. Liberty does not mean licence: the Fundamental Rights that give it effect are subject to reasonable restrictions.
  • Equality of status and of opportunity: no special privileges for any section, and equal chances for all. Articles 14 to 18 put this into practice.
  • Fraternity, a sense of common brotherhood, assuring two things: the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation. The word "integrity" was added by the 42nd Amendment.

The 42nd Amendment and the Preamble

The Preamble has been amended only once, by the 42nd Amendment (1976), which added three words: socialist, secular and integrity. The date of adoption in the last paragraph was not changed.

docs.title: 2.3 The Preamble's legal status
docs.text:
Two questions about the Preamble have come before the Supreme Court.

Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution? In the Berubari Union reference (1960), the Court said that the Preamble shows the general purposes of the framers and is a key to their minds, but that it is not part of the Constitution. In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), a larger bench took the opposite view: the Preamble is part of the Constitution, and it is of great importance in interpreting the rest of the text. The Court repeated this in LIC of India v. Consumer Education and Research Centre (1995).

Can the Preamble be amended? Since it is part of the Constitution, Kesavananda Bharati held that it can be amended under Article 368, but, like every other part, only so far as the amendment does not destroy the basic structure. The 42nd Amendment's additions have not been held to violate the basic structure.

Two further points are settled.

  • The Preamble is not a source of power for the legislature, nor a limit on its power. A law cannot be challenged only on the ground that it conflicts with the Preamble.
  • The Preamble is not enforceable in a court. It is used to interpret articles that are ambiguous: where words can bear two meanings, the one more consistent with the Preamble is preferred.

Common confusion

Students often write that the Preamble "is not part of the Constitution". That was the view in Berubari (1960), and it was overruled by Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The present position is that the Preamble is part of the Constitution, can be amended subject to the basic structure, and is not enforceable on its own.

docs.title: 2.4 The Union and its territory
docs.text: Part I of the Constitution (Articles 1 to 4) deals with the territory of India.

docs.title: Article 1: a Union of States
docs.text:
Article 1(1) begins: "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States." Dr Ambedkar explained the choice of words in the Constituent Assembly. The Indian federation was not the result of an agreement among States, as the American one was, and no State has the right to secede. The Union is indestructible; the States, whose boundaries can be changed by Parliament, are not.

Under Article 1(3), the territory of India comprises the territories of the States, the Union Territories specified in the First Schedule, and such other territories as may be acquired. "Territory of India" is thus wider than "Union of States", which covers the States only.

docs.title: Articles 2 and 3: new States and changes to existing ones
docs.text:
• Article 2 allows Parliament, by law, to admit into the Union, or establish, new States on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit. It refers to territories that were not part of India. Sikkim, which became a State in 1975 by the 36th Amendment, is the main example.
  • Article 3 allows Parliament, by law, to form a new State by separating territory from a State or by uniting States or parts of States, to increase or diminish the area of any State, and to alter the boundaries or name of any State.

Article 3 lays down a procedure. A bill under it can be introduced in Parliament only on the recommendation of the President. Before recommending it, the President must refer the bill to the legislature of the affected State for its views within a period the President specifies. Parliament is not bound by those views: it may go ahead even if the State legislature objects.

docs.title: Article 4: not an amendment
docs.text:
Article 4 says that laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not amendments of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368, even though they change the First and Fourth Schedules. They are passed by a simple majority, like ordinary laws. This is one of the clearest unitary features of the Constitution: Parliament can redraw the map of the States without their consent.

Ceding territory is different

Article 3 lets Parliament diminish the area of a State, but not hand Indian territory to a foreign country. In the Berubari Union reference (1960) the Supreme Court held that cession of territory needs a constitutional amendment under Article 368. The 9th Amendment (1960) was passed for Berubari, and the 100th Amendment (2015) gave effect to the land boundary agreement with Bangladesh, under which enclaves were exchanged. Settling a boundary dispute, as distinct from ceding territory, does not need an amendment.

docs.title: How the map changed
docs.text:
At the commencement of the Constitution, the States were grouped into four categories (Part A, B, C and D). The demand for States based on language grew quickly. After a popular movement, Andhra State was formed in 1953 for Telugu speakers. The government then appointed the States Reorganisation Commission (1953) under Fazl Ali. On its report, the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, together with the 7th Amendment, abolished the four categories and created 14 States and 6 Union Territories, largely along linguistic lines.

Year Change 1960 Bombay State divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat 1963 Nagaland 1966 Punjab reorganised; Haryana formed; Chandigarh a Union Territory 1971 Himachal Pradesh becomes a State 1972 Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya become States 1975 Sikkim becomes a State (36th Amendment) 1987 Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa become States 2000 Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand (then Uttaranchal) and Jharkhand 2014 Telangana formed from Andhra Pradesh 2019 State of Jammu and Kashmir reorganised into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and of Ladakh 2020 Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu merged into one Union Territory

Table 2.1. Main changes to the States and Union Territories since 1956.

At the time of writing there are 28 States and 8 Union Territories. The Union Territories are the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Delhi (the National Capital Territory), Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, and Puducherry.

Worked example 2.1: Forming a new State

Situation. A region within a large State demands a State of its own. The State's legislature passes a resolution opposing the division. Can Parliament create the new State, and how?

Answer. Yes. Under Article 3, a bill to form the new State is introduced in Parliament on the recommendation of the President. Before recommending it, the President refers it to the State legislature for its views within a fixed time. The legislature's opposition must be heard but does not bind Parliament. The bill is passed by a simple majority in each House, and by Article 4 it is not treated as a constitutional amendment, though it will amend the First Schedule (the list of States) and the Fourth Schedule (seats in the Rajya Sabha). This is how Telangana was created in 2014.

docs.title: 2.5 Citizenship under the Constitution
docs.text:
A citizen is a full member of the State, with all civil and political rights. An alien is a citizen of another country. Some rights in the Constitution belong to citizens only:

  • the Fundamental Rights in Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30;
  • the right to vote in elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies (Article 326);
  • the right to be a member of Parliament or of a State legislature;
  • eligibility for certain offices: President, Vice-President, judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court, Governor, Attorney General, Comptroller and Auditor-General, and Advocate General.

India has a single citizenship. A person is a citizen of India, not of a State; all citizens enjoy the same rights wherever they live in the country (subject to special provisions for some regions).

docs.title: Part II: citizenship at the commencement
docs.text:
Part II (Articles 5 to 11) does not set out a full law of citizenship. It only says who were citizens on 26 January 1950, and leaves everything else to Parliament.

Article Who it covers 5 Persons domiciled in India at the commencement who were born in India, or either of whose parents was born in India, or who had been ordinarily resident in India for at least five years 6 Persons who migrated to India from Pakistan, if they or a parent or grandparent were born in undivided India; those who came before 19 July 1948 became citizens if ordinarily resident since, those who came later had to be registered 7 Persons who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 were not citizens, unless they returned under a permit for resettlement 8 Persons of Indian origin living abroad could be registered as citizens by Indian diplomatic or consular representatives 9 A person who voluntarily acquired the citizenship of a foreign State was not a citizen 10 Every citizen continues to be a citizen, subject to any law made by Parliament 11 Parliament has the power to make any provision on the acquisition and termination of citizenship

Table 2.2. Articles 5 to 11.

Under Article 11, Parliament enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955, which is the main source of citizenship law today. It has been amended several times, notably in 1986, 1992, 2003, 2005, 2015 and 2019.

Citizenship provisions came first

Articles 5 to 9 came into force on 26 November 1949, the day the Constitution was adopted, not on 26 January 1950. It was necessary to know who the citizens were before the new system started.

docs.title: Five ways of acquiring citizenship
docs.text:
The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides five ways.

1. By birth. The rule depends on the date of birth, because Parliament has tightened it twice.

Born in India Citizen by birth if... On or after 26 January 1950 and before 1 July 1987 always, whatever the nationality of the parents On or after 1 July 1987 and before 3 December 2004 either parent was a citizen of India at the time of birth On or after 3 December 2004 both parents are citizens, or one parent is a citizen and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of birth

Table 2.3. Citizenship by birth under Section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.

Children of foreign diplomats posted in India and of enemy aliens born in occupied territory do not acquire citizenship by birth.

2. By descent. A person born outside India may be a citizen by descent if a parent was an Indian citizen at the time of birth. (For births before 10 December 1992 only the father's citizenship counted; for births since then, either parent's does.) Since 2004, the birth must be registered at an Indian consulate, normally within one year.

3. By registration. Certain persons may apply to be registered as citizens: for example, persons of Indian origin who have been ordinarily resident in India for seven years, persons married to citizens of India who have been ordinarily resident for seven years, and minor children of citizens. Illegal migrants cannot be registered.

4. By naturalisation. A foreigner who is not an illegal migrant may be granted a certificate of naturalisation if he or she has lived in India for twelve months immediately before applying and for eleven years in all during the fourteen years before that, is of good character, knows a language of the Eighth Schedule and intends to live in India. The person must renounce his or her previous citizenship. The government may waive conditions for a person who has rendered distinguished service to science, philosophy, art, literature, world peace or human progress.

5. By incorporation of territory. When a foreign territory becomes part of India, the Government of India specifies by order which persons of that territory become citizens. This was done, for example, when Goa, Daman and Diu, and Puducherry became part of India.

Worked example 2.2: Citizenship by birth

Decide whether each person is a citizen of India by birth.

  1. A child born in Kolkata in March 1985 to two parents who are citizens of Nepal living in India legally (neither is a diplomat).
  2. A child born in Pune in May 1995 to the same kind of parents.
  3. A child born in Chennai in 2012 to a father who is a citizen of India and a mother who is a German citizen living in India on a valid visa.
  4. A child born in Delhi in 2012 to a father who is a citizen of India and a mother who entered India without valid documents.

Answers.

  1. Yes. Born before 1 July 1987: birth in India is enough.
  2. No. Born between 1 July 1987 and 3 December 2004: at least one parent must have been a citizen. Neither was. (The child may still acquire citizenship later by another route.)
  3. Yes. Born after 3 December 2004: one parent is a citizen and the other, being in India on a valid visa, is not an illegal migrant.
  4. No, not by birth. One parent is a citizen, but the other is an illegal migrant at the time of birth. (The child may be eligible for citizenship by registration as the minor child of a citizen.)

docs.title: Three ways of losing citizenship
docs.text:
• Renunciation. A citizen of full age and capacity who is also a citizen of another country may renounce Indian citizenship by declaration. Minor children of that person also cease to be citizens, but may resume citizenship within a year of turning eighteen.
  • Termination. A citizen who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country ceases to be an Indian citizen automatically. India does not allow dual citizenship.
  • Deprivation. The Central Government may, by order, deprive a person of citizenship acquired by registration or naturalisation (not by birth) on grounds such as fraud in obtaining it, disloyalty to the Constitution, unlawful dealings with an enemy during war, or certain prison sentences or long residence abroad within a few years of acquiring it.

Key idea

Citizenship at the commencement is in the Constitution (Articles 5 to 9); everything after that is in the Citizenship Act, 1955, made under Article 11. Acquisition: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory. Loss: renunciation, termination, deprivation.

docs.title: Overseas Citizenship of India
docs.text:
Many people of Indian origin have taken the citizenship of other countries, and so lost Indian citizenship. To keep their connection with India, Parliament created the status of Overseas Citizen of India (OCI), introduced in 2005. In 2015 the older Person of Indian Origin (PIO) card scheme was merged into it. Broadly, a foreign citizen who was, or whose parent, grandparent or great-grandparent was, a citizen of India (or eligible to become one in 1950), and the foreign spouse of a citizen or OCI cardholder in certain cases, may be registered as an OCI cardholder. Persons who are or were citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh, or whose ancestors were, are excluded.

OCI is not dual citizenship. An OCI cardholder receives a lifelong visa and may live and work in India, but does not have the right to vote, to be elected, to hold constitutional offices or, as a rule, to buy agricultural land.

docs.title: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019
docs.text:
The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 provides that persons belonging to the Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi or Christian communities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh or Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014 are not to be treated as illegal migrants, and it reduces the residence period for their naturalisation from eleven years to five. Tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura covered by the Sixth Schedule, and areas under the Inner Line Permit system, are excluded. The rules under the Act were notified in March 2024.

The Act has been strongly debated. Its supporters describe it as a humanitarian measure for religious minorities facing persecution in neighbouring countries. Its critics argue that classification by religion is inconsistent with equality before the law (Article 14) and with secularism. Petitions challenging its validity were filed in the Supreme Court; check the current position before relying on any statement about them.

Assam and Section 6A

Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, inserted in 1985 after the Assam Accord, contains special rules for persons who came to Assam from what is now Bangladesh before 25 March 1971. A Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld its validity in 2024.

Summary

  • The Preamble states the source of the Constitution's authority (the people), the nature of the State (sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic), its objectives (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity) and the date of adoption (26 November 1949).
  • "Socialist", "secular" and "integrity" were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), the only amendment of the Preamble.
  • The Preamble is part of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, overruling Berubari, 1960); it can be amended subject to the basic structure; it is neither a source of power nor enforceable in court, but it guides interpretation.
  • India is a Union of States (Article 1). Parliament can form new States and change boundaries and names by ordinary law under Article 3, after hearing the views of the State legislature; such laws are not amendments (Article 4). Ceding territory needs an amendment.
  • Part II deals only with citizenship at the commencement; the Citizenship Act, 1955 governs the rest: acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory, and loss by renunciation, termination and deprivation.
  • India has single citizenship and no dual citizenship; OCI is a status for foreign citizens of Indian origin, not citizenship.

docs.title: 2.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Which three words were added to the Preamble in 1976, and by which amendment?

Answer

Socialist, secular and integrity, by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

Exercise 2

In about 80 words, explain the meaning of "secular" in the Indian Constitution, and how it differs from a strict separation of State and religion.

Answer

Indian secularism means that the State has no religion of its own, treats all religions with equal respect, does not discriminate on the ground of religion, and protects every person's freedom of conscience and religion. It is not a strict wall of separation: the State may regulate secular activities associated with religion, carry out social reform, and give aid to educational institutions run by religious groups on equal terms. The emphasis is on equal treatment and principled distance rather than total non-involvement.

Exercise 3

A student says, "Parliament needs the consent of a State legislature before changing that State's boundaries." Correct the statement.

Answer

Under Article 3, the President must refer the bill to the State legislature for its views, but Parliament is not bound by those views. Consent is not required. The bill is introduced on the President's recommendation and passed by a simple majority; under Article 4 it is not a constitutional amendment.

Exercise 4

Why did the Berubari case need a constitutional amendment, when Parliament can alter the boundaries of States by ordinary law?

Answer

Article 3 allows Parliament to redraw boundaries among the States of India, but transferring Indian territory to a foreign country (cession) is not covered by it. The Supreme Court held in the Berubari Union reference (1960) that cession requires an amendment under Article 368; hence the 9th Amendment (1960).

Exercise 5

A child is born in India in 2008. Her mother is a citizen of India; her father is a citizen of Sri Lanka who is living in India on a valid work visa. Is she a citizen by birth? Give the rule.

Answer

Yes. For births on or after 3 December 2004, a child born in India is a citizen by birth if both parents are citizens, or if one parent is a citizen and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of birth. The father is lawfully in India, so he is not an illegal migrant.

Exercise 6

List three rights or privileges that an Indian citizen has and an OCI cardholder does not.

Answer

Any three of: the right to vote; the right to be elected to Parliament or a State legislature; eligibility for constitutional offices such as President, Vice-President or judge of the Supreme Court; and, as a rule, the right to buy agricultural land. (The Fundamental Rights reserved for citizens, such as those in Article 19, are also not available to OCI cardholders, who are foreign citizens.)

docs.title: 2.9 Quiz
docs.text:
Check yourself: Preamble, Union and citizenship

Exercise 1

Which case held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution?

  1. Berubari Union (1960)
  2. Golaknath (1967)
  3. Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
  4. Minerva Mills (1980)
Answer

Kesavananda Bharati (1973)

Exercise 2

How many times has the Preamble been amended?

  1. Never
  2. Once
  3. Twice
  4. Three times
Answer

Once

Only by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

Exercise 3

Article 1 says: India, that is Bharat, shall be a ___ of States.

Answer

Union

Exercise 4

A bill to form a new State can be introduced in Parliament only on the recommendation of whom?

  1. The Prime Minister
  2. The President
  3. The Speaker
  4. The State Governor
Answer

The President

Exercise 5

A person born in India in 1980 to two foreign parents (not diplomats) is...

  1. a citizen by birth
  2. not a citizen by birth
  3. a citizen only if registered
  4. an OCI cardholder
Answer

a citizen by birth

For births before 1 July 1987, birth in India was enough.

Exercise 6

Which of these is NOT a way of losing Indian citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955?

  1. Renunciation
  2. Termination
  3. Deprivation
  4. Residence in another State of India
Answer

Residence in another State of India

Exercise 7

Match each Preamble word with its meaning.

ABSovereignNo State religionRepublicCommon brotherhoodSecularFree from external controlFraternityElected head of State Answer

Sovereign — Free from external control; Republic — Elected head of State; Secular — No State religion; Fraternity — Common brotherhood

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
How India is governed, and how to read this book

Current as of late 2026

Current as of late 2026; constitutional law changes: check the latest official text (the Constitution of India as published by the Legislative Department) before relying on details. Numbers of seats, the count of amendments and the position on questions still before the courts are the details most likely to change.

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
This book explains how India is governed. It starts from the document at the centre of the whole system, the Constitution of India, and follows it outwards into the institutions it creates: the President and the Council of Ministers, Parliament, the courts, the States, the panchayats and municipalities, the Election Commission and the other bodies that keep the system honest. Along the way it explains the rights the Constitution guarantees to every person, the goals it sets for the State, and the ways in which the Constitution itself can be changed and has been changed.

The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. It is a long document, and it can feel like a list of articles to be memorised. This book tries to show it instead as a working design. Every provision answers a question that the framers had to face: who should choose the head of state, how a law should be made, what should happen when the Centre and a State disagree, what a citizen can do when a right is taken away. When you know the question, the answer is much easier to remember, and much easier to judge.

The book is neutral. It describes the Constitution, the main judgments of the Supreme Court and the arguments on each side of the debates that surround them. It does not take sides between political parties, and where a question is still disputed it says so.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The book is written for a reader who is meeting the subject for the first time:

  • a student in a first university course in political science, law or public administration;
  • a candidate preparing for a competitive examination with a paper on polity;
  • a school leaver, a teacher, a journalist or any citizen who wants to understand the system they live in.

No background is needed beyond school. Legal words are explained the first time they appear, and the glossary at the end collects them.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
The fourteen chapters follow the order in which the system is usually built up in the mind.

Part of the subject Chapters Foundations: how the Constitution was made, its Preamble, the Union and citizenship 1, 2 Rights and goals: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties 3, 4 The organs of the Union: executive, Parliament, judiciary 5, 6, 7 The federal design: Centre and States, State governments, local government 8, 9 Changing and protecting the system: emergencies, amendment and the basic structure 10, 11 Watchdogs and the people: constitutional bodies, elections and parties 12, 13 Putting it together: the Constitution in practice 14

Table P.1. The plan of the book.

docs.title: How each chapter is built
docs.text:
Every chapter has the same parts, so that you always know where you are.

  • Learning outcomes at the top say what you should be able to do when you have finished.
  • Numbered sections explain the topic, starting from the reason a provision exists and moving to its exact terms: the article number, who acts, what majority is needed.
  • Boxes pick out what matters. A key idea box states the one thing in a section not to forget. A note adds a detail or a piece of history. A caution marks a common confusion, the kind that costs marks in examinations.
  • Worked examples take a situation (a bill rejected by one House, a State asking for more money, a person arrested at night) and walk through how the Constitution deals with it.
  • Figures and tables show structures and comparisons that are hard to hold in words.
  • A summary collects the chapter in a few points.
  • Exercises come with answers folded under them. Try each one before you open the answer.
  • A short quiz at the end lets you check yourself; it remembers your answers in your browser.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Read the chapters in order the first time: later chapters lean on earlier ones. Keep a copy of the Constitution beside you; the official text is published by the Legislative Department of the Ministry of Law and Justice and can be read free of charge. When the book cites an article, look it up and read the actual words. The articles are usually short, and reading them is the single best habit you can form.

Three further habits help.

  1. Ask who decides. For any provision, find out which person or body acts, on whose advice, and who can check them.
  2. Count the majority. Many provisions turn on the kind of majority needed: a simple majority of those present and voting, a majority of the total membership, or two-thirds of those present and voting. Chapter 6 explains the differences, and they come back in almost every chapter after it.
  3. Separate the text from the interpretation. Much of Indian constitutional law is found not in the text but in what the Supreme Court has said the text means. The book marks clearly which is which.

docs.title: A note on numbers and names
docs.text: Articles are written as "Article 21" and parts of an article as "Article 19(1)(a)". Amendments are named by number and year, for example "the 42nd Amendment (1976)"; the year is the year of the amending Act. Court cases are cited by their short names, with the year of the judgment, for example Kesavananda Bharati (1973). The book avoids naming present holders of offices, since they change; it names historical figures where they are part of the story.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Government in the States and Local Government
docs.text:
The Governor, the Chief Minister, State legislatures, Union Territories, and panchayats and municipalities

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe the appointment, term, powers and position of the Governor, and distinguish the Governor's constitutional and situational discretion;
  • explain the role of the Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers;
  • describe the composition and powers of the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council, and how a Council is created or abolished;
  • outline how Union Territories are governed and list the main special provisions for particular States and areas;
  • trace the history of local government in India up to the 73rd and 74th Amendments;
  • state the compulsory and voluntary provisions of the 73rd Amendment and the main provisions of the 74th Amendment;
  • discuss the strengths and weaknesses of local government in practice.

docs.title: 9.1 The State executive: the Governor
docs.text: Part VI of the Constitution (Articles 152 to 237) deals with the States. The design follows that of the Union closely: a nominal head (the Governor), a real executive (the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister) responsible to the lower House of the legislature, a legislature, and a High Court. The differences lie mainly in the Governor's office.

docs.title: Appointment, term and removal
docs.text:
There is a Governor for each State, though the same person may be appointed Governor of two or more States (Article 153, as amended by the 7th Amendment, 1956). The Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal (Article 155), that is, in practice, by the Union government. The Governor must be a citizen and at least 35 years old (Article 157), must not be a member of a legislature or hold any office of profit (Article 158), and takes the oath before the Chief Justice of the State's High Court.

The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President (Article 156). The normal term is five years, but the Governor may resign earlier or be removed by the President at any time, and continues in office until a successor takes over. The Constitution lays down no grounds or procedure for removal.

The pleasure doctrine and its limits

In B. P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010), the Supreme Court held that although the President's pleasure can be withdrawn at any time without giving reasons, it cannot be withdrawn arbitrarily, capriciously or unreasonably. A Governor cannot be removed merely because he or she is out of sympathy with the policies of the Union government or because a different party has come to power at the Centre. If a removal is challenged, the courts can examine it on limited grounds.

Two conventions are commonly followed in appointments: the Governor should be from outside the State, and the Chief Minister of the State should be consulted. The Sarkaria Commission recommended both, along with the suggestion that Governors should be eminent persons not closely connected with active politics.

docs.title: The Governor's powers
docs.text:
The Governor's formal powers mirror the President's.

  • Executive. All executive action of the State is taken in the Governor's name. The Governor appoints the Chief Minister and, on the Chief Minister's advice, the other ministers; the Advocate General; the State Election Commissioner; and the chairman and members of the State Public Service Commission (who can, however, be removed only by the President).
  • Legislative. The Governor summons and prorogues the State legislature and can dissolve the Legislative Assembly; addresses the legislature; nominates one-sixth of the members of the Legislative Council, where there is one; gives or withholds assent to bills, returns them for reconsideration, or reserves them for the President (Article 200); and promulgates ordinances when the legislature is not in session (Article 213), on the same terms as the President's under Article 123.
  • Financial. Money bills are introduced only with the Governor's recommendation; the State budget is laid before the legislature in the Governor's name; the Governor constitutes a State Finance Commission every five years for panchayats and municipalities.
  • Judicial. Under Article 161, the Governor can grant pardons and other forms of clemency for offences against State laws. The Governor is consulted by the President in appointing High Court judges, and appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court.

docs.title: Discretion
docs.text:
Article 163 says that the Governor shall act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers "except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions or any of them in his discretion", and that the Governor's decision on whether a matter falls within his discretion is final. This is a real difference from the President, who has no such clause.

The Governor's constitutional discretion covers matters such as:

  • reserving a bill for the consideration of the President (Article 200);
  • recommending President's rule by reporting to the President that the government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution (Article 356);
  • acting as administrator of an adjoining Union Territory, if so appointed;
  • certain functions under the Sixth Schedule, for example determining the amount payable by the State to an autonomous district council from mining royalties;
  • special responsibilities under Article 371 and related articles in some States, such as Nagaland, Manipur, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh, and for development boards in parts of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka;
  • seeking information from the Chief Minister on administrative and legislative matters (Article 167).

Like the President, the Governor also has situational discretion: in appointing a Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority in the Assembly, in dismissing a ministry that has lost the confidence of the Assembly and refuses to resign, and in deciding whether to dissolve the Assembly in such a situation.

Discretion is not a licence

The courts have narrowed the Governor's discretion. In S. R. Bommai (1994), the Supreme Court held that the majority of a ministry must be tested on the floor of the House, not by the Governor's personal assessment. In Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016), it held that the Governor cannot, on his own, summon or advance a session of the Assembly or interfere in its internal proceedings, except in limited circumstances. The Governor's role, the Court has repeatedly said, is that of a constitutional head who acts on ministerial advice save where the Constitution clearly says otherwise.

Worked example 9.1: A bill on the Governor's desk

Situation. The Legislative Assembly of a State with no Legislative Council passes a bill (not a money bill) that the Governor believes would reduce the powers of the High Court. What may the Governor do?

Answer. Under Article 200, the Governor has four options: assent; withhold assent; return the bill (with a message) for reconsideration, in which case, if the legislature passes it again, the Governor cannot withhold assent; or reserve it for the President. But for a bill that would so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger its constitutional position, Article 200 makes reservation compulsory: the Governor must not assent to it, but must reserve it for the consideration of the President. The President may then assent or withhold assent, or direct that it be returned to the legislature for reconsideration (Article 201). On the question of time limits for these decisions, see the note in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 9.2 The Chief Minister and the Council of Ministers
docs.text:
The Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor (Article 164); by convention, the Governor appoints the leader of the party or coalition with a majority in the Legislative Assembly. The other ministers are appointed by the Governor on the Chief Minister's advice. A non-member may be appointed a minister but must become a member of the legislature within six months.

Under the 91st Amendment (2003), the total number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, must not exceed 15 per cent of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly, but must not be less than twelve (Article 164(1A)). The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly (Article 164(2)). The Chief Minister must communicate the decisions of the Council to the Governor and furnish information the Governor asks for (Article 167).

The Chief Minister's position in the State resembles that of the Prime Minister at the Centre: head of the Council of Ministers, leader of the majority in the Assembly, chief adviser to the Governor, and the chief spokesperson of the State government. In addition, the Chief Minister represents the State in bodies such as the Inter-State Council, the Governing Council of NITI Aayog and the Zonal Councils.

The Advocate General (Article 165) is the State's highest law officer. He or she must be qualified to be a High Court judge, is appointed by the Governor and holds office during the Governor's pleasure, and has the right to speak in the State legislature without a vote.

docs.title: One House or two
docs.text:
Every State has a Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha). Some States also have a Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad), forming a bicameral legislature (Article 168). At the time of writing, six States have Councils: Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.

A Council may be created or abolished by Parliament by law, if the Legislative Assembly of the State passes a resolution to that effect by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting (Article 169). Such a law is not a constitutional amendment for the purposes of Article 368 and is passed by a simple majority.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
• The Legislative Assembly consists of not more than 500 and not less than 60 members, directly elected from territorial constituencies (Article 170). Some small States have been allowed fewer members by law; for example, Sikkim's Assembly has 32 members and those of Goa and Mizoram have 40. Its normal term is five years, and it may be dissolved earlier. Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and (after the next delimitation) one-third will be reserved for women.
  • The Legislative Council has not more than one-third of the total membership of the Assembly and not less than 40 members (Article 171). It is a permanent body; one-third of its members retire every second year, and each serves six years. Its members are chosen as follows:
Share Chosen by One-third Members of local bodies (municipalities, district boards and similar authorities) One-twelfth Graduates of at least three years' standing residing in the State One-twelfth Teachers of at least three years' standing in institutions of secondary level or higher One-third Members of the Legislative Assembly, from among persons who are not members of the Assembly One-sixth (the rest) Nominated by the Governor from persons with special knowledge or practical experience of literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service

Table 9.1. Composition of a Legislative Council.

The minimum age is 25 for the Assembly and 30 for the Council. The presiding officers are the Speaker (and Deputy Speaker) of the Assembly and the Chairman (and Deputy Chairman) of the Council, each elected by the House from among its members.

docs.title: The Council's limited powers
docs.text:
The Legislative Council is much weaker than the Rajya Sabha.

  • A money bill can be introduced only in the Assembly. The Council must return it within 14 days, with recommendations that the Assembly may accept or reject, as in Parliament.
  • For an ordinary bill passed by the Assembly, if the Council rejects it, or does not pass it within three months, or proposes amendments the Assembly does not accept, the Assembly may pass it again. If the Council then rejects it, or does not pass it within one month, or proposes unacceptable amendments, the bill is deemed passed in the form the Assembly passed it the second time (Article 197). The Council can therefore delay an ordinary bill by at most about four months, but cannot stop it.
  • There is no joint sitting in a State legislature.
  • The Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Assembly.

Worked example 9.2: How long can a Council delay a bill?

Situation. A bill passed by the Assembly of a bicameral State is sent to the Council on 1 March. The Council does nothing. What happens?

Answer. If the Council has not passed the bill within three months, by about 1 June, the Assembly may pass it again (with or without amendments suggested by the Council). Suppose it does so on 10 June and sends it back. If the Council again does nothing for one month, by about 10 July, the bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form in which the Assembly passed it the second time. It then goes to the Governor for assent. The Council has delayed the bill but not defeated it.

docs.title: Union Territories
docs.text:
Union Territories are administered by the President through an administrator appointed by the President, with whatever designation the President chooses, such as Lieutenant Governor or Administrator (Article 239). Parliament can make laws for them on any subject, including subjects in the State List.

Three Union Territories have legislatures and councils of ministers.

  • Delhi, the National Capital Territory, under Article 239AA (inserted by the 69th Amendment, 1991), has a Legislative Assembly that may make laws on State and Concurrent List subjects except public order, police and land. The relationship between the elected government and the Lieutenant Governor has been the subject of Constitution Bench judgments of the Supreme Court (in 2018 and 2023) and of later legislation by Parliament.
  • Puducherry has a legislature created by Parliament under Article 239A.
  • Jammu and Kashmir became a Union Territory with a legislature under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.

The other Union Territories (the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Ladakh and Lakshadweep) have no legislature.

Article 370

Article 370, a "temporary provision" in Part XXI, gave the former State of Jammu and Kashmir a special status: most provisions of the Constitution applied to it only as modified by Presidential orders, with the concurrence of the State government, and it had its own constitution. In August 2019, by a Presidential order and a resolution of Parliament, all provisions of the Constitution were applied to Jammu and Kashmir and the special status ended; the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 divided the State into two Union Territories. In In re Article 370 of the Constitution (December 2023), a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld these steps and directed that elections to the Legislative Assembly be held, which took place in 2024.

docs.title: Special provisions for some States
docs.text:
Articles 371 to 371J contain special provisions for particular States, reflecting historical agreements and regional needs. Examples:

  • Article 371: development boards for regions of Maharashtra and Gujarat, for which the Governor has special responsibility.
  • Article 371A: in Nagaland, no Act of Parliament on the religious or social practices of the Nagas, Naga customary law and procedure, civil and criminal justice according to customary law, or the ownership and transfer of land applies unless the State Assembly so decides.
  • Articles 371B to 371I: provisions for Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh (and Telangana), Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa.
  • Article 371J (98th Amendment, 2012): a development board and reservation in education and employment for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region.

docs.title: Scheduled and tribal areas
docs.text:
• The Fifth Schedule deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. A Tribes Advisory Council advises on tribal welfare, and the Governor may direct that a law shall not apply, or apply with modifications, to a Scheduled Area, and may make regulations for its peace and good government.
  • The Sixth Schedule provides for autonomous district councils in the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, with powers to make laws on matters such as land, forests, inheritance and social customs, to administer justice in certain cases, and to levy some taxes.

docs.title: 9.5 Local government: the background
docs.text:
Democracy is not complete if it stops at the Union and the States. Many matters of daily life, such as drinking water, local roads, sanitation, primary schools and markets, are best handled close to the people who use them. Local self-government means the management of local affairs by bodies elected by the local people.

Local bodies have a long history in India. Village councils existed in many forms for centuries. In the colonial period, a resolution of 1882 associated with the Viceroy Lord Ripon encouraged elected local boards, and Ripon is often called the father of local self-government in India. The Constitution as adopted, however, mentioned village panchayats only in a Directive Principle, Article 40, which asks the State to organise them and give them the powers needed to function as units of self-government. Local government was a State subject, and its fortunes depended on each State's laws.

Year Step 1952–53 Community Development Programme and National Extension Service launched 1957 Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommends "democratic decentralisation" through a three-tier system: gram panchayat (village), panchayat samiti (block) and zila parishad (district) 1959 Rajasthan becomes the first State to establish Panchayati Raj (inaugurated at Nagaur on 2 October 1959) 1977–78 Ashok Mehta Committee recommends a two-tier system and open participation of political parties 1986 L. M. Singhvi Committee recommends constitutional recognition of panchayats 1989 64th Amendment Bill passed by the Lok Sabha but defeated in the Rajya Sabha 1992 73rd and 74th Amendments passed 1993 73rd Amendment in force on 24 April 1993 (now National Panchayati Raj Day); 74th on 1 June 1993

Table 9.2. Milestones in local government.

By the 1980s, panchayats had declined in many States: elections were postponed for years, bodies were superseded, and they had little money or power. The 73rd and 74th Amendments were designed to give local bodies constitutional status, regular elections and a guaranteed share in power.

docs.title: 9.6 Panchayats: the 73rd Amendment
docs.text:
The 73rd Amendment (1992) added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243-O), titled "The Panchayats", and the Eleventh Schedule, which lists 29 subjects that may be devolved to panchayats. Its provisions are of two kinds: compulsory provisions, which every State law must include, and voluntary provisions, which States may adopt at their discretion.

Figure 9.1 Rural and urban local government. The structure of local government. Rural (Part IX): the Gram Sabha of all voters, and above it the gram panchayat, the panchayat samiti (intermediate level, which may be omitted in small States) and the zila parishad. Urban (Part IXA): nagar panchayats for transitional areas, municipal councils for smaller urban areas and municipal corporations for larger ones, with ward committees where the population is 3 lakh or more.

docs.title: Compulsory provisions
docs.text:
• Gram Sabha (Article 243A): a body of all persons registered on the electoral rolls of a village, exercising such powers as the State legislature gives it.
  • Three tiers (Article 243B): panchayats at the village, intermediate and district levels. A State with a population not exceeding 20 lakh need not have the intermediate level.
  • Direct election of all members at all levels (Article 243C). The chairpersons of the intermediate and district panchayats are elected indirectly, by and from among the elected members.
  • Minimum age of 21 years for membership (Article 243F).
  • Reservation (Article 243D): seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their share of the population, at every level; not less than one-third of the seats (including those reserved for SCs and STs) for women; and reservation of the offices of chairpersons for SCs, STs and women in the same way. Many States have raised the reservation for women to one-half.
  • Term of five years (Article 243E). If a panchayat is dissolved earlier, elections must be held within six months.
  • State Election Commission (Article 243K) to conduct panchayat elections, appointed by the Governor and removable only like a High Court judge.
  • State Finance Commission (Article 243I), constituted by the Governor every five years, to review the finances of panchayats and recommend the sharing of State taxes and grants.
  • Audit of panchayat accounts as provided by State law (Article 243J), and a bar on courts interfering in electoral matters except through election petitions (Article 243-O).

docs.title: Voluntary provisions
docs.text:
• representation of members of Parliament and of the State legislature in panchayats;
  • reservation of seats and offices for backward classes;
  • the extent to which panchayats are given powers and functions to work as institutions of self-government, including the preparation and implementation of plans on the subjects of the Eleventh Schedule (Article 243G);
  • the financial powers of panchayats to levy taxes, duties, tolls and fees (Article 243H).

Key idea

The 73rd Amendment made the existence, elections, reservations and term of panchayats compulsory, and created State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions to protect them. But how much power and money panchayats actually get is left to each State, and this is where practice differs most.

The Eleventh Schedule's 29 subjects include agriculture and land improvement, minor irrigation, animal husbandry and fisheries, social forestry and minor forest produce, small-scale and cottage industries, rural housing, drinking water, roads, rural electrification, poverty alleviation, primary and secondary education, adult education, libraries, health and sanitation, women and child development, social welfare, the public distribution system and the maintenance of community assets.

docs.title: Exemptions and PESA
docs.text:
Under Article 243M, Part IX does not apply to Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram, to the Scheduled Areas and the tribal areas of the Sixth Schedule, and to certain hill areas, which have their own institutions. Parliament extended Part IX to the Fifth Schedule areas, with modifications, by the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, known as PESA. It gives the Gram Sabha in these areas special powers: for example, to safeguard community resources and customary modes of dispute resolution, to approve development plans, to be consulted before land is acquired, and to own minor forest produce.

Worked example 9.3: Reserving seats in a panchayat

Situation. A gram panchayat has 15 elected seats. Scheduled Castes form 20 per cent and Scheduled Tribes 7 per cent of the village population. The State law provides only the minimum reservation for women required by the Constitution. How many seats must be reserved?

Answer.

  • Scheduled Castes: in proportion to population, as nearly as may be: \(0.20 \times 15 = 3\) seats.
  • Scheduled Tribes: \(0.07 \times 15 = 1.05\), so 1 seat.
  • Women: at least one-third of the total, \(\tfrac{1}{3} \times 15 = 5\) seats. Within the SC seats, at least one-third must go to SC women: one of the three SC seats. (For a single ST seat, one-third is less than one; States handle such fractions through their rules, usually by rotating the women's seat between elections.) The seats for SC and ST women count towards the total of five, so at least four further seats, or three if the ST seat also goes to a woman, are reserved for women from the general seats.

Reserved seats are rotated among the wards of the panchayat at successive elections.

docs.title: 9.7 Municipalities: the 74th Amendment
docs.text:
The 74th Amendment (1992) added Part IXA (Articles 243P to 243ZG), titled "The Municipalities", and the Twelfth Schedule, which lists 18 subjects for municipalities. Its provisions parallel those for panchayats, with features suited to towns and cities.

  • Three kinds of municipality (Article 243Q): a Nagar Panchayat for an area in transition from rural to urban, a Municipal Council for a smaller urban area, and a Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area. The Governor decides the category, considering population, density, revenue, employment in non-agricultural activities and other factors. An industrial township may be exempted.
  • Composition (Article 243R): members directly elected from wards. The State may also provide for representation of persons with special knowledge of municipal administration (without voting rights), and of MPs and MLAs.
  • Ward committees (Article 243S) in municipalities with a population of three lakh or more.
  • Reservation for SCs, STs and women (not less than one-third) on the same lines as panchayats (Article 243T).
  • Term of five years, with elections within six months of a premature dissolution (Article 243U).
  • The State Finance Commission and State Election Commission serve municipalities as well (Articles 243Y and 243ZA).
  • A District Planning Committee in every district consolidates the plans of panchayats and municipalities (Article 243ZD).
  • A Metropolitan Planning Committee prepares a draft development plan for each metropolitan area, defined as an area with a population of ten lakh or more (Article 243ZE).

The Twelfth Schedule's 18 subjects include urban planning, regulation of land use and construction of buildings, roads and bridges, water supply, public health, sanitation and solid waste management, fire services, urban forestry and the environment, slum improvement, urban poverty alleviation, parks and playgrounds, burial and cremation grounds, registration of births and deaths, public amenities such as street lighting, and slaughterhouses.

Feature Panchayats (73rd) Municipalities (74th) Part and articles IX, 243–243-O IXA, 243P–243ZG Schedule and subjects Eleventh, 29 Twelfth, 18 Structure Three tiers: village, intermediate, district Three types by size: nagar panchayat, municipal council, municipal corporation Assembly of all voters Gram Sabha None (ward committees in large cities) Planning body District Planning Committee District and Metropolitan Planning Committees In force 24 April 1993 1 June 1993

Table 9.3. The 73rd and 74th Amendments compared.

Other urban bodies exist outside Part IXA, such as cantonment boards (under the Cantonments Act, 2006), township authorities, port trusts and special-purpose agencies for housing or water supply.

docs.title: 9.8 Local government in practice
docs.text:
Three decades after the 73rd and 74th Amendments, local government is far more firmly established than before. Regular elections have been held in most States, and several million representatives are elected to local bodies, a large share of them women and members of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Many observers see this as one of the largest experiments in grassroots democracy anywhere.

The weaknesses are usually summarised as the problem of the three Fs: functions, funds and functionaries.

  • Functions. Many States have not transferred the Eleventh and Twelfth Schedule subjects in full, or have kept parallel State bodies doing the same work.
  • Funds. Local bodies raise little revenue of their own and depend on grants from the Union and the States, often tied to specific schemes. Finance Commissions at both levels have recommended grants to local bodies, but the recommendations of State Finance Commissions have not always been acted on.
  • Functionaries. Local bodies often lack their own staff and depend on State officials who answer to State departments.

Other concerns include delays in local elections in some States, the influence of family members over women representatives in some places (sometimes called proxy representation), and limited capacity for planning. On the other hand, the reservation of seats has brought large numbers of women and members of disadvantaged groups into public life, and studies have found that this can change the priorities of local spending.

Summary

  • The Governor, appointed by the President and holding office during the President's pleasure (subject to B. P. Singhal, 2010), is the constitutional head of the State and acts on ministerial advice except where the Constitution gives discretion (Article 163), notably in reserving bills and recommending President's rule.
  • The Chief Minister heads a Council of Ministers of at most 15 per cent of the Assembly (minimum 12), collectively responsible to the Assembly.
  • Every State has a Legislative Assembly (60 to 500 members, with exceptions); six have Legislative Councils, created or abolished by Parliament on an Assembly resolution (Article 169). The Council can delay an ordinary bill for about four months and a money bill for 14 days, but cannot defeat either.
  • Union Territories are administered by the President through administrators; Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir have legislatures. Articles 371 to 371J, and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, make special provisions for certain States and tribal areas.
  • After the Balwant Rai Mehta, Ashok Mehta and L. M. Singhvi committees, the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to panchayats (three tiers, Gram Sabha, Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects) and municipalities (three types, Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects), with five-year terms, reservation for SCs, STs and women, State Election Commissions and State Finance Commissions.
  • In practice, local democracy has deepened, but devolution of functions, funds and functionaries remains incomplete.

docs.title: 9.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

How does Article 163 make the Governor's position different from the President's?

Answer

Article 163 says that the Governor acts on ministerial advice "except in so far as he is by or under this Constitution required to exercise his functions ... in his discretion", and that the Governor's decision on whether a matter is within his discretion is final. There is no equivalent clause for the President, who must act on advice under Article 74 (with only the power to return it once).

Exercise 2

Name the six States that have Legislative Councils, and state the procedure for creating a new Council.

Answer

Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh (at the time of writing). The State's Legislative Assembly must pass a resolution by a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of the members present and voting; Parliament then passes a law by simple majority (Article 169). This is not a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

Exercise 3

A State Legislative Assembly has 180 members. What are the maximum and minimum sizes of its Legislative Council, if it has one?

Answer

Maximum: one-third of 180 = 60. Minimum: 40 (Article 171).

Exercise 4

List five compulsory provisions of the 73rd Amendment.

Answer

Any five of: a Gram Sabha in every village; three tiers (village, intermediate, district), with the intermediate tier optional for States with population up to 20 lakh; direct election of members at all levels; indirect election of chairpersons at the intermediate and district levels; minimum age of 21; reservation of seats for SCs and STs in proportion to population; at least one-third of seats and chairpersons' offices for women; a five-year term with elections within six months of dissolution; a State Election Commission; a State Finance Commission every five years.

Exercise 5

What are the three kinds of municipality under the 74th Amendment, and who decides which kind an area gets?

Answer

A Nagar Panchayat (area in transition from rural to urban), a Municipal Council (smaller urban area) and a Municipal Corporation (larger urban area). The Governor specifies the category, considering population, density, revenue, non-agricultural employment and other factors.

Exercise 6

What is PESA, and what does it do?

Answer

The Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996. It extends Part IX of the Constitution, with modifications, to the Fifth Schedule (Scheduled) Areas, and gives the Gram Sabha there special powers, such as safeguarding community resources and customs, approving development plans, being consulted before land acquisition, and owning minor forest produce.

docs.title: 9.10 Quiz
docs.text:
Check yourself: States and local government

Exercise 1

  1. The Chief Minister
  2. The President
  3. The Chief Justice of the High Court

Exercise 2

  1. Article 123
  2. Article 161

Exercise 3

  2. About two months

Exercise 4

Answer

Exercise 5

  1. Ashok Mehta Committee
  2. Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
  3. L. M. Singhvi Committee

Exercise 6

Exercise 7

ABGram SabhaArticle 243KState Finance CommissionArticle 243ZEState Election CommissionArticle 243AMetropolitan Planning CommitteeArticle 243I Answer

Exercise 8
