docs.title: Chapter 7: The Judiciary
docs.text:
The Supreme Court, the High Courts, the subordinate courts and the power of judicial review

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe the integrated structure of the Indian judiciary;
  • explain how judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are appointed, including the collegium system and the fate of the National Judicial Appointments Commission;
  • state the qualifications, tenure and procedure for removal of judges, and the safeguards of judicial independence;
  • classify the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court (original, writ, appellate, advisory) and of the High Courts;
  • explain the meaning, basis and limits of judicial review;
  • describe the subordinate courts, tribunals and Lok Adalats;
  • discuss judicial activism and its critics in a balanced way.

docs.title: 7.1 An integrated judiciary
docs.text:
In a federation like the United States there are two sets of courts: federal courts that apply federal law and state courts that apply state law. India chose differently. It has a single integrated judiciary: one hierarchy of courts, with the Supreme Court at the top, the High Courts below it and the subordinate courts below them. The same courts enforce both Union and State laws. An appeal from a village magistrate's decision can, in principle, travel all the way to the Supreme Court.

Figure 7.1 The hierarchy of courts. The hierarchy of courts. The Supreme Court is at the top, the High Courts below it, and the subordinate courts (district and sessions judges, civil judges and judicial magistrates) below the High Courts. Appeals go upwards, and the law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts.

This design came largely from the Government of India Act, 1935, which had created a Federal Court above the provincial High Courts. The Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, which had been the final court of appeal for India. It was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.

The judiciary has three main functions under the Constitution: it decides disputes between persons and between governments; it is the guardian and final interpreter of the Constitution; and it protects the Fundamental Rights of individuals.

Key idea

India has one integrated hierarchy of courts that applies both Union and State law. At its head, the Supreme Court is the final court of appeal, the guardian of the Constitution, the protector of Fundamental Rights and the arbiter of disputes between the Centre and the States.

docs.title: 7.2 The Supreme Court: composition and appointment
Composition
docs.text:
Article 124 provides for a Supreme Court consisting of a Chief Justice of India and such number of other judges as Parliament may fix by law. The original Constitution provided for seven other judges. Parliament has increased the number several times; since 2019 the sanctioned strength is the Chief Justice and 33 other judges, 34 in all. The Court sits in Delhi, or in such other places as the Chief Justice may decide with the approval of the President (Article 130).

The Chief Justice may, with the President's consent, appoint a High Court judge as an ad hoc judge of the Supreme Court when there is no quorum of permanent judges (Article 127), and may request retired judges to sit and act as judges (Article 128).

docs.title: Qualifications
docs.text:
A person is qualified to be a judge of the Supreme Court if he or she is a citizen of India and

  • has been a judge of a High Court (or of two or more High Courts in succession) for at least five years; or
  • has been an advocate of a High Court (or two or more High Courts in succession) for at least ten years; or
  • is, in the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist.

No minimum age is prescribed.

docs.title: Appointment: from consultation to collegium
docs.text:
Article 124(2) says that judges are appointed by the President after consultation with such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as the President thinks necessary, and that in appointing a judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of India shall always be consulted. The meaning of "consultation" has been the subject of four major cases, known as the Judges cases.

Case Year Holding S. P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges case) 1981 "Consultation" does not mean concurrence; the executive has the final say. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Second Judges case) 1993 Overruled the first case: the opinion of the Chief Justice, formed after consulting senior judges, has primacy. This created the collegium system. In re Special Reference 1 of 1998 (Third Judges case) 1998 On a Presidential reference: the Chief Justice must consult a collegium of the four senior-most judges for Supreme Court appointments (two for High Court appointments). Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (Fourth Judges case) 2015 Struck down the 99th Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act as violating the independence of the judiciary, a part of the basic structure. The collegium system continues.

Table 7.1. The Judges cases.

Under the collegium system as it now works, the Chief Justice of India and the four senior-most judges of the Supreme Court recommend names for appointment to the Supreme Court; for High Courts, the High Court's own collegium recommends names, which are considered by the Supreme Court collegium. The government may return a recommendation for reconsideration once, but if the collegium reiterates it, the appointment should be made. Procedural details are set out in a Memorandum of Procedure agreed between the judiciary and the government.

The 99th Amendment (2014) had sought to replace the collegium with a National Judicial Appointments Commission consisting of the Chief Justice of India, the two senior-most judges, the Union Law Minister and two eminent persons. In the Fourth Judges case (2015), the Supreme Court held, by four to one, that giving the executive and lay members a role that could veto judicial members compromised judicial independence.

A continuing debate

The collegium system is unusual: in few countries do judges in effect choose judges. Its defenders say it protects courts from political influence. Its critics say it lacks transparency and accountability. Even the judgment that struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission acknowledged that the collegium system needed improvement. The question remains open.

By a long-standing convention, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court is appointed Chief Justice of India. The convention was departed from in 1973 and 1977, which led to much criticism, and it has been followed since.

docs.title: Tenure and removal
docs.text:
A Supreme Court judge holds office until the age of 65. He or she may resign by writing to the President, and may be removed only in the manner laid down in Article 124(4): by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament, supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by two-thirds of the members present and voting, presented in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

The procedure is laid down in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968:

  1. A motion for removal must be signed by at least 100 members of the Lok Sabha or 50 members of the Rajya Sabha.
  2. The Speaker or Chairman may admit or refuse it.
  3. If admitted, a three-member committee is set up: the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a Chief Justice of a High Court, and a distinguished jurist. It frames charges and investigates.
  4. If the committee finds the judge guilty, the House takes up the motion. If both Houses pass it by the special majority, an address is presented to the President, who orders removal.

No judge of the Supreme Court has ever been removed. A motion against one judge failed in the Lok Sabha in 1993, and in 2011 a High Court judge resigned after the Rajya Sabha had voted for his removal and before the Lok Sabha took up the motion.

Worked example 7.1: Removing a judge

Situation. A removal motion against a High Court judge, supported by the committee's finding of misbehaviour, is voted on in the Lok Sabha. The House has a total membership of 543. 420 members are present and voting; 300 vote in favour. Is the motion carried in the Lok Sabha?

Answer. Two conditions apply. (1) A majority of the total membership: more than half of 543, that is at least 272. 300 is more than 272, so this is met. (2) Two-thirds of those present and voting: \(\tfrac{2}{3} \times 420 = 280\). 300 is more than 280, so this is met too. The motion is carried in the Lok Sabha. It must also be carried by the same special majority in the Rajya Sabha in the same session before the President can order removal.

docs.title: Safeguards of independence
docs.text:
The framers wanted judges to decide cases without fear of the government. The Constitution protects their independence in several ways:

  • Appointment involves the judiciary itself, not the executive alone.
  • Security of tenure: judges can be removed only by the difficult procedure of Article 124(4).
  • Fixed service conditions: salaries, allowances and rights cannot be varied to a judge's disadvantage after appointment, except during a financial emergency (Article 125).
  • Expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so they are not voted by Parliament (Article 146).
  • No discussion of the conduct of a judge in Parliament or a State legislature, except on a motion for removal (Articles 121 and 211).
  • Ban on practice after retirement: a retired Supreme Court judge may not plead or act before any court or authority in India (Article 124(7)).
  • Power to punish for contempt of itself (Article 129).
  • Separation of the judiciary from the executive (Article 50).

docs.title: 7.3 The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
docs.text:
Jurisdiction means the authority of a court to hear and decide cases. The Supreme Court has several kinds.

Jurisdiction Article(s) What it covers Original 131 Disputes between the Union and one or more States, or between States, involving a legal right Writ 32 Enforcement of Fundamental Rights Appellate 132–134, 136 Appeals in constitutional, civil and criminal cases; special leave to appeal Advisory 143 Opinions on questions referred by the President Court of record 129 Its records are evidence; it can punish for contempt Review 137 Review of its own judgments Other 139A, 141, 142 Transfer of cases; law declared binding on all courts; orders for complete justice

Table 7.2. The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

docs.title: Original jurisdiction (Article 131)
docs.text: The Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction in any dispute between the Government of India and one or more States, between the Government of India and any State or States on one side and one or more other States on the other, or between two or more States, if the dispute involves a question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends. This is the federal function of the Court. It does not extend to disputes arising out of pre-Constitution treaties and similar instruments, and Parliament has excluded inter-State river water disputes, which go to tribunals under a law made under Article 262.

docs.title: Writ jurisdiction (Article 32)
docs.text: As Chapter 3 explained, any person can move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of a Fundamental Right. Strictly, this is part of the Court's original jurisdiction, since the case begins in the Supreme Court, but it is usually treated separately. The High Courts have a concurrent and wider jurisdiction under Article 226.

docs.title: Appellate jurisdiction
docs.text:
The Supreme Court is the highest court of appeal.

  • Constitutional matters (Article 132). An appeal lies from a judgment of a High Court if the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution.
  • Civil matters (Article 133). An appeal lies if the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance that needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.
  • Criminal matters (Article 134). An appeal lies as of right if the High Court has reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death, or has withdrawn a case from a lower court, convicted the accused and sentenced him or her to death; and in other cases if the High Court certifies that the case is fit for appeal.
  • Special leave to appeal (Article 136). The Supreme Court may, in its discretion, grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree or order of any court or tribunal in India, except military tribunals. This is the widest appellate power and the source of most of the Court's appeals.

docs.title: Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143)
docs.text: The President may refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact of public importance on which it is expedient to obtain the Court's opinion. The Court may report its opinion; it is not bound to answer, and its opinion is advisory, not binding on the President. (For disputes arising out of certain pre-Constitution treaties, the Court must give its opinion.) Well-known references include those on the Kerala Education Bill (1958), the Berubari Union (1960), the powers of legislatures over privileges (1964) and judicial appointments (1998). The Court declined to answer a reference made in 1993 on the Ayodhya dispute.

docs.title: Other powers
docs.text:
• Court of record (Article 129). Its judgments are recorded for perpetual memory and testimony and can be cited as precedents, and it can punish for contempt of itself.
  • Review (Article 137). The Court can review its own judgments. Beyond review, it has created the curative petition, which allows a final judgment to be re-examined in rare cases to prevent abuse of process or a gross miscarriage of justice (Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra, 2002).
  • Binding law (Article 141). The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.
  • Complete justice (Article 142). The Court may pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in any matter before it.
  • Constitution benches (Article 145(3)). A case involving a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution must be heard by at least five judges.

Worked example 7.2: Which jurisdiction?

Identify the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court involved in each case.

  1. Two States disagree about whether a law of one of them unlawfully restricts the legal rights of the other over a shared resource (not a river).
  2. A journalist is detained under a preventive detention law and claims that her rights under Articles 21 and 22 have been violated.
  3. The President asks the Court whether a proposed law would be constitutional.
  4. A company loses a tax case in a High Court and wants the Supreme Court to hear an appeal, though the High Court has refused a certificate.

Answers. (1) Original jurisdiction under Article 131. (2) Writ jurisdiction under Article 32 (she could also go to the High Court under Article 226). (3) Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. (4) It can seek special leave to appeal under Article 136, which the Court grants in its discretion.

docs.title: 7.4 The High Courts
docs.text: Article 214 provides that there shall be a High Court for each State, but Article 231 allows Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States and a Union Territory. At the time of writing there are 25 High Courts. Some serve more than one State or Union Territory; for example, the Gauhati High Court serves Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh, and the Punjab and Haryana High Court serves the two States and Chandigarh.

docs.title: Appointment and tenure
docs.text: Each High Court has a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President appoints. The judges are appointed by the President (Article 217) after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State, and, for a judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of the High Court; in practice through the collegium system described above. A judge must be a citizen and have held judicial office in India for ten years or been an advocate of a High Court for ten years. High Court judges retire at 62 (raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment, 1963). They are removed in the same way as Supreme Court judges. The President may transfer a judge from one High Court to another after consulting the Chief Justice of India (Article 222).

docs.title: Jurisdiction
docs.text:
• Original jurisdiction. Some High Courts hear certain civil suits in the first instance, and all hear matters such as election petitions.
  • Writ jurisdiction (Article 226). The High Courts can issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, which makes this jurisdiction wider than the Supreme Court's under Article 32.
  • Appellate jurisdiction. Appeals from district and subordinate courts in civil and criminal matters.
  • Supervisory jurisdiction (Article 227). Superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territory, except military tribunals.
  • Control over subordinate courts (Article 235). Postings, promotions and discipline of district judges and other judicial officers.
  • Court of record (Article 215), with the power to punish for contempt.

In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227 is part of the basic structure; tribunals may supplement the High Courts but cannot exclude their review.

docs.title: 7.5 Subordinate courts, tribunals and Lok Adalats
Subordinate courts
docs.text:
Articles 233 to 237 deal with the subordinate courts. District judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court (Article 233); other judicial officers are appointed by the Governor after consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the High Court (Article 234). The High Court controls the subordinate courts (Article 235).

The structure varies a little from State to State, but in each district the District Judge is the highest judicial authority. When dealing with civil cases he or she is called the District Judge, and when dealing with criminal cases, the Sessions Judge. Below are civil judges (senior and junior division) for civil cases and judicial magistrates, headed by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, for criminal cases. Laws such as the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 provide for village-level courts.

docs.title: Tribunals
docs.text: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Part XIVA. Article 323A allows Parliament to set up administrative tribunals to decide disputes about the recruitment and conditions of service of public servants; the Central Administrative Tribunal was established in 1985. Article 323B allows Parliament and the State legislatures to set up tribunals for other matters, such as taxation, land reform and industrial disputes. After L. Chandra Kumar (1997), the decisions of tribunals can be challenged before a High Court.

docs.title: Lok Adalats
docs.text: Lok Adalats ("people's courts") are forums for the amicable settlement of disputes, given statutory status by the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. They deal with cases pending in courts or at the pre-litigation stage, such as motor accident claims, family disputes and bank recovery cases. Their awards are deemed to be decrees of civil courts and are final; there is no appeal. The same Act sets up legal services authorities at the national, State and district levels to provide free legal aid, giving effect to Article 39A.

docs.title: 7.6 Judicial review
docs.text: Judicial review is the power of the courts to examine whether a law made by a legislature, or an action taken by the executive, is consistent with the Constitution, and to declare it void if it is not. The idea is usually traced to the American case Marbury v. Madison (1803), in which the United States Supreme Court asserted this power although the American Constitution does not mention it expressly.

docs.title: Basis in the Constitution
docs.text:
The Indian Constitution does not use the phrase "judicial review", but the power is plain from several provisions:

  • Article 13: laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void;
  • Articles 32 and 226: the courts' power to enforce Fundamental Rights;
  • Articles 245 and 246, with the Seventh Schedule: the division of legislative power, which the courts must police;
  • Articles 131 to 136 and 143: the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court;
  • Article 254: inconsistency between Union and State laws;
  • Article 372: pre-Constitution laws continue only subject to the Constitution.

docs.title: Grounds
docs.text:
A law can be struck down on three broad grounds:

  1. it violates a Fundamental Right;
  2. it is beyond the competence of the authority that made it (for example, a State law on a Union List subject); or
  3. it is repugnant to another provision of the Constitution.

Executive actions can be struck down for these reasons and also for being illegal, irrational, procedurally unfair or disproportionate.

docs.title: Scope and limits
docs.text:
In the United States, judicial review rests on "due process of law", which allows courts to examine the fairness of laws; Indian courts began with the narrower "procedure established by law" (Chapter 3). Over time, through Maneka Gandhi and later cases, Indian review has become broad. The courts now apply doctrines such as:

  • presumption of constitutionality: a law is presumed valid, and the person challenging it must show otherwise;
  • pith and substance: to decide which list a law falls under, the court looks at its true nature, not its incidental effects (Chapter 8);
  • colourable legislation: what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly;
  • proportionality: a restriction on a right must pursue a legitimate aim, be suitable and necessary for it, and balance the harm against the benefit, a test applied in K. S. Puttaswamy (2017) and other cases.

Since Kesavananda Bharati (1973), even constitutional amendments are subject to review under the basic structure doctrine, discussed in Chapter 11. In Minerva Mills (1980) and L. Chandra Kumar (1997), the Supreme Court held that judicial review itself is part of the basic structure, so it cannot be abolished even by amendment.

Judicial review is not judicial supremacy

Judicial review does not mean that judges may substitute their own policy preferences for those of the legislature. Courts examine the legality and constitutionality of laws, not their wisdom. And in India, Parliament can respond to a judgment by changing the law, or by amending the Constitution, provided the amendment respects the basic structure. The system balances parliamentary sovereignty and judicial review.

docs.title: 7.7 Judicial activism and its critics
docs.text:
From the late 1970s, the Supreme Court and the High Courts became markedly more active. They relaxed the rules of standing to allow public interest litigation (Chapter 3), read many new rights into Article 21, issued detailed guidelines where the legislature had not acted (for example, on sexual harassment at the workplace in Vishaka, 1997, and on arrest in D. K. Basu, 1997), and supervised the implementation of their orders through continuing mandamus.

Supporters of this judicial activism argue that it gave a voice to the poor and powerless, filled gaps left by inactive legislatures and executives, and protected the environment and human rights. Critics argue that courts lack the expertise and democratic accountability to make policy, that some orders have been difficult to implement, and that judicial overreach can upset the separation of powers. Judges themselves have often called for judicial restraint. A balanced view is that activism is justified where it protects constitutional rights that would otherwise go unprotected, and that restraint is wise where questions of policy are properly for elected bodies.

The judiciary also faces practical challenges: a very large backlog of pending cases, vacancies in the courts, delay, and the cost of litigation. Measures such as Lok Adalats, fast-track courts, the use of technology and alternative dispute resolution aim to address them.

docs.title: Landmark cases met in this book
docs.text:
Case Year Principle Chapter A. K. Gopalan 1950 Narrow reading of Article 21 3 Golaknath 1967 Fundamental Rights cannot be amended (later overruled) 11 Kesavananda Bharati 1973 Basic structure doctrine 11 Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain 1975 Free and fair elections part of basic structure 11 Maneka Gandhi 1978 Just, fair and reasonable procedure 3 Minerva Mills 1980 Limited amending power; balance of Parts III and IV 4, 11 Indra Sawhney 1992 Reservations, creamy layer, 50 per cent ceiling 3 S. R. Bommai 1994 Limits on Article 356; secularism and federalism basic 10 K. S. Puttaswamy 2017 Right to privacy 3

Table 7.3. Landmark cases and the chapters where they are discussed.

Summary

  • India has a single integrated judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts and subordinate courts, applying both Union and State law.
  • The Supreme Court has a Chief Justice and up to 33 other judges. Judges are appointed by the President on the recommendation of the collegium (the Chief Justice and four senior-most judges), a system created by the Second and Third Judges cases; the National Judicial Appointments Commission was struck down in 2015.
  • Supreme Court judges retire at 65 (High Court judges at 62) and can be removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity, by the special majority of each House in the same session, under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
  • The Supreme Court's jurisdiction is original (Article 131), writ (32), appellate (132–134, 136), advisory (143), and it is a court of record (129) whose law binds all courts (141) and which can do complete justice (142).
  • High Courts have wide writ jurisdiction under Article 226 and supervise all courts in their territory under Article 227. Subordinate courts are headed in each district by the District and Sessions Judge.
  • Judicial review rests on Articles 13, 32, 226, 245–246 and others; it covers laws, executive action and amendments (through the basic structure doctrine), and is itself part of the basic structure.

docs.title: 7.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court at present, and who fixes it?

Answer

The Chief Justice of India and 33 other judges (34 in all), fixed by Parliament by law under Article 124(1); the present number dates from 2019.

Exercise 2

Summarise in two or three sentences what the Second and Fourth Judges cases decided.

Answer

The Second Judges case (1993) held that in appointments the opinion of the Chief Justice of India, formed after consulting senior judges, has primacy, creating the collegium system. The Fourth Judges case (2015) struck down the 99th Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission as violating the independence of the judiciary, a part of the basic structure, so the collegium system continues.

Exercise 3

Give five constitutional safeguards of the independence of judges.

Answer

Any five of: appointment involving the judiciary; removal only by the special parliamentary procedure for proved misbehaviour or incapacity; service conditions that cannot be varied to their disadvantage (except in a financial emergency); expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund; no discussion of their conduct in legislatures except on a removal motion; ban on practice after retirement; power to punish for contempt; separation of the judiciary from the executive.

Exercise 4

How is the writ jurisdiction of a High Court wider than that of the Supreme Court?

Answer

Under Article 226 a High Court can issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, that is, for ordinary legal rights as well. Under Article 32 the Supreme Court issues writs only for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

Exercise 5

Is the President bound by the Supreme Court's opinion under Article 143? Is the Court bound to give one?

Answer

No to both, in general. The opinion is advisory and does not bind the President, and the Court may decline to answer a reference (as it did with the Ayodhya reference made in 1993). The exception is a dispute arising out of certain pre-Constitution treaties under Article 143(2), on which the Court must give its opinion.

Exercise 6

State the three broad grounds on which a court may declare a law unconstitutional.

Answer

(1) It violates a Fundamental Right; (2) it is outside the legislative competence of the body that made it; (3) it is repugnant to another provision of the Constitution.

docs.text:
Check yourself: the judiciary

Exercise 1

  1. Article 32
  2. Article 131

Answer

Exercise 2

Exercise 3

Exercise 4

  1. Article 129
  2. Article 137
  3. Article 141

Answer

Exercise 5

Answer

Exercise 6

Exercise 7

ABArticle 32Advisory jurisdictionArticle 136Court of recordArticle 143Writ jurisdictionArticle 129Special leave to appeal Answer

docs.title: Chapter 5: The Union Executive
docs.text:
The President, the Vice-President, the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • distinguish the nominal executive from the real executive in a parliamentary system;
  • explain how the President is elected, and compute the value of the votes of legislators in a simple case;
  • state the qualifications, term and procedure for impeachment of the President;
  • describe the President's executive, legislative, financial, judicial, diplomatic, military and emergency powers, including the veto and the ordinance power;
  • explain Article 74 and the situations in which the President may act with some discretion;
  • describe the election, functions and removal of the Vice-President;
  • explain the position and powers of the Prime Minister and the principle of collective responsibility;
  • describe the composition of the Council of Ministers and the role of the Attorney General.

docs.title: 5.1 Two executives
docs.text:
Part V of the Constitution begins with the Union executive (Articles 52 to 78). It consists of the President, the Vice-President, the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers, and the Attorney General.

India has a parliamentary system of government, borrowed from Britain. In such a system there are two executives:

  • a nominal (or formal, or constitutional) executive, in whose name government is carried on: in India, the President;
  • a real executive, which actually takes the decisions: the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister.

The real executive is drawn from the legislature and is collectively responsible to its lower House, the Lok Sabha. It stays in office only so long as it has the confidence of the Lok Sabha. This is the central difference from the presidential system of the United States, where the President is both head of State and head of government, is elected for a fixed term and is not responsible to the legislature.

Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, to be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him. Article 74 then provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at its head to aid and advise the President, who shall act in accordance with that advice. Read together, these two articles create the parliamentary executive.

Key idea

The President is the head of the State; the Prime Minister is the head of the government. Executive power is vested in the President (Article 53), but the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister (Article 74), which is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)).

docs.title: 5.2 The President: election, term and removal
The electoral college
docs.text:
The President is not elected directly by the people. Under Article 54, the President is elected by an electoral college consisting of:

  • the elected members of both Houses of Parliament; and
  • the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, including (since the 70th Amendment, 1992) the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union Territory of Puducherry.

Nominated members of Parliament and of the Assemblies, and members of the State Legislative Councils, do not take part.

Figure 5.1 Electing the President and the Vice-President. The two electoral colleges. The President is elected by the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry), with votes weighted by population. The Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses of Parliament, each vote counting equally.

docs.title: The value of each vote
docs.text:
Article 55 aims at two kinds of fairness. There should be uniformity among the States, so that a legislator from a large State carries more weight than one from a small State in proportion to population; and there should be parity between the States taken together and the Union, so that the total weight of the members of Parliament equals the total weight of all the members of the Assemblies.

The value of the vote of an elected member of a State Legislative Assembly is

\[ \text{value of an MLA's vote} = \frac{\text{population of the State}}{\text{number of elected MLAs in the State}} \times \frac{1}{1000}, \]

rounded to the nearest whole number. The value of the vote of an elected member of Parliament is

\[ \text{value of an MP's vote} = \frac{\text{total value of the votes of all MLAs}}{\text{total number of elected MPs}}, \]

again rounded. The population used is that of the 1971 census; under the 84th Amendment (2001), this will continue until the figures of the first census taken after the year 2026 have been published.

Worked example 5.1: Weighting the votes

Situation. Imagine a small country with three States and fifteen elected members of Parliament. The populations (at the relevant census) and the numbers of elected MLAs are as follows.

  • State A: population 60,00,000 (six million); 60 elected MLAs.
  • State B: population 24,00,000 (2.4 million); 40 elected MLAs.
  • State C: population 9,00,000 (0.9 million); 30 elected MLAs.

Find the value of each MLA's vote, the total value of the MLAs' votes, and the value of each MP's vote.

Answer.

  • State A: \(6{,}000{,}000 / 60 = 100{,}000\); divided by 1000 gives 100 per MLA; total \(60 \times 100 = 6{,}000\).
  • State B: \(2{,}400{,}000 / 40 = 60{,}000\); divided by 1000 gives 60 per MLA; total \(40 \times 60 = 2{,}400\).
  • State C: \(900{,}000 / 30 = 30{,}000\); divided by 1000 gives 30 per MLA; total \(30 \times 30 = 900\).

Total value of the MLAs' votes \(= 6{,}000 + 2{,}400 + 900 = 9{,}300\). Each MP's vote is worth \(9{,}300 / 15 = 620\), so the fifteen MPs together also carry \(9{,}300\). The whole electoral college carries \(18{,}600\), half from the States and half from Parliament. An MLA from State A carries more weight than one from State C because each represents more people.

docs.title: The single transferable vote
docs.text:
The election is held by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, by secret ballot (Article 55(3)). Each elector ranks the candidates in order of preference. To win, a candidate must obtain a quota of more than half the total value of the valid votes. If no candidate reaches the quota on first preferences, the candidate with the lowest value is eliminated and his or her ballots are transferred to the next preference marked on them. This continues until a candidate reaches the quota.

A misleading name

The phrase "proportional representation" is a misnomer here. Proportional representation normally applies where two or more seats are to be filled. In the election of the President only one seat is to be filled, so the system is really a preferential (or alternative) vote with a majority requirement.

Disputes about the election of the President or the Vice-President are decided by the Supreme Court, whose decision is final (Article 71). An election cannot be challenged on the ground that the electoral college was incomplete because some seats were vacant.

docs.title: Qualifications, term and vacancy
docs.text:
A candidate for President must be a citizen of India, have completed 35 years of age, be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha, and not hold an office of profit under the Union, a State or a local authority (Article 58). (The President, Vice-President, Governors and ministers are not treated as holding offices of profit for this purpose.) The nomination must be supported by fifty electors as proposers and fifty as seconders, under the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.

The President holds office for five years and is eligible for re-election (Articles 56 and 57). The oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India (Article 60). The President may resign by writing to the Vice-President. When the office falls vacant through death, resignation or removal, an election must be held within six months, and in the meantime the Vice-President acts as President (Articles 62 and 65).

docs.title: Impeachment
docs.text:
The President can be removed by impeachment for "violation of the Constitution" (Article 61). The procedure is quasi-judicial.

  1. A charge is brought in either House of Parliament by a resolution, moved after at least 14 days' written notice signed by at least one-quarter of the total members of that House.
  2. The resolution must be passed by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the total membership of that House.
  3. The other House then investigates the charge, or causes it to be investigated. The President has the right to appear and to be represented.
  4. If the other House also passes a resolution, by two-thirds of its total membership, declaring that the charge has been sustained, the President is removed from the date of the resolution.

Note that nominated members of Parliament, who do not vote in the election, do take part in impeachment, while the elected members of the State Assemblies, who do vote in the election, do not. No President has ever been impeached.

docs.title: 5.3 The powers of the President
docs.text: The President's powers are wide on paper. In practice almost all are exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers (section 5.4).

docs.title: Executive powers
docs.text: All executive action of the Government of India is taken in the President's name. The President appoints the Prime Minister and, on the Prime Minister's advice, the other ministers; and appoints the Attorney General, the Comptroller and Auditor-General, the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners, the chairman and members of the Union Public Service Commission, the Governors of States, the members of the Finance Commission, and the judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. The President administers the Union Territories through administrators, and can declare areas to be Scheduled Areas.

docs.title: Legislative powers
docs.text:
The President is a part of Parliament (Article 79). The President:

  • summons and prorogues the Houses and can dissolve the Lok Sabha (Article 85);
  • addresses Parliament at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year (Article 87);
  • nominates 12 members of the Rajya Sabha with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service (Article 80);
  • recommends certain bills, such as money bills and bills to form new States, before they can be introduced;
  • gives or withholds assent to bills (Article 111); and
  • promulgates ordinances (Article 123).

Anglo-Indian nominations ended

Until January 2020, the President could also nominate up to two members of the Anglo-Indian community to the Lok Sabha (Article 331). The 104th Amendment (2019) did not extend this provision, so it has lapsed.

The veto. When a bill passed by both Houses is presented, the President has three choices under Article 111.

Type of veto What the President does When it is available Absolute veto Withholds assent; the bill does not become law In practice used for private members' bills, or for a government bill when the government has changed and the new ministry advises against it Suspensive veto Returns the bill for reconsideration; if Parliament passes it again, with or without amendment, the President must give assent Not for money bills Pocket veto Takes no action; the Constitution fixes no time limit for the President's decision Used rarely; the best-known instance was the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986

Table 5.1. The President's veto over bills of Parliament.

The President has no veto over constitutional amendment bills: since the 24th Amendment (1971), the President must give assent to them (Article 368(2)). For a money bill, which is introduced with the President's prior recommendation, the President may give or withhold assent but cannot return it; in practice assent is given.

State bills and time limits

A Governor may reserve a State bill for the consideration of the President (Article 200). The President may then assent, withhold assent or, for a bill other than a money bill, direct the Governor to return it to the State legislature, which must reconsider it within six months; even if it is passed again, the President is not bound to assent (Article 201). Whether the courts can set time limits for decisions of Governors and the President on bills was the subject of significant litigation and of a Presidential reference to the Supreme Court in 2025. Check the latest position before relying on any statement about time limits.

Ordinances. When either House of Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that circumstances exist that make immediate action necessary, the President may promulgate an ordinance (Article 123). An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament, but:

  • it can be made only on subjects on which Parliament can legislate, and is subject to the same limits (it cannot, for example, violate Fundamental Rights or amend the Constitution);
  • it must be laid before both Houses when they reassemble, and it ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles, unless the Houses disapprove it earlier;
  • the President may withdraw it at any time.

Since the gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months (Article 85), an ordinance can last at most about six months and six weeks without parliamentary approval. In Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), the Supreme Court held that re-promulgating ordinances repeatedly without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution, and that the President's or Governor's satisfaction is open to judicial review on limited grounds.

docs.title: Financial powers
docs.text: Money bills and demands for grants can be introduced only on the President's recommendation. The President causes the annual financial statement (the budget) to be laid before Parliament (Article 112), can make advances from the Contingency Fund of India, and constitutes a Finance Commission every five years (Article 280).

docs.title: Judicial powers: pardon
docs.text:
Under Article 72, the President can grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment, or suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of an offence, in three kinds of case: offences against a Union law, sentences by a court martial, and all sentences of death.

Term Meaning Pardon Removes both the sentence and the conviction Commutation Substitutes a lighter form of punishment (for example, life imprisonment for death) Remission Reduces the period of a sentence without changing its character Respite Awards a lesser sentence because of a special fact, such as pregnancy or physical disability Reprieve Temporarily stays the execution of a sentence, especially a death sentence, pending a decision

Table 5.2. Forms of clemency under Article 72.

The power is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Maru Ram v. Union of India, 1980). The courts can review a decision on limited grounds, such as that it was arbitrary, mala fide or made without considering relevant material (Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, 2006). The Governor has a similar but narrower power under Article 161; only the President can grant clemency for a sentence by court martial, and only the President can pardon a sentence of death.

docs.title: Diplomatic, military and emergency powers
docs.text: International treaties and agreements are negotiated and concluded in the President's name, and the President receives and sends diplomats. The President is the Supreme Commander of the Defence Forces, though the exercise of this command is regulated by law. Finally, the President can proclaim three kinds of emergency: national (Article 352), in a State (Article 356) and financial (Article 360), studied in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 5.4 The position of the President
docs.text:
The framers intended the President to be a constitutional head, like the British monarch. The original Article 74 said that the Council of Ministers would "aid and advise" the President, but did not say in so many words that the advice was binding. Two amendments settled the question.

  • The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice binding: the President "shall act in accordance with such advice".
  • The 44th Amendment (1978) added a proviso: the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice, once; but the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after reconsideration.

The Supreme Court had already taken the same view in Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974): the President and Governors exercise their formal powers on the advice of their ministers, save in a few well-known exceptional situations.

docs.title: Situational discretion
docs.text:
The President has no constitutional discretion in the way some Governors do (Chapter 9), but certain situations leave room for judgement, because there is no Council of Ministers whose advice can be followed, or because that Council has lost its authority.

  1. Appointing a Prime Minister when no party or coalition has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha, or when the Prime Minister dies in office and there is no obvious successor. The President must then choose the person most likely to command the confidence of the House, and may ask that person to prove a majority on the floor of the House within a stated time.
  2. Dismissing a Council of Ministers that has clearly lost the confidence of the Lok Sabha and refuses to resign.
  3. Dissolving the Lok Sabha on the advice of a Council of Ministers that has lost its majority; the President may then consider whether an alternative government can be formed.

In addition, the President has the right, under Article 78, to be informed by the Prime Minister of all decisions of the Council of Ministers and proposals for legislation, and may ask that a matter decided by a single minister be considered by the whole Council.

Worked example 5.2: A hung Parliament

Situation. After a general election, no party has a majority in the 543-member Lok Sabha. Party X has 230 seats and Party Y has 190. Party Y presents letters showing that it has the support of smaller parties and independents bringing its total to 280. Party X claims it will win over enough members once in office. Whom should the President invite?

Answer. The test is who is most likely to command the confidence of the Lok Sabha, not who leads the largest single party. A majority of the full House is 272. Party Y has shown written support of 280 members, which is a stronger claim than Party X's expectation. The President may invite the leader of Party Y to form the government and ask him or her to seek a vote of confidence within a fixed period. The floor of the House, not the President's estimate, finally decides: S. R. Bommai (1994) emphasised the floor test as the proper way to determine majority support.

docs.title: 5.5 The Vice-President
docs.text:
The office of Vice-President was modelled on that of the American Vice-President. It is the second highest office in the country.

  • Election (Article 66). By an electoral college of all members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated, by proportional representation by single transferable vote and secret ballot. State legislators do not take part, and each vote has the same value.
  • Qualifications. A citizen, at least 35 years old, qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha, and not holding an office of profit.
  • Term. Five years; eligible for re-election. Resignation is addressed to the President.
  • Removal (Article 67). By a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all its then members (an "effective majority") and agreed to by the Lok Sabha (by a simple majority). At least 14 days' notice is needed. No grounds are stated in the Constitution.

Functions. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64) and presides over its proceedings. When the office of President falls vacant, the Vice-President acts as President until a new President takes office, for at most six months; while doing so, the Vice-President does not perform the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 65).

Common confusion

The President is removed by impeachment for violation of the Constitution, with a two-thirds majority of the total membership in both Houses. The Vice-President is removed by a resolution that starts in the Rajya Sabha, with an effective majority there and a simple majority in the Lok Sabha, and no grounds are specified. Do not use the word "impeachment" for the Vice-President.

docs.title: Appointment
docs.text:
Article 75(1) says only that the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President. By convention, the President appoints the leader of the party or coalition that has a majority in the Lok Sabha. The Prime Minister may be a member of either House. A person who is not a member of either House may be appointed, but must become a member within six months (Article 75(5)).

The Prime Minister has no fixed term. Formally, he or she holds office during the pleasure of the President; in practice, so long as the Council of Ministers retains the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

docs.title: Powers and functions
docs.text:
• Head of the Council of Ministers. The other ministers are appointed by the President on the Prime Minister's advice. The Prime Minister allocates and reshuffles portfolios, can ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss one, and presides over meetings of the Council and the Cabinet. The resignation or death of the Prime Minister dissolves the whole Council.
  • Link between President and Council. Under Article 78, the Prime Minister communicates to the President all decisions of the Council and furnishes information on administration and legislation.
  • Leader in Parliament. The Prime Minister advises the President on summoning and proroguing sessions and on dissolving the Lok Sabha, and announces government policies on the floor of the House.
  • Other roles. The Prime Minister chairs bodies such as NITI Aayog, the National Development Council and the Inter-State Council, and is the chief spokesperson of the government at home and abroad.

The Prime Minister was once described in British theory as "first among equals" (primus inter pares) among ministers. In practice the office is far more powerful than that phrase suggests, especially when the Prime Minister's party has a clear majority.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
The Council of Ministers has three ranks:

  1. Cabinet Ministers, who head the most important ministries and form the Cabinet;
  2. Ministers of State, who may hold independent charge of a ministry or be attached to a Cabinet Minister;
  3. Deputy Ministers, who assist other ministers. (This rank has not been used in recent decades.)

The 91st Amendment (2003) introduced two limits (Article 75(1A) and (1B)): the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15 per cent of the total number of members of the Lok Sabha; and a member disqualified for defection under the Tenth Schedule cannot be appointed a minister until the end of his or her term or re-election.

The word "Cabinet" did not appear in the original Constitution. It was inserted in Article 352 by the 44th Amendment (1978), which requires a written decision of the Union Cabinet before a national emergency is proclaimed. The Cabinet works through Cabinet committees (for example, on appointments, security and economic affairs), which are set up under the Government of India (Transaction of Business) Rules and are not mentioned in the Constitution.

docs.title: Responsibility
docs.text:
• Collective responsibility (Article 75(3)). The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. All ministers share responsibility for every decision of the Cabinet; a minister who disagrees must either support the decision in public or resign. If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the Council (or rejects a confidence motion, or defeats a major government measure such as the budget), the whole Council must resign.
  • Individual responsibility (Article 75(2)). Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, which in practice means that the Prime Minister can have any minister removed.
  • No legal responsibility. In India there is no requirement that an order of the President be countersigned by a minister, and courts may not inquire into what advice was given (Article 74(2)).

The no-confidence motion

The Constitution does not mention a no-confidence motion; it is provided by the rules of procedure of the Lok Sabha. A motion of no confidence in the Council of Ministers needs the support of at least 50 members to be admitted. It can be moved only in the Lok Sabha, since the Council is responsible only to that House.

docs.title: 5.8 The Attorney General
docs.text:
The Attorney General for India (Article 76) is the highest law officer of the Union government. He or she must be qualified to be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court, is appointed by the President and holds office during the pleasure of the President. The Attorney General gives advice to the Government of India on legal matters referred by the President, appears on its behalf in the Supreme Court and High Courts, and has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament and their committees, but not to vote (Article 88). The Attorney General is assisted by the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General, whose offices are not created by the Constitution.

Summary

  • India has a parliamentary executive: the President is the nominal head of State; the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister is the real executive, collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
  • The President is elected by the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry), with votes weighted by population so as to secure uniformity among States and parity between States and Union, by single transferable vote.
  • The President must be a citizen, at least 35, qualified for the Lok Sabha; serves five years; can be impeached for violation of the Constitution by two-thirds of the total membership of each House.
  • Powers: executive, legislative (including the absolute, suspensive and pocket veto and ordinances under Article 123), financial, judicial (pardons under Article 72), diplomatic, military and emergency.
  • Under Article 74, as amended in 1976 and 1978, the President must act on ministerial advice, but may return it once for reconsideration; real discretion arises only in exceptional situations such as a hung Parliament.
  • The Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses, is ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, acts as President in a vacancy, and is removed by a Rajya Sabha resolution agreed to by the Lok Sabha.
  • The Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, which is limited to 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha's strength (91st Amendment) and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

docs.title: 5.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Who are members of the electoral college for the President? Name two groups of legislators who are excluded.

Answer

The elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States, Delhi and Puducherry. Excluded: nominated members of Parliament and of the Assemblies, and members of the State Legislative Councils.

Exercise 2

A State had a population of 1,20,00,000 at the 1971 census and has 150 elected MLAs. Compute the value of the vote of each MLA and the total value of the State's MLAs' votes.

Answer

\(12{,}000{,}000 / 150 = 80{,}000\); divided by 1000 gives 80 per MLA. Total: \(150 \times 80 =\) 12,000.

Exercise 3

Explain the difference between a suspensive veto and a pocket veto. Can either be used against a constitutional amendment bill?

Answer

Under a suspensive veto, the President returns a bill (other than a money bill) for reconsideration; if Parliament passes it again, the President must assent. Under a pocket veto, the President neither assents nor returns the bill, relying on the absence of any time limit in Article 111. Neither can be used against a constitutional amendment bill: since the 24th Amendment (1971), the President is bound to give assent to it.

Exercise 4

An ordinance is promulgated on 1 March, while Parliament is in recess. Parliament reassembles on 15 April and does nothing about the ordinance. On what date will it cease to operate?

Answer

Six weeks (42 days) after reassembly. Counting from 15 April: 15 days remain in April after the 15th, so 42 days fall on 27 May. (Exact counting conventions aside, the principle is that it lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless disapproved earlier.)

Exercise 5

How does the removal of the Vice-President differ from that of the President?

Answer

The President is impeached for "violation of the Constitution": a charge in either House, with 14 days' notice signed by a quarter of its members, passed by two-thirds of its total membership, investigated and sustained by two-thirds of the total membership of the other House. The Vice-President is removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of all its then members and agreed to by the Lok Sabha, after 14 days' notice; no grounds are specified.

Exercise 6

What did the 91st Amendment (2003) provide about the Council of Ministers?

Answer

The total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, may not exceed 15 per cent of the total membership of the Lok Sabha (Article 75(1A)), and a member disqualified for defection may not be appointed a minister until the end of the term or re-election (Article 75(1B)). (It made similar provisions for the States, with a minimum of twelve ministers.)

Exercise 7

In which situations may the President exercise some personal judgement despite Article 74?

Answer

When appointing a Prime Minister if no party or coalition has a clear majority (or on the death of a Prime Minister with no obvious successor); when dismissing a Council of Ministers that has lost the confidence of the Lok Sabha but refuses to resign; and when deciding on dissolution of the Lok Sabha on the advice of a ministry that has lost its majority. The President may also return advice once for reconsideration.
